title: Falcons vs. Packers: Michael Penix Jr. and other key players to watch
summary: After an agonizing 0-2 start, the Atlanta Falcons seek a jolt as they head into the first of three consecutive primetime matchups. First up are the Green Bay Packers, who present a daunting road test on Thursday Night Football. The intrigue is sky-high as Atlanta looks for an adrenaline shot at quarterback to jump-start its […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons stands on the field prior to an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images After an agonizing 0-2 start, the Atlanta Falcons seek a jolt as they head into the first of three consecutive primetime matchups. First up are the Green Bay Packers , who present a daunting road test on Thursday Night Football . The intrigue is sky-high as Atlanta looks for an adrenaline shot at quarterback to jump-start its offense, awaken dormant playmakers, and navigate shifting personnel in the secondary. Michael Penix Jr. All eyes will be on Penix as he returns from a 10-month absence to make his 2026 debut . The pressure is on Penix to revitalize the Falcons offense after two weeks of abysmal quarterback play. But how ready will he be to help this Falcons passing attack take flight? He has the big arm, which is a welcome upgrade to watching Cooper Rush’s throws over the past two games. But will the Falcons let him unleash it, or will they play it safe and ease him into the offense? So much of the team’s future hinges on this question. Not only because it could help decide whether Penix can be the team’s long-term answer at quarterback beyond this season, but also because it will tell us a lot about how this coaching staff might handle a different young quarterback taking over next season . It’s not fair to Penix to already be looking beyond this year to the next potential quarterback option, which is why he’s such an intriguing presence not only against the Packers, but for the remainder of the season. We’ve seen flashes from Penix through his first 12 NFL starts, but he’s now at a critical point in his career where those flashes need to become a more consistent, steady pulse to show there is light at the end of the tunnel for the Falcons at quarterback. Kyle Pitts Offensive coordinator Tommy Rees has stated he wants to get tight end Kyle Pitts going this week . Running back Bijan Robinson shined in Week 1, and wide receiver Drake London was the star of Week 2 , so it seems like the natural progression to get the third member of the Falcons’ “Big 3” more involved this week. Penix’s presence should help expedite things. Pitts faces scrutiny after the team decided to pay him this summer. He’s no longer working on a prove-it deal under the franchise tag. In the team’s eyes, he’s already proven he’s worth the price tag. Yet, he has only one reception in two games, far below expectations for the league’s third-highest-paid tight end. Instead, the Falcons need to justify that price tag by making him a core part of their offense, starting Thursday night. Zachariah Branch Like Pitts, Falcons rookie wideout Zachariah Branch has been an afterthought in the Falcons’ offense through two games, and he’s worth injecting to see if he can ignite things against the Packers. Branch did get two targets last week on screens, which was a step in the right direction for Rees as a play-caller. But Branch saw only seven snaps on passing downs last Sunday, and beyond those two manufactured touches, he was mostly relegated to getting his steps in by running clear-out routes for other players. Over the years, all we hear about the Falcons offense is how loaded they are at the skill positions, and Branch is just the latest dynamic addition to that group. But one throughline has been consistent: no coaching staff or quarterback can bring that weaponry to bear each week. With Penix back in the lineup, they have fewer excuses for not finding ways to maximize someone like Branch. Za’Darius Smith “Big Z” returns to Lambeau for the first time in four years, after having a lot of success there across his three seasons with the Packers from 2019 to 2021. In 21 career games played in that stadium, he’s recorded 16.5 sacks. He can continue that production in a favorable matchup against a beat-up Packers offensive line that will be without its best blocker , right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele. The Falcons will need Smith and the rest of the pass rush to keep smothering opposing quarterbacks if they want to slow down Packers quarterback Jordan Love and mask any deficiencies on the defensive back end now that top cornerback A.J. Terrell is out of the lineup . Avieon Terrell While backup cornerback C.J. Henderson will be tasked with the huge burden of directly replacing A.J. Terrell, the latter’s younger brother, Avieon, could help ease that burden if he gets increased reps as an outside corner . Avieon has worked exclusively as a nickel since the end of training camp, with Mike Hughes entrenched as the starter opposite A.J. But now that former starting nickel Billy Bowman is slowly working his way back into the lineup as he recovers from a 2025 torn Achilles tendon, coupled with the emergence of safety Sydney Brown in the team’s big nickel looks, the Falcons have more flexibility to give Avieon a longer look outside. If things go well for Avieon in that new role, there’s a world where, upon A.J.’s return, along with Bowman being fully ramped up to play a full-time role, we might see a newer, better cornerback triumvirate to fulfill Jeff Ulbrich’s vision for the defense. Thursday night in Green Bay will reveal whether a change under center and a secondary reshuffle can finally get the Falcons into the win column. Can you name any other Falcon who needs to step up most under the bright lights of Lambeau Field?
author: Aaron Freeman

title: How the Falcons can recover from hitting rock bottom
summary: The Falcons have had their share of 0-2 starts over the years. It’s hard to recall a bleaker beginning to the season. While they were competitive against Pittsburgh, the number of missed opportunities left a bitter taste. They were uncompetitive against a team that has owned them in recent matchups, which was a real troubling […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Drake London #5 of the Atlanta Falcons looks on from the bench against the Carolina Panthers during the third quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Falcons have had their share of 0-2 starts over the years. It’s hard to recall a bleaker beginning to the season. While they were competitive against Pittsburgh, the number of missed opportunities left a bitter taste. They were uncompetitive against a team that has owned them in recent matchups, which was a real troubling sign. To look hopeless offensively against a Carolina team that previously allowed 59 points was alarming. Hitting rock bottom after two games may seem dramatic, but it has truly felt like the Falcons have already crashed into a total state of misery. They have a golden opportunity to pick themselves up with three upcoming primetime games in either difficult environments or against stellar quarterbacks. Doing this will require substantial improvement on both sides of the ball. Here are four things the Falcons must do to revive what is quickly becoming a lost season. Professional quarterback play leads to professional operation We’ll never know the severity of Cooper Rush’s back spasms. No matter how much it hindered him, the reality is the Falcons haven’t looked like an NFL offense with him under center. His mistakes resembled those of an overmatched rookie, from his decision-making to managing pressure to staring down his intended target. Combine that with his lack of arm strength and baffling inaccuracy on intermediate-to-deep throws, Rush didn’t offer anything in relief. The offense should receive a much-needed jolt with Michael Penix Jr. returning on Thursday . Skill position players should get the ball without being forced to make an enormous effort to catch an off-target throw. They shouldn’t be left dejected like Kyle Pitts and Jahan Dotson were downfield, where the ball was severely underthrown when the opportunity was there to produce an explosive play. Penix Jr. will have some rust to shake off in a hostile environment, as this is Green Bay’s home opener. He is still more than capable of getting the ball to the Falcons’ dynamic trio and other skill-position players, who possess the attributes to make a difference. Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees can tap into more vertical concepts with Penix Jr. returning to stretch the field and force opposing defenses into more coverage breakdowns. Penix Jr. shouldn’t be viewed as a savior, but his presence should help rejuvenate a furious locker room, especially Drake London, who can use a lift after Sunday’s debacle. The chemistry between Penix Jr. and London has been evident consistently when they have been on the field together. That can only help the Falcons gain some semblance of an offensive identity, as they climb out of the abyss of what has transpired so far this season. Offensive line providing more stability and push up front It’s been a tale of two games for an offensive line that fans had high hopes for. They understandably struggled to keep the pocket clean against Pittsburgh, but managed to open some holes and establish a fairly solid running game. They held up well in pass protection against Carolina, but failed to create any movement up front on the ground. A strong, complete performance is critical for the offense to become more efficient and score 24 or more points. It can be hard to gauge the offensive line’s overall performance based on how limited the offense has been with Rush as the signal caller. Rees has used more 12 and 13 personnel to try to get the running game going and create safe throwing windows. That added protection hasn’t translated into much success, albeit it’s understandable given how the quarterback was incapable of making even the most standard plays. Individual player performances can be analyzed, especially when it comes to penalties. Every offensive lineman except Ryan Neuzil was penalized in pass protection against Pittsburgh. The issues lingered into the home opener, where Jake Matthews’ ugly facemask penalty after getting beat negated a highlight-reel catch by Drake London across the middle of the field. Before getting injured later in the game, Jawaan Taylor looked a step behind on several snaps. A team with quarterback instability can’t afford to have two underperforming tackles. Both veterans will have to raise their game to help bring solidity to the offense. While Matthew Bergeron bounced back against Carolina, consistency has been a career-long issue for him. He needs to prove he can sustain high-level performances after his massive contract extension last August. As much as the Falcons are in transition as an organization, they have made numerous significant investments offensively. Under Bill Callahan’s guidance, this group has the infrastructure and pieces to be an above-average unit. Secondary needs to level up and tighten up Entering the season, the Falcons’ defensive back group looked like the most capable unit on the roster to take a substantial leap. Two established stars and leaders lead them in Jessie Bates and A.J. Terrell. They have an emerging playmaker in Xavier Watts who plays like a five-year veteran. Young, intriguing corners like Avieon Terrell and Billy Bowman Jr. have raised expectations. With veterans and solid contributors like Mike Hughes and C.J. Henderson, this is a well-rounded group that should be at the forefront of the defense’s success. It’s been an undermanned front, with Divine Deablo flying across the field, doing most of the heavy lifting in the first two games. The defensive line has played far better than anticipated, generating a decent amount of pressure with four. Collapsing opposing pockets should only benefit the secondary, yet they allowed far too many high-percentage completions against Pittsburgh and Carolina. Despite having nine pass breakups as a team this season, some were fairly fortunate plays made by A.J. Terrell and Hughes. Terrell has been overwhelmed when he’s been on the field. His poor start to the season doesn’t diminish his value as an above-average corner as he heads to injured reserve. After a strong performance against Pittsburgh, Hughes allowed his share of big plays versus Carolina. For what is supposed to be one of the best safety tandems in the league, Bates and Watts have been caught out of position on throws outside the numbers. That most notably happened when Bates got caught up in the flat and failed to get enough depth behind him to contest Darren Waller’s second receiving touchdown. Even without Terrell, the secondary must step up against a more pass-oriented Packers attack, the Saints’ surging offense, and Lamar Jackson’s brilliance. They need to start contesting more passes and forcing quarterbacks into making mistakes. Aaron Rodgers and Bryce Young were never at risk of turning the ball over. That has to change for an ultra-talented unit. Time for the coaching staff to expand With Penix Jr. back in the starting lineup, it’s time for the coaching staff to show what it’s made of. The decision to start Rush against Carolina and be persistent in keeping him in will be long remembered by fans, especially those in attendance at the home opener. Stefanski couldn’t have gotten off to a worse start toward proving he is the leader to guide the franchise back to winning ways. It hasn’t been an encouraging beginning for Tommy Rees either. From not dialing up much play action against Pittsburgh to calling runs designed straight into Carolina’s biggest strength on the interior, there have been some odd tendencies. The short-yardage play calling has been problematic, with run calls that the opposition easily telegraphed. That was exemplified by calling a jet sweep for Drake London on fourth down, which Carolina instantly swarmed in to get the big stop. Stefanski and Rees should get some grace…

title: Falcons vs. Packers: What will Week 3’s win or loss mean for Atlanta?
summary: We’ve barely begun the season, yet the Falcons are already reeling following back to back weeks with Cooper Rush as the starter. The latest, a 34-3 home opener humiliation at the hands of the division rival Panthers, prompted a rain of boos from a frustrated fanbase. Next for the Falcons is the start of three […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - SEPTEMBER 17: Green Bay Packers running back AJ Dillon #28 runs the football as Atlanta Falcons cornerback A.J. Terrell #24 defends during the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and the Atlanta Falcons on September 17, 2023 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Jeff Robinson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We’ve barely begun the season, yet the Falcons are already reeling following back to back weeks with Cooper Rush as the starter. The latest, a 34-3 home opener humiliation at the hands of the division rival Panthers, prompted a rain of boos from a frustrated fanbase. Next for the Falcons is the start of three consecutive prime time matchups, starting with a trip to Lambeau Field to face the Green Bay Packers, who have gotten off to a disappointing start in their own right. The good news for the Falcons is that Michael Penix Jr. has been announced as the starter for that game , as he will make his highly anticipated season debut. It’s a short week, and the Birds have no time to lick their wounds after the mauling they just took at the hands of the Panthers. The entire country will have a chance to watch Atlanta, who kick off Week 3 on Thursday Night Football. Here is the scenario the Falcons face if they beat the Green Bay Packers in Week 3, as well as if they lose. If the Falcons win It will be a much needed bounce back and will work to regain the confidence of what looks to be a broken fanbase. Not that anybody at Flowery Branch seems to or should care about media narratives, but it will give them some positive PR after weeks of getting crushed by the media. The team would finally have some liftoff, and could in theory find themselves tied for the division lead if all other scores around the NFC South work in their favor (however, they will remain at best in third place due to early season tiebreakers). This would be a big blow dealt to the Packers, who would fall to 1-2 in a season of expectations. Atlanta would pull very close to .500 in their all time history against Green Bay, as the mark would be 18-19. They would also get a massive confidence boost going into the Monday night grudge match against the New Orleans Saints next week. If the Falcons lose This train will begin derailing not too far from the starting station, as the Birds will fall to 0-3 with the hard part of their schedule still lingering in the near future. The vibes around the fanbase will continue to sink as next week’s Monday Night Football game against the Saints will really turn into a must win. In truth, even if they win that one it may not make much of a difference long term after an 0-3 start. As for the early division race, Atlanta could find themselves a quick 2.0 games behind both Carolina and New Orleans (who will both likely be favored in their matchups this weekend). Tampa will also be ahead of Atlanta even if they also lose and fall to 0-3, due to the divisional record tiebreaker, keeping the Falcons in the cellar of the NFC South for yet another week. It’s a lot earlier than expected but we will likely need to begin tracking draft standings in this article series as early as next week.
author: Adnan Ikic

title: The under-looked cause to the Ravens’ 1-1 start
summary: Much has been made of yet another Ravens’ fourth quarter collapse during their loss to the Saints in Week 2. “It was the defense’s fault!” or “it was Declan Doyle’s fault!” have been reccuring phrases from fans. While we are all quick to scapegoat, there is actually a much simpler issue that, if fixed, would […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Head Coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens looks on against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Much has been made of yet another Ravens’ fourth quarter collapse during their loss to the Saints in Week 2. “It was the defense’s fault!” or “it was Declan Doyle’s fault!” have been reccuring phrases from fans. While we are all quick to scapegoat, there is actually a much simpler issue that, if fixed, would have the Ravens sitting at the top of the NFL standings — penalties. Not just any type of penalties, though, but specifically ones that absolutely kill drives and positive plays. Through two weeks, the Ravens have lost -11.0 EPA on the penalties themselves, second-most in the NFL behind only the Carolin Panthers. That number undersells the damage, though. It only captures what happened on the flag, not what the flag took away. Add in the value of the plays those penalties erased and the picture gets worse. The Ravens’ nullified plays were worth a combined +9.2 EPA, by far the most in the league. Baltimore isn’t getting flagged for holding on a stuffed run or an incomplete pass. It’s having productive plays called back again and again: a Ja’Kobi Lane touchdown, a 19-yard catch by Rashod Bateman, an 11-yard grab by Mark Andrews, a Lamar Jackson first down scramble. Combine the two, and the Ravens’ total penalty cost comes to -20.1 EPA, just a hair behind Carolina’s -20.2. Unfortunately, there’s more . . . most offenses make back some of what they lose by drawing flags from opposing defenses. The Panthers have recovered +3.1 EPA that way, and Minnesota and Buffalo have each gained more than +19. Baltimore has gained, drum roll . . . zero. The Ravens are the only offense in the league without a single accepted defensive penalty. That leaves Baltimore with a net offensive penalty EPA of -20.1, the worst mark in the NFL. No team has lost more to penalties on offense, and no team has gotten less back. Then, you factor in some of the questionable calls at the end of the Saints game – that’s really when I started scratching my head. Is it possible that the Ravens are only committing offensive penalties on very successful plays, and the opposing defense hasn’t committed a penalty? A number of the team’s offensive penalties have certainly been valid but there are some that haven’t been. Chris Moore’s holding penalty last week and John Simpson’s “chop block” in Week 1 were highly questionable. The opposing team hasn’t been the victim of any of these 50/50 calls — especially on plays that yield very positive results. Obviously, you would surmise that these penalties are in-part leading to some of these eventually negated plays, but the Ravens have also generated explosive plays without them, so that doesn’t seem valid. These penalties had a major swing factor against the Saints, especially the ones in the 3rd quarter, which led to them losing ~5 expected points. The Ravens had reached the Saints 28 yard line, but were backed all the way up by penalties, resulting in a field goal. They were moving the ball effortlessly and would have probably scored a touchdown. For some quick back of hand math, the Ravens lost by seven points. If those flags did not occur, they should have theoretically been in position to win or tie the game at the end with a field goal – at the very least. Obviously, none of this really matters now and the result is the result. However, the Ravens clearly need to clean up this penalty mess. It’s costing them big time and while part of this is on the Ravens technique, you would clearly expect some of the penalty luck to naturally start swinging in their favor soon. Two weeks isn’t a large sample size but at this pace, they are on track to shatter the NFL record for the most net expected points lost to penalties on offense. What does all this mean? Yes, the Ravens need to clean some things up – but I have a feeling some good luck might be coming their way. They are currently on pace to quadruple the NFL record for net penalty EPA lost on offense, and that probably won’t continue.
author: Stephen Bopst

title: Ravens vs Saints Rookie Report
summary: The Ravens’ 2026 rookie class suffered their first NFL loss in the home opener against the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Let’s see how the rookies did in the game. OG Vega Ioane After a strong NFL debut in Week 1, Ioane had a much rougher time in Week 2. Ioane was charted with […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Chandler Rivers #29 of the Baltimore Ravens reacts as he runs against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens’ 2026 rookie class suffered their first NFL loss in the home opener against the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Let’s see how the rookies did in the game. OG Vega Ioane After a strong NFL debut in Week 1, Ioane had a much rougher time in Week 2. Ioane was charted with four pressures on 40 pass-blocking snaps according to PFF. The Saints countered the new Ravens under-center offense with a lot of A-gap blitzes and Ioane, paired with center Jovaughn Gywn, struggled to sort through the noise. PFF also gave him a low run-blocking grade, but the Ravens ran the ball effectively on Sunday, with clips showing Ioane moving bodies, so I’m not buying into that grade as much. While many, myself included, touted Ioane as one of the most NFL-ready prospects in the draft with an All-Pro ceiling, he’s still just a rookie in his second start next to a first-time starter at center. I’m not discouraged. His Week 1 performance was great, and I’ll buy we see more games like that than this one. DE Zion Young Young had an up-and-down day against New Orleans. He continued to flash that raw strength that is the cornerstone of his game, which gave him one pressure on seven pass-rush snaps according to PFF rate, with a 16.3% win rate. He graded out fairly well in pass rush (63.1), run defense (68.7), and special teams (72.6). That being said, Young had two noticeable mistakes on Sunday. First, on the Saints’ first scoring drive, Tyler Shough absolutely shook Young out of his cleats on what should have been an easy tackle for loss that could have helped force a longer field goal attempt. Then, after the Ravens responded to that field goal with their own touchdown and should have been going into halftime with a 14-3 lead, Young failed to keep contain with Malaki Starks on the kick return right before halftime, which allowed the Saints to tag on another three. These aren’t massive mistakes and most rookies do make them, but they were impactful and it’s the little details that can win or lose you a game. Otherwise, I think Young has been as advertised — a guy who’s been able to knock linemen back with his incredible play strength and push the pocket. WR Elijah Sarratt After being specifically mentioned by the coaching staff before the game against New Orleans as a guy who could find rhythm with Zay Flowers and Ja’Kobi Lane down, Sarratt got the game-day activation after being a healthy scratch Week 1. Sarratt then proceeded to get zero snaps on offense or special teams. This is frustrating, considering the Ravens did lose and how much they’ve struggled on offense since Flowers went down. Sarratt’s steady hands should be utilized. TE Matt Hibner and TE Josh Cuevas I wouldn’t normally put two rookies together, but that’s how little they were both used in this one. Neither tight end saw a target, and they played a combined 24 snaps total against the Saints. Hibner ran 10 routes according to TruMedia and earned a 57.8 run-blocking grade on nine blocking snaps, per PFF. Cuevas ran four routes and had a run-blocking grade of 59.7 on one snap. I specifically mentioned Hibner a couple of times leading up to the game, as I would have liked to have seen him get targets. Fellow tight end Mark Andrews was effective in his safety valve role but didn’t offer much downfield or after the catch. Hibner seems to be a guy who could become an explosive tight end receiving option for this team but hasn’t received much a chance. We’ll have to see if his role gets bigger as the Ravens continue to navigate operating without Flowers and Lane. CB Chandler Rivers After being a healthy scratch Week 1, Rivers got the activation against the Saints following T.J. Tampa’s move to IR. Rivers immediately factored into the rotation, out-snapping both Chido Awuzie and Keyon Martin. Rivers flashed throughout the day in coverage, limiting yards after the catch and being a solid tackler — something the rest of the Ravens’ defense struggled with against the Saints. Coming out of the draft, some of the best things scouted from Rivers were his physicality despite his smaller stature, play recognition and IQ, and how well he got downhill to bust screens and on blitzes. That was exactly what he showed in this game, especially on his tackle for loss in the red zone, where he immediately eliminated an Alvin Kamara designed touch out near the boundary. Expect Rivers to keep his playing time in a secondary that’s still looking to find its footing. P Ryan Eckley After a great Week 1 where all three of his punts pinned the Colts inside the 20, Eckley’s day against the Saints was less banner-worthy. Eckley only averaged 41.3 yards on his three punts, and none were even caught inside of the 20. With Flowers’ absence continuing to linger, this Ravens team might need to lean on its defense for some wins. That starts with Eckley giving opposing teams a long field to drive on. He’ll need to be better moving forward. Wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane and running back Adam Randall remain on injured reserve, with defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny on the practice squad.

Madubuike was noncommittal during his locker room media availability on Thursday, saying only, “We’ll see.” But his upgraded status this week – his first full practices since injuring his neck in Week 2 of last year – represent a major step forward in his return process. Buchanan, meanwhile, is expected to play, according to CBS Sports’ Matt Zenitz . Sunday’s game will mark roughly nine-and-a-half months since he tore his ACL last December, ending the fourth-round pick’s mini-rookie breakout next to Roquan Smith in the middle of Baltimore’s defense. title: AFC North Week 2 Recap: 2-0 Bengals alone atop division
summary: Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books. Only one team remains undefeated in the AFC North after just two games. Cincinnati Bengals (2-0) The Bengals are now the lone undefeated team in the division after a 20-6 victory over the Houston Texans. Cincinnati’s revamped defense had another strong outing in Week […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 20: Ja'marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals celebrates after scoring a touch down against the Houston Texans during the third quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books. Only one team remains undefeated in the AFC North after just two games. Cincinnati Bengals (2-0) The Bengals are now the lone undefeated team in the division after a 20-6 victory over the Houston Texans. Cincinnati’s revamped defense had another strong outing in Week 2. Spearheaded by defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence, the unit held the Texans’ running backs to just 18 rushing yards. Demetrius Knight Jr. led the team with 12 total tackles. The Bengals sacked C.J. Stroud four times, with two coming from Cedric Johnson. Cincinnati could be one of the top teams in the AFC if their defense can continue to play near this level. The highlight for the Bengals’ offense was Ja’Marr Chase and his two touchdowns. The superstar receiver’s first touchdown catch was particularly impressive as he contorted his body to reel in the pass. WHAT A CATCH BY JA'MARR CHASE FOR THE TD pic.twitter.com/M1vbRIiESS — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) September 20, 2026 Chase finished with seven catches for 75 yards and two scores while his running mate Tee Higgins led the way with 95 yards on five targets. Chase Brown led the ground attack with 80 yards on 20 carries. Joe Burrow completed 20 of 31 passes for 207 yards and two touchdowns. Burrow’s back was a concern entering the game before being sacked five times by Houston’s defense. He admitted it was a little sore after the game, but that he was “good to go.” Given Burrow’s injury history, his back tightness will likely remain a talking point each week. Baltimore Ravens (1-1) The Ravens experienced the first disappointment of the Jesse Minter era with a 27-17 loss to the New Orleans Saints in the team’s home opener. Baltimore’s defense found itself in an all-too-familiar position with their backs against the wall in the fourth quarter after blowing a double-digit lead. Similar to many of those prior instances, the unit was unable to get the game-sealing stop. Tyler Shough had little trouble marching down the field with the game on the line before scoring on a quarterback sneak. The Ravens sacked Shough just three times despite constant blitzes and his starting left tackle leaving the game due to an ankle injury. Baltimore’s offense shoulders blame as well after scoring just three points in the second half. The offense had the ball for four drives in the second half, two of which were three-and-outs while the final ended in an interception. Lamar Jackson was solid for much of the day, completing 21 of 31 passes for 235 yards and a touchdown before the game-losing interception on the final drive. Rashod Bateman led the team with 88 receiving yards and a touchdown on seven catches in Zay Flowers’ absence. Derrick Henry finished the game with 68 rushing yards and a touchdown on 16 carries, with just five carries in the second half. Pittsburgh Steelers (1-1) The Steelers dropped to 1-1 with a 20-3 loss to the reigning AFC champion New England Patriots. The decision to run it back another year with 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers at quarterback is looking questionable, to say the least, through two games of the season. Pittsburgh’s offense has scored just one touchdown through two games with the future Hall of Famer under center. Rodgers completed 23 of 39 passes against the Patriots for 187 yards and an interception while being sacked four times and losing a fumble. D.K. Metcalf, whom the Steelers acquired for a second-round pick and awarded a massive contract to a year ago, has had a rough start to the season, hauling in four catches for just 27 yards against New England. Germie Bernard was the leading receiver with 35 yards on four catches. Jaylen Warren led the rushing attack with 43 yards on 11 carries. Rico Dowdle left the game with a toe injury after carrying the ball seven times for 22 yards. Pittsburgh’s defense did what it could by forcing two turnovers: an interception by Patrick Queen and a forced fumble on Rhamondre Stevenson by Nick Herbig. The defense sacked Drake Maye three times, with T.J. Watt accounting for 1.5 sacks. There is only so much the talented unit can do with so little help from the Steelers’ offense at the moment. Cleveland Browns (1-1) The Browns got their first win of the season on Sunday with a 23-19 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. After a rough start to the season in Week 1, Deshaun Watson rebounded with a solid day against the Buccaneers, completing 24 of 30 pass attempts for 238 yards and two touchdowns while avoiding any turnovers. The biggest play of the day for Cleveland’s offense once again came from rookie Denzel Boston, as the second-round receiver scored a 55-yard touchdown. Boston finished the game with 95 yards to go with his one score on five catches. The run game was quiet for the Browns as Deshaun Watson led the team with 22 rushing yards on seven carries. Cleveland’s defense faced a familiar foe in former Cleveland quarterback Baker Mayfield, picking him off once and sacking him three times. Carson Schwesinger led the unit with 10 total tackles. Jared Verse, acquired in the blockbuster trade that sent Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams, has yet to make his impact felt in two games with his new team.

title: Buffalo Bills rookie WR Skyler Bell is probably going to make his NFL debut in Week 3 vs. Chargers
summary: The Buffalo Bills are experiencing some receiver injuries ahead of Week 3’s game against the Chargers, but we can’t forget the team drafted a wideout in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Skyler Bell has been a healthy scratch for the first two contests of the season after he worked his way back […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are experiencing some receiver injuries ahead of Week 3’s game against the Chargers, but we can’t forget the team drafted a wideout in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft. Skyler Bell has been a healthy scratch for the first two contests of the season after he worked his way back from an injury in the summer that kept him out of the first two preseason games in August. In the final exhibition outing, draft pick from UConn led the team with seven snags for 49 yards and took a jet sweep 28 yards for a touchdown in Buffalo’s 28-27 win. I’m ready to see Bell in a real game, aren’t you? D.J. Moore was downgraded from limited Wednesday to DNP on Thursday . Keon Coleman has yet to practice this week. When two receivers are DNP on Thursday during a week with a Sunday game, chances are another receiver is going to be called upon in the upcoming contest. That’s why Bell is almost assuredly going to be running routes for the first time as a professional in Week 3 against a Chargers secondary that ranks 26th in EPA per drop back allowed through two games. Regarding Bell the player, as a refresher, here’s what I wrote about him before the draft: “ Skyler Bell is a modern inside–outside wide receiver with a lighter, compact build and enough length through his limbs to play bigger than his listed size. He’s nimble and light on his feet, showing noticeable quickness off the line and smooth acceleration into his routes. Bell isn’t physically imposing, but he moves easily and fluidly, giving him the flexibility to align both in the slot and outside depending on matchup and usage. From a skill standpoint, Bell wins with suddenness more than power. He shows clean footwork on underneath routes and has double moves in his bag thanks to his ability to change speeds and directions without gearing down. He’s a clear hands-catcher who consistently plucks the ball away from his frame, and despite his size, he’s a respectable contested-catch finisher due to strong tracking instincts rather than leaping ability or physical dominance. After the catch, Bell is functional but not dynamic — he won’t consistently break tackles, yet he has enough juking ability and spatial awareness to avoid clean hits and steal extra yards in space. Physical coverage gives him trouble early in routes, and his route running, while solid, doesn’t consistently uncover defenders with nuance alone. Speed is slightly above average, and concentration lapses show up at times with a few too many easy drops on film. Bell projects as a rotational NFL receiver whose value comes from versatility, reliable hands mechanics, and functional route ability rather than any standout trait. There’s no glaring weakness in his profile, but also no defining calling card that elevates him beyond a complementary role at this stage. He profiles best as a WR3/WR4 option who can move around formations, contribute underneath, and win selectively in contested situations, but likely won’t tilt coverage or demand schemed touches.” I had a late second/early third-round grade on him and compared him to Sterling Shepard. Not only did they appear similar on the field, they were almost mirror images of each other with very comparable combine workouts. Shepard was 5’10” and 194 pounds with 4.48 speed, a 41-inch vertical, and 128” broad jump all the way back in 2016. Bell measured in at 5’11 5/8” with 4.41 speed, a 41-inch vertical, and 133” broad jump. So Buffalo’s receiver is a little bigger with slightly more juice. And the Bills offense has exuded juice through two games. Josh Allen’s enormous arm is being accentuated by head coach Joe Brady. Don’t be surprised if Bell is thrown into the mix and targeted downfield in this one. To me, his best bet to get open against sizable veteran outside corners Tarheeb Still and Cam Hart, who have 4.52 and 4.50 speed respectively, is on vertical routes. While the gadget plays haven’t been part of Buffalo’s offense through two games beyond a jet sweep to Moore, expect Bell to get schemed up on some high-percentage throws or even credited with a carry simply because of his speed and explosiveness. That’s a more sensible ask for a rookie in his NFL debut than hoping he gets open on his own underneath or at the intermediate level. In Week 2, a huge opportunity was thrust upon Coleman, and he delivered with six catches for 63 yards, including four grabs that went for first downs. Bell will likely get a few chances to demonstrate the burst, long speed, and edge that were all very apparent on film during his 101-catch, 1,278-yard, 13-touchdown final season in college last year.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills trending up, trending down ahead of Chargers game in Week 3
summary: The Bills are 2-0 with the league’s top offense by DVOA. Facing a desperate Los Angeles Chargers team will offer a unique Week 3 test. Justin Herbert has faced pressure on 45.5% of his dropbacks through two games, the second-highest rate in the league, and PFF has him at 28.7 when he’s under duress. The […]
full_text: The Bills are 2-0 with the league’s top offense by DVOA. Facing a desperate Los Angeles Chargers team will offer a unique Week 3 test. Justin Herbert has faced pressure on 45.5% of his dropbacks through two games, the second-highest rate in the league, and PFF has him at 28.7 when he’s under duress. The Chargers are 0-2, and their offense sits 27th in DVOA at -20.6%. The Bills sit second overall at 52.7%, with the league’s top offense at 56.8%, although the defense is 19th at +9.0%. It’s a two-game sample, and the adjustments still lean on last season. Still, gives us an idea of where Sunday can be decided: can Buffalo’s defense get to Herbert before Herbert gets to it? Here are my choices for which Buffalo players could be decisive in next Sunday’s matchup. HEROES Greg Rousseau, OLB: the pass rush runs through him Rousseau earned an 84.5 PFF grade against Houston and a 90.8 against Detroit, second among Bills defenders behind Deone Walker on Thursday. He has four sacks and three forced fumbles, including the strip-sack that closed out the Texans with 16 seconds left. He has looked like a natural fit at outside linebacker in Jim Leonhard’s defense, and I think the move was the best thing to happen to his production. He lined up mostly over the right tackle in Week 1, which is Joe Alt this Sunday. I don’t expect him to simply beat Alt. Alt has a 75.3 PFF pass-block grade (23rd among tackles) with only two pressures allowed, and Bleacher Report ranked him the No. 2 right tackle in the league this summer. His weakness has been discipline: five penalties, four against the Raiders. Rousseau will have a tougher test than the matchups he’s had so far. Hopefully, he can continue to impress and impact the game as he has done this season. Buffalo’s defense needs it. Dion Dawkins, LT: the answer to Tuipulotu and Mack Dawkins posted an 81.7 PFF grade against the Lions, fifth-best on the roster, and Bleacher Report graded him an A for a nearly perfect night against Aidan Hutchinson. In Week 1, he led the line with an 87.5% pass-block win rate in one-on-one situations, and Danielle Hunter had one of the quietest games of his career. It wasn’t perfect, though. He whiffed on a key fourth-down block that day, and PFF had his run-blocking grade at 39.9. I think that matters, because the Chargers swallowed Ashton Jeanty last week, holding him to 2.4 yards per carry, for just 48 yards. However, we know the Shnowman can do his 1/11th in the run game, and the pass rush is where the challenge is bigger. Tuli Tuipulotu had 13 sacks and a 17.9% pressure rate last season, sixth in the league, and rookie Akheem Mesidor is the only Charger in the top 40 of PFF’s pass rush win rate at 20%. Against the Cardinals, Los Angeles produced just eight pressures, so the production hasn’t matched the names yet. Dawkins will decide whether that stays true on Sunday. HEAD-SCRATCHERS Christian Benford, CB: the best chance to get right Benford was the third-lowest-graded Bill in Week 1 by PFF, and he has allowed 11 receptions, the most among corners before Monday night. That comes to roughly 118 yards and two touchdowns. He’s been beaten too often in man coverage for a number one corner who travels with the opponent’s WR1. Also, pairing a nice pass breakup with a pass interference in the end zone didn’t help. To be fair, he drew Nico Collins and Amon-Ra St. Brown, and those two combined for 16 catches, 217 yards, and five touchdowns on 23 targets against the Bills’ defense as a whole, not against Benford alone. The Chargers offer a much easier week, at least on paper. Ladd McConkey is dealing with rib trouble and has eight catches, while every other Chargers wideout combined has the same number. If Benford stays home in coverage and doesn’t give Herbert clean throws, it’s a real chance he can start his comeback this season. Landon Jackson, DE: I expected more Jackson graded 33.1 in Week 1 and 36.1 in Week 2, the lowest on the roster against Detroit and a bottom-five grade both weeks. After a promising preseason, I expected him to make the most of the opportunity in TJ Sanders’ absence. So far, he has struggled with penalties and a lack of push, being almost invisible in the middle, and has allowed others like DeWayne Carter and Greg Gaines to outplay him. The Chargers’ run game isn’t scary: Omarion Hampton had 43 yards on 12 carries in Week 1 and has fumbled in both games. It’s time for Jackson to start showing more, or he could be in danger of losing snaps to other teammates who have done better. The Bills can quietly get something from other guys inside, as Deone Walker starts to get all the attention from opposing offenses. HONORABLE MENTIONS Trending up Deone Walker, DT: He was last week’s hero and is still climbing. Walker earned a 93.0 PFF grade, the best of any Bill against Detroit, with three quarterback hits and three batted balls, two of them on the same fourth-quarter drive. He has nine pressures and a sack on the season, per PFF, and the Chargers’ interior gives him a good target. Keon Coleman, WR: He caught all six passes thrown to him against Detroit, with two third-down conversions on touchdown drives, and earned a 79.0 PFF grade. With DJ Moore’s shoulder in question, Coleman’s role matters more. (If his ankle allows him to play) DeWayne Carter, DL: He earned a 75.5 PFF grade with Ed Oliver and T.J. Sanders inactive, and was very noticeable in his snps against the run. Trending down Spencer Brown, RT: Brown has been one of the best run-blocking tackles in football, ranking seventh in PFF’s run-block grade last season, and Bleacher Report placed him third among right tackles this summer. But his pass protection went the other way in 2025, dropping from 76.2 to 61.3 in PFF pass-block grade with 36 pressures allowed. Hutchinson beat him on the third play of Thursday’s game for a sack and forced fumble. With Khalil Mack coming to town, Brown will need to rebound this week. Davison Igbinosun, CB: He has graded in the bottom five both weeks, at 41.2 and 38.8, though on limited snaps , and for a man corner, he’s been too grabby. Final Thoughts This defense is still a work in progress, but it isn’t as awful as some people believe, with a DVOA rank of 19th. Despite sitting at 0-2 now, the Chargers will be another good test for this unit, especially with Herbert being good from a clean pocket. The pass rush is the answer to that problem, and Rousseau and Walker are the ones producing it. Dawkins and Brown have to hold up on the other side to allow Josh Allen and the offense to continue to put up points on the board. No matter if it’s Rousseau getting home or Benford keeping the receivers in front of him, the defense will have one job: hold the Chargers offense down, scoring less than the Bills. The players I mentioned today will be key, in my opinion. Let me know in the comments if you have more names to share. Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!
author: Fernando Schmude

title: Bills news: Deone Walker has taken a giant leap forward
summary: Alongside outside linebacker Greg Rousseau, defensive tackle Deone Walker has been one of the most disruptive defensive forces through the first two weeks of the season for the Buffalo Bills, amassing one sack to go with nine quarterback pressures, four tackles and three batted down passes as the Bills have raced off to a 2-0 […]
full_text: Alongside outside linebacker Greg Rousseau, defensive tackle Deone Walker has been one of the most disruptive defensive forces through the first two weeks of the season for the Buffalo Bills, amassing one sack to go with nine quarterback pressures, four tackles and three batted down passes as the Bills have raced off to a 2-0 start. In victories against the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions, there have been plenty of plays where Walker has been nearly unblockable, having a tremendous impact on a play even if he isn’t the one to get the sack or make the tackle. It’s been an encouraging start to the 2026 campaign for Walker, a fourth-round pick by the Bills in the 2025 NFL Draft who showed flashes of his immense talent and potential during his rookie season. But after two outstanding performances, today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by dissecting Walker’s dominant start to the season. Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts in the comments section. DT Deone Walker has become a disruptor Anyone who has watched a Bills game has noticed that Greg Rousseau and Deone Walker have led the way in creating disruptive plays through the first two weeks of the season. Walker’s rise to dominance has been impressive to see, as he followed up a successful rookie season that saw him generate 13 pressures on 214 pass rush snaps (a pressure rate of 8%) by generating seven pressures in just 53 pass rush snaps so far this year (good for a pressure rate of 17.9%). Walker has been a dominant, disruptive force in the middle of Jim Leonhard’s defense, and his stellar play has Walker positioned to become a rising star for the Bills. “I think the scheme fits him,” head coach Joe Brady said Walker. “He made a jump from year one to year two, but we’ve only played two games right now. The consistency, I want to be able to see that game in and game out, and him being able to keep that competitive stamina. He has a style of play that fits exactly what we’re looking for, so it’s important for him to just continue finding ways to get better. We’re putting stuff on tape now and teams are obviously going to have to prepare for him and him being able to adjust and kind of handle that, but I’ve been pleased with his progress thus far.” Walker is looking to build upon a rookie season that saw him land on the NFL’s All-Rookie Team after making 39 tackles to go with 16 pressures, one sack, four batted down passes and a fumble recovery. title: NFL Power Rankings, Week 3: Buffalo Bills remain AFC favorites
summary: Buffalo Rumblings’ weekly look at where the Buffalo Bills land in the latest batch of power rankings is back this time with an extensive group of list-making experts. No one is ever wrong when it comes to their power rankings, but very seldom are most people right. Except when it comes to favorable conversations about […]
full_text: Buffalo Rumblings’ weekly look at where the Buffalo Bills land in the latest batch of power rankings is back this time with an extensive group of list-making experts. No one is ever wrong when it comes to their power rankings, but very seldom are most people right. Except when it comes to favorable conversations about the Bills, right? Last week before Buffalo tamed the Detroit Lions, NFL writers, analysts, and more were riding high on the Bills. Clearly that must be true ahead of the team’s Week 3 home game against the Los Angeles Chargers — and it is, mostly. Buffalo is among the league’s top three teams in 23 of the 25 rankings listed below. Does that mean you shouldn’t check out what opinionated experts had to say? Hardly true. Do the Bills fall in any of these rankings? You’ll have to scroll to find out. This week, we pick up rankings from a few new sites, which lead off the group below. So, are the Bills the NFL’s best team in most peoples’ eyes at the moment? Not so fast, at least not everywhere. At such an early stage, it may not even be accurate to suggest they’re the NFL’s most complete team. As you may have guessed, where there are concerns… things center around the defense. That makes Buffalo’s positioning in many of these rankings all the more impressive when you consider it’s really Josh Allen (and James Cook III, thank you) raising the bar. Still, the hope is that the Bills’ defense eventually comes around. Maybe that’s true as soon as this Sunday. But failing that, would anyone readily count out Josh Allen and the team’s postseason quest? Right, foolish if that’s the case. On that note, let’s put aside the the small talk and get down to the very serious business that is NFL power rankings. Yes, you love it. Everyone loves this stuff! Here’s the Week 2 Bills power rankings article for reference, if you’re keeping score. Let’s get to it… Windy City Gridiron : 1 “ Contender, pretender, or TBD: Contender ” “The offense is legit, and even if there are questions about the defense (they’ve given up 31 points in consecutive weeks), it should be enough to keep them as strong Super Bowl contenders all season. Josh Allen looks primed for another MVP run, so assuming the defense can get their sea legs under them at some point soon, they might be the most complete team in the AFC.” — Aaron Leming Bleeding Green Nation : 3 “With nine total touchdowns and zero giveaways through two wins, Josh Allen is currently the betting favorite to win MVP. His odds are listed at +250 while the next closest player is Mahomes at +750.” — Brandon Lee Gowton Sharp Football Analysis : 1 “After a big road win in Week 1, the Bills opened their new stadium with a 41-31 victory over the Lions, cementing their spot at the top of these rankings. Buffalo is averaging 7.1 yards per play (1st) after two games, and Josh Allen is averaging a massive 9.7 yards per attempt. The defense needs to take a step forward, and the schedule remains tough with the Chargers, Patriots, and Rams the next three weeks. Still, Buffalo has opened the season with two impressive wins.” — Raymond Summerlin Gridiron Experts : 1 “It’s hard to move the Bills out of the top spot; they look great this year, and maybe even better than in years past. This week they take on a very desperate Chargers team. The mark of a great football team is not overlooking anyone and taking care of business, which they should do in Week 3.” — Adam Henley ClutchPoints : 1 “The Josh Allen MVP conversation is fully back on, as Buffalo’s standout quarterback put everything on full display against the Detroit Lions on Thursday Night Football. Allen threw for three touchdowns and ran in two more, as the Bills outlasted the Lions in a fun shootout, 41-31. Allen’s performance helps keep the Bills locked into the top spot of the Week 3 NFL Power Rankings.” — Mike Johrendt NFL Spin Zone : 3 “Much has been made about the Buffalo Bills thus far. Through two weeks, Josh Allen looks every bit like an MVP candidate, and the offense looks unstoppable in the Joe Brady era. With that said, it’s only been two games, and I feel like this exact thing happens each year: the Bills enjoy a short stretch during the regular season where people wonder if they’ll be beat and if this year is the year…. But as we have seen, it has never been the year thus far. The truth is, unfortunately, that the Bills will again be a very good team, likely win the AFC East, but may fall flat on their faces in the playoffs when it matters the most, or simply won’t be good enough. It’s happened for years now, so while Buffalo is very good, let’s pump the brakes for the time being. The defense has been putrid across the first two weeks, for what that’s worth.” — Lou Scataglia NFL.com : 2 (down from 1 in Week 2) “Joe Brady’s promotion from offensive coordinator to head coach has elevated Buffalo’s offense from a productive and versatile group to an incredibly diverse, efficient and explosive attack that looks like a juggernaut through two weeks. Josh Allen is playing the best football of his career and he’s on an early track to win his second MVP award. If I trusted the Bills’ defense a bit more, I’d move them up to No. 1.” — Nick Shook The Athletic : 2 (up from 3 in Week 2) “ Rookie spotlight : Davison Igbinosun” “The Bills aren’t getting much from their rookie class, but they don’t need much with the way Josh Allen is playing. Buffalo’s quarterback has accounted for nine touchdowns through two weeks. That gives you some flexibility on defense, and the Bills are using it to give Igbinosun, a cornerback, a few snaps each week behind Max Hairston to get the rookie ready. He had three tackles against the Lions.” — Josh Kendall, Chad Graff ESPN : 1 (up from 3 in Week 2) “ One thing we know about the QB1: Josh Allen is going to make defenses pay either way.“ “Allen has kept his eyes downfield through two games, averaging a career-best 9.7 yards per attempt on his deepest average depth of target (10.5) since 2018, his rookie season. That has led to three touchdowns on throws of 20-plus air yards. But Allen is just as dangerous when defenses bail out to protect against the deep ball. Of his 92 rushing yards on 20 carries this season, 70 have come on six scramble plays.” — Nick Suss FOX Sports : 1 (up from 4 in Week 2) “Josh Allen has five passing touchdowns and four rushing touchdowns through two games. If he keeps playing anywhere close to this the rest of the way, there may be no stopping the Bills.” — Ralph Vacchiano CBS Sports : 2 (up from 3 in Week 2) “Josh Allen is playing at an unreal level right now. He is the leader for the MVP after two games. The defense does need to be better.” — Pete Prisco USA Today : 2 (up from 3 in Week 2) “They’ve got the league’s best player (Josh Allen) and, apparently, have paired him with the right coach at the right time. Also feels like an upgraded home-field advantage is already in (lake) effect.” — Nate Davis NFL Trade Rumors : 3 (up from 4 in Week 2) “Even through two games, the historical comps for Bills QB Josh Allen are ludicrous. It would be silly to name MVP favorites this early in the season, but he’s putting together quite the resume already. While Buffalo’s defense won’t win them many games by itself, this defensive line continues to impress. Wiht their ability to get pressure on opposing quarterbacks and the unstoppable duo of Allen and RB James Cook on offense, this Bills team is checking a lot of Super Bowl-contender boxes.” — Ethan Woodie Fansided : 6 (up from 10 in Week 2) “Joe Brady can definitely walk and chew gum at the same time or coach and call plays on offense. Josh Allen looks even more possessed than ever; they are getting a little more off the edge than usual. full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Michael Penix Jr. #9 of the Atlanta Falcons warms up prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 3 of NFL action begins this evening with a primetime NFC matchup for Thursday Night Football on Prime. On the surface, there’s not a lot of intrigue here for Buffalo Bills fans, but we’ve brought back the featured open threads for readers because no one circles the football wagon like Buffalo Rumblers! Buffalo does head to Lambeau Field later this season to take on the Packers in Week 14, so you can consider this a very early sneak preview if you’ve yet to watch the Pack in 2026. Green Bay is currently in last place in the NFC West with a 1-1 record. What’s there to say about the Packers? Quarterback Jordan Love continues to mystify those who watch the game of football closely, while many analysts and “experts” continue buying in on his talent and potential. So far, Love has only a lot to prove beyond any prior season’s statistical success. There’s also edge rusher Micah Parsons, whose trade last year tried to tilt the Earth’s axis, but instead an injury had other plans. As such, it’s fair to wonder if he’s now flying a bit under the radar. As for the Falcons, they’re also in last place in their division (NFC South) and currently 0-2. There’s a lot to like about Atlanta, especially running back Bijan Robinson, tight end Kyle Pitts, and wide receiver Drake London, but so far they seem to be spoiling any matchup advantage their roster holds. Quarterback Michael Penix Jr. returns tonight, which may allow London to settle back down and into a groove. Always drama with a wide receiver, right? Will the Packers continue to sputter? Will the Falcons pick up their first win of the 2026 NFL season? Hey, at least we don’t have to watch that Aaron Rodgers guy this evening. If you weren’t aware, this is the first of three consecutive primetime games for Atlanta. What could go wrong? Here we go, and with that we also turn things over to you, Rumblers, with tonight’s open thread for ‘TNF’! As always, be kind to one another, and in all things — even this matchup… Go Bills!

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Los Angeles Chargers Week 3 Thursday injury report
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will renew their AFL-roots rivalry on Sunday for a Week 3 showdown at Highmark Stadium. full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 17: Keon Coleman #0 of the Buffalo Bills runs the ball during an NFL game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will renew their AFL-roots rivalry on Sunday for a Week 3 showdown at Highmark Stadium. It’s a matchup that represents two teams seemingly headed in opposite directions, but a pair of rosters in the midst of some roster challenges. Will the Bills have two important wide receivers in their starting lineup Sunday? What about the Chargers and their offensive line? Read on below for updates on those situations and quite a few other injury statuses we’re monitoring with only one practice left on Friday for this week. Buffalo Bills Thursday injury report Thursday injury report pic.twitter.com/hrbmh3GriL — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 24, 2026 No practice: WR Keon Coleman (ankle) DB Jordan Hancock (hamstring) WR DJ Moore (shoulder) DL T.J. Sanders (illness) Limited practice: DL Ed Oliver (hip) OG Ar’maj Reed-Adams (elbow) Full practice: ILB Joe Andreessen (knee) ILB Terrel Bernard (knee) OLB Bradley Chubb (thumb) RB Ty Johnson (hamstring) What we’re watching The Bills have a total of six regular starters listed with injuries this week. Keon Coleman has now been a “DNP” for two consecutive practices after landing on the injury list Wednesday. All signs point to him dealing with an ankle injury that occurred in-action against the Detroit Lions in Week 2. DJ Moore was downgraded to “DNP” for Thursday’s session, after being a limited participant on Wednesday. We’ve been told that Moore’s injury is an AC joint shoulder sprain, and that he has a chance to suit up in Week 3. His status Thursday could be about rest and soreness, but it’s impossible to know without hearing directly from the team — including the prospects of him playing Sunday afternoon. Regardless, Moore is unlikely to be fully healed by Sunday. Buffalo could find itself scrambling to fill two main voids at wide receiver if Coleman and Moore are sidelined. Wide receivers Greg Dortch, Stephen Gosnell, Ja’Mori Maclin, and Trent Sherfield Sr. are all on the team’s practice squad. Dortch has one more call-up in the regular season before he’d need to be signed to the 53-man roster. Of important note is that Dortch cannot be released and later signed back to the practice squad with a renewed set of call-ups in the current regular season. Practice-squad call-ups don’t reset until the NFL playoffs. Beyond Dortch, the team could roll with Sherfield’s game experience, or toss the dice with a pair of unproven players in Gosnell and Maclin. Also missing two practices in a row is T.J. Sanders, who is listed with an illness. There’s no additional information to better understand this situation. Jordan Hancock was downgraded to “DNP” after logging a limited practice session on Wednesday. There’s good news out of Thursday’s injury list, namely that Ed Oliver was able to practice in a limited capacity after a “DNP” on Wednesday. Also, it’s likely Buffalo will get Ty Johnson back in Week 3, which could once again put the brakes on running back Frank Gore Jr.‘s playing opportunity (who also has one remaining practice-squad call-up). Los Angeles Chargers Thursday injury report thursday's injury report for week 3 at BUF pic.twitter.com/7wqhIT6mWE — Los Angeles Chargers (@chargers) September 24, 2026 No practice: OG Kayode Awosika (fibula) TE Charlie Kolar (forearm) DB Elijah Molden (hamstring) OG/OT Trey Pipkins III (knee) CB Rodney Shelley (hamstring) WR Brenen Thompson (quadriceps) DL Dalvin Tomlinson (hamstring) Limited practice: OLB Tuli Tuipulotu (hamstring) Full practice: S Derwin James Jr. (finger/NIR-rest) DB Deane Leonhard (abdomen) OLB Khalil Mack (NIR-rest) WR Ladd McConkey (ribs) OT Rashawn Slater (groin) OG Cole Strange (pectoral) What we’re watching The Chargers have a lot to manage, with 14 players on this week’s injury report. It’s not an ideal situation for a team looking to pick up its first win with a road date against the 2-0 Bills in Week 3. This list also doesn’t reflect those players placed on Injured Reserve (IR), notably tight end David Njoku. Charlie Kolar avoided the IR term, but his recent forearm surgery will likely keep him out of the lineup in Week 3. The only players who improved from “DNP” statuses on Wednesday were Derwin James Jr. and Khalil Mack, who both received scheduled vet rest days. A pair of offensive linemen improved from “Limited” to “FULL” for Los Angeles, which should help them in sorting Sunday’s roster. We’ll see if both offensive tackle Rashawn Slater and offensive guard Cole Strange are able to play in Week 3. Unfortunately, cornerback Rodney Shelley was downgraded to “DNP” Thursday after putting together a limited session on Wednesday.

title: Buffalo Bills facing Justin Herbert who’s prime example of under-pressure play not being predictive
summary: Josh Allen and Justin Herbert are similar in some ways and drastically different in others. They’re arguably the NFL’s two most physically intimidating quarterbacks. Allen is listed at 6’5” and 237 pounds. Herbert is 6’6” and 236 pounds on the Chargers official website. They both have rocket-launcher arms. But the number of differences between the […]
full_text: Josh Allen and Justin Herbert are similar in some ways and drastically different in others. They’re arguably the NFL’s two most physically intimidating quarterbacks. Allen is listed at 6’5” and 237 pounds. Herbert is 6’6” and 236 pounds on the Chargers official website. They both have rocket-launcher arms. But the number of differences between the two towering passers has grown over the years, particularly after Herbert’s tremendous rookie season in 2020. Allen and Herbert took the league by storm that season. Allen erupted to the tune of 4,544 yards with 37 passing touchdowns and eight on the ground with only 10 interception. Also that year, Herbert set plenty of league records for a first-year quarterback en route to winning Offensive Rookie of the Year. One superhuman feat from Herbert’s debut season as a professional has not stayed with him to date in the NFL. In that legendary 2020 campaign, Herbert had the league’s highest passer rating under pressure at 99.4 (among qualifiers). Given his mobility, arm talent, and plus accuracy, it felt like Herbert was bound to regularly rock while pressure mounted inside and outside the pocket. Since then, he’s done a 180 against pressure. In Herbert’s second season, his passing rating in those situations was 77.9, the 21st-best in football. The following season, his under-pressure rating was 70.3, the 28th-best among qualifiers. In 2023, Herbert only managed a rating of 62.6, which ranked 40th out of 50 qualifiers. In 2024, it raised slightly to 72.1, the 29th-best in the NFL. Last year, Herbert’s pressure it stabilized at 74.2, which was the 27th-highest among 50 qualifiers. So for as much as his drastic dip from his rookie season in this key area originally felt like a prime example of how under-pressure play isn’t sticky year-to-year, we’ve now seen him struggle in this area five-consecutive seasons. Through two games this season, it’s only 61.8, the 19th-highest in the NFL. Allen has been inside the Top 20 in under-pressure passer rating every since 2021, and is currently second with a rating of 106.3 while under duress through two games. Another area in which these two quarterbacks are different. How Herbert performs, when pressured behind a reserve-laden offensive line on Sunday against the Bills, will be a key storyline of this Week 3 game.
