title: How the Denver Broncos can beat the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football
summary: The Denver Broncos are coming off an impressive Week 2 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars. Their Week 3 opponent is the Los Angeles Rams, who earned a decisive victory over the New York Giants on Monday Night Football. They will be another tough opponent in Denver’s gridiron gauntlet to start the season. Here is what […]
full_text: ENGLEWOOD, COLORADO - AUGUST 1: Defensive coordinator Vance Joseph of the Denver Broncos looks on during training camp at Broncos Park Powered by CommonSpirit on August 1, 2026 in Englewood, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos are coming off an impressive Week 2 victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars. Their Week 3 opponent is the Los Angeles Rams, who earned a decisive victory over the New York Giants on Monday Night Football . They will be another tough opponent in Denver’s gridiron gauntlet to start the season. Here is what the Broncos need to do to beat the Rams on Sunday Night Football . Do what you can to slow down Matthew Stafford At 38 years of age, Matthew Stafford is in his eighteenth season in the NFL. Interestingly enough, the Broncos have only faced him twice. Both of those matchups were when he was playing the Detroit Lions. In 2025, Stafford had a career year with 4,707 passing yards and 46 touchdowns. Those marks topped the NFL and earned him a Pro-Bowl nod, a first-team All-Pro honor, and the first MVP award of his historic career. He had a rough start to his 2026 season against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1. However, the longtime veteran played much better against the Giants and was 22-of-31 for 327 yards with 4 touchdowns and 1 interception. Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph had a tremendous gameplan to combat Trevor Lawrence and the high-powered Jacksonville Jaguars defense in Week 2. Joseph and his players will have to execute well again in order for the Broncos to earn a primetime victory Sunday night. Stafford was without star wide receiver Puka Nacua on MNF, but if he is available for SNF, that will make this task even harder. Keep committed to the running game It wasn’t an easy, but the Broncos were able to top the 100-yard mark with their rushing attack last weekend against the Jaguars. That was without RJ Harvey who missed the game with a hamstring injury and J.K. Dobbins for most of the second half. In turn, the Broncos looked to rookie running back Jonah Coleman late in the game. The fourth-round draft pick had several key runs, including the go-ahead touchdown to cement a victory for Denver. He displayed tremendous patience, vision, and nose for the endzone in his small sample size. It’s too early to know whether Harvey or Dobbins will suit up on Sunday. Though Head Coach Sean Payton remained optimistic at that possibility in his Monday morning presser. Regardless, Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb needs to commit to the run game. The Rams’ defensive front will be without Myles Garrett which should help in this matter. Against the 49ers, the Rams struggled to stop Kyle Shanahan’s rushing attack and gave up 174 yards on the ground. Though against the Giants, they performed much better and allowed just 52 yards on the ground. The Broncos had a lot of success in heavier personnel and running the ball under center in the second half versus the Jaguars. Let’s see more of that moving forward. A strong rushing attack will be essential to control the clock and limit the opportunities Stafford and the Rams have on offense. Operate better on third down and perform better in the red zone Two issues have been constant for the Broncos’ offense in their first two games of the season: struggling to convert on third down and missing opportunities in the redzone. To be competitive on Sunday Night Football and compete at a high level throughout the entire season, both of these issues need to be corrected. The Broncos have converted just 6 of 23 third down attempts this season. Meanwhile, they are just 3 of 7 in the redzone. A big part of this can also be attributed Denver’s ongoing penchant for penalties. Denver has seventeen thus far, which makes them one of the most penalized teams in the NFL. This is an area the team has to get much better at. They can’t settle for field goals or turn the ball over in the redzone. They also can’t afford to keep having so many three-and-outs. I don’t want to see Denver have to try and rally back or outduel Stafford in a shootout. Improvement and efficiency in these areas will be an absolute must for the Broncos to earn their second win of the year.

title: Lions vs. Jets predictions: 4 keys to victory in Week 3
summary: The Detroit Lions (1-1) and New York Jets (1-1) will square off in a Week 3 battle as coach Dan Campbell welcomes back his protégé, Aaron Glenn, to Ford Field for the first time since the former defensive coordinator left for the Big Apple. “Our players know exactly what’s coming in here because the defensive […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 17: Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 of the Detroit Lions runs a route during an NFL game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (1-1) and New York Jets (1-1) will square off in a Week 3 battle as coach Dan Campbell welcomes back his protégé, Aaron Glenn, to Ford Field for the first time since the former defensive coordinator left for the Big Apple. “Our players know exactly what’s coming in here because the defensive coordinator was here for (four) years,” Campbell said of Glenn and the Jets. “Turn on the tape. … This is not going to be a trap game. This is gonna be a knockout, 60-minute brawl.“ Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Jets in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1900 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 6.5-point favorites in Week 3 . Jets base schemes For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 3 preview: Breaking down the Jets’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Lions attack forward to offset Jets’ aggressiveness Glenn’s Jets’ defense won’t look like the one he ran in Detroit (the Jets run a 3-4 base with a 2-4 subpackage), but the principles remain the same: Stop the run, press at the line of scrimmage, and take the fight to the offense. On paper, the Jets defense ranks very highly in most statistics (including allowing the fewest yards per game this season with just 197 total ypg), and on film, they fly to the football in both the run and the pass. They plug rushing lanes up the middle with big space occupiers and downhill linebackers, and also have the range to chase laterally down the line of scrimmage. Against the pass, they play press-man coverage at the line, look comfortable in man and zone schemes, and spread out their coverages to the sidelines with their defensive backs. The Jets’ aggressiveness has been a key catalyst in their defensive success in 2026, but this approach also leaves them vulnerable in certain areas. For example, against the run, the Jets ask their defensive tackles to occupy multiple offensive linemen, thus freeing up gap lanes for their linebackers to fill and stop the ball carrier quickly. To offset this, the Lions will need their interior offensive linemen to win one-on-one or run movement-based blocking schemes, such as Duo or pulling guards. Jared Goff will also need to make quick decisions because the Jets defensive line has the fastest “get off” at the snap (0.71 seconds). That being said, their time to pressure is 2.69 seconds (21st in the NFL), meaning that while the Jets have elite quickness, they can get stuck on blocks, creating opportunities for a decisive quarterback. Over two weeks, the Jets’ aggressiveness showed up most when the Titans and/or Packers tried to move laterally with quick screens, passes to the flat, or stretch outside zone runs. The Jets are far too quick and athletic, and New York often chewed up these plays. However, with linebackers attacking downhill, the secondary living in two-high safety shells, and the corners pressing the line, there is often space to operate in the middle of the field. Look for the Lions to be creative with a run-blocking scheme that opens lanes for Gibbs to speed through, and a forward-moving passing approach that attacks the middle of the field with their best skill players, like Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta. Prediction 2: Lots of 11 personnel, keep Jets defense in nickel While Glenn ran a ton of “Base” defense in Detroit and a fair amount during his first year with the Jets, their 2026 approach has seen them play more nickel sets (roughly 77% of the time). While this brings them closer to the league average, their production in Base has been higher. When in a Base defensive set, the Jets have produced impressive numbers, including a -0.58 EPA, best in the NFL. However, when the Jets move to a subpackage look, their production dips, producing a 0.18 EPA and ranking 13th in the NFL. This shows up against both the run and the pass, as they drop from the top of the rankings in Base to the middle of the pack in subpackages. By running a lot of 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR sets), the Lions will not only get their best skill players on the field at the same time, but it will also help lighten the box, set up cleaner rush lanes, and open up opportunities with play-action and in the intermediate passing game. Prediction 3: Lions deploy Base defense to stop the run On the flip side, the Lions will want to stay in their Base defense, especially early in the game, and work to take the Jets’ rushing attack away. NFL teams strive for a balanced run/pass split with their offensive play calls, but the reality is, this is a passing league, and more often than not, teams default to throwing the ball to gain positive yards quickly. Glenn, like Campbell, wants to control the game with the run, and through two weeks, their run/pass split is roughly 44%/56%, resulting in the eighth-highest rushing rate and fourth-most rushing attempts entering Week 3. Despite the dedication to and opportunities in the run game, the Jets are only producing 3.3 yards per rushing attempt (28th) with a -0.20 EPA (28th). One main reason for this lack of production is that their offensive line isn’t getting much push. Most blocking calls are one-on-one matchups where the offensive line is asked to win, or simple inside/outside zone calls, and over two games, New York hasn’t shown much creativity in blocking assignments. As a result, about 30% of their runs gain no positive yardage, and their rushing yards before contact are just 0.76 (24th) as a team, and 0.6 for starting running back Breece Hall. The Jets have shown a dedication to the run, the Lions a dedication to stopping it, and Base defense allows the Lions to get their best run defenders on the field to win this battle in the trenches. Prediction 4: Lions pass rush turns pressures into sacks While the Jets’ run blocking has lacked impact, their pass blocking has been very good, as Jeremy Reisman pointed out in his game observations post; the Jets offensive line currently has PFF’s highest pass-blocking grade (77.4) . In Week 1, the Jets didn’t allow a sack to the Titans, and while they did give up four sacks to the Packers, many were coverage-based rather than pressure getting home, as shown by their time-to-pressure allowed numbers (2.76 seconds, 13th in the NFL). However, the Jets have surrendered 33 pressures through two games (28th), indicating a few things. First, quarterback Geno Smith is holding onto the ball (he averages 2.97 seconds per throw, 7th longest), and his line is holding up just long enough to keep him upright. Second, Smith still has enough mobility (at 35 years old) to stretch his time in the pocket. And lastly, neither the Titans nor the Packers could consistently generate a pass rush that could finish. Bottom line, the Jets’ offensive line and veteran quarterback have felt some heat, but have mitigated that pressure for the most part. If the Lions want to disrupt the Jets’ success, they’ll need to turn those pressures into sacks. For this to happen, the Lions will need to keep their aggressive approach on the defensive line, deploying stunts and pulls and continuing to generate pressure at a high rate. Through two games, the Lions’ time to pressure is 2.51 seconds (sixth fastest in the NFL), resulting in 39 pressures (fifth most in the NFL) and seven sacks (fourth). Entering Week 3, Aidan Hutchinson ranks third in the NFL in pressures (14) and sacks (3), but he’ll need help from his other starting defensive linemen: DJ Wonnum (six pressures, no sacks), Alim McNeill (four pressures, one sack), and Tyleik Williams (four…

title: Detroit Lions vs. New York Jets preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The Detroit Lions are looking for a rebound this Sunday after a pretty sound defeat at the hands of the Buffalo Bills. Prior to the start of the 2026 season, Week 3 against a New York Jets team that finished 3-14 last year looked like an easy win. But Aaron Glenn has the Jets inches […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions celebrates after scoring a touchdown with Jared Goff #16 against the New Orleans Saints during the third quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions are looking for a rebound this Sunday after a pretty sound defeat at the hands of the Buffalo Bills. Prior to the start of the 2026 season, Week 3 against a New York Jets team that finished 3-14 last year looked like an easy win. But Aaron Glenn has the Jets inches away from a 2-0 start this year. Is that start a mirage, or are the Jets truly a formidable foe this year? Let’s take a closer look in our Lions vs. Jets Week 3 preview and prediction. It’s “On Paper” time. Note: This is the last week we’ll be using any 2025 data. Lions pass offense (13th in DVOA) vs. Jets pass defense (4th) 2025 rankings: Lions pass offense (6th) vs. Jets pass defense (32nd) Week 1 (Saints): 204 passing yards, 96.7 passer rating Week 2 (Bills): 289 passing yards, 130.0 passer rating It took a while for things to get going, but Jared Goff and the Lions’ passing offense finally looked like itself in the second half of the Bills game. Is that a legitimate data point or did the Bills play Detroit differently while up two or three scores? It’s a very fair question to ask, and one that probably will keep my confidence in this unit at “cautiously optimistic” until we get more information. So far this year, the Lions rank: 22nd in yards per attempt (6.9) Fifth in passer rating (113.2) Fifth in dropback EPA (0.270) 10th in dropback success rate (49.4%) I see no reason to believe this can’t be a top-10 passing attack yet again, although there was one significant step back last week: pass protection. Last week, the Bills produced 29 pressures, according to PFF, and four sacks on 42 dropbacks. Detroit now has the 27th ranked pass blocking grade by PFF, although they oddly rank eighth in ESPN’s pass block win rate. The good news is that the biggest culprits of last week’s protection breakdowns were backups. Right tackle Larry Borom allowed 11 pressures vs. the Bills, and left guard Ben Bartch wasn’t far behind with six. Both of those players are expected to go back to the bench this week with Blake Miller and Christian Mahogany on track to return. Week 1 (Titans): 127 passing yards allowed, 80.2 passer rating Week 2 (Packers): 136 passing yards allowed, 91.9 passer rating Last year, the Jets were an absolutely awful passing defense, ranking in the bottom 10 of most statistical categories, including passer rating allowed (110.9, 32nd), yards per attempt (7.5, 25th), dropback EPA (29th), and DVOA (32nd). This year is off to a much more promising start, although they’ve done it against a Titans passing offense that was bottom three last year, and against a Packers team in the rain with no offensive line. Still, the stats are impressive. The Jets pass defense ranks: Second in yards per attempt (4.7) 12th in passer rating (85.8) 11th in dropback EPA (-0.051) 6th in dropback success rate (39.7%) The highlight of their pass defense is their pass rush. Led by rookie and second overall pick David Bailey (2.0 sacks, eight pressures), the Jets have produced an 8.5% sack rate on dropbacks (fifth highest), despite the fact that their pressure rate is just 36.6% (16th). They’re selectively aggressive, sporting just a 23.9% blitz rate (23rd), but that jumps to 28.6% on third down (18th). Their secondary is full of a rag-tag group, but 2025 third-round pick Azareye’h Thomas is playing quite well (77.2 PFF grade, eighth among CBs). Player to watch: Bailey vs. Miller. Bailey has insane speed to deal with (4.50) and Miller is dealing with a knee injury. Not an ideal matchup for Detroit, but it’ll be a good, early test for both rookies. Advantage: Lions +1.5. Maybe I’m being too dismissive of the Jets after watching the Packers get run out of their own house against the Falcons, but I’m just not quite buying that significant of a turnaround for the Jets defense. They’ve yet to really be tested, while the Lions passing offense can be trusted after years of consistently top-10 play. Protection should be better this week, which should help Detroit get off to a faster start. Lions run offense (4th) vs. Jets run defense (1st) 2025 rankings: Lions run offense (10th) vs. Jets run defense (16th) Week 1 (Saints): 165 rushing yards, 5.0 YPC Week 2 (Bills): 66 rushing yards, 3.3 YPC I find it a bit odd that the Lions’ run offense DVOA is ranked so high because that isn’t matching any other statistical benchmarks. They currently rank: 10th in YPC (4.4) 15th in rush EPA (-0.133) 10th in rush success rate (43.6%) Obviously last week was a significant step back, but Detroit was harmed by a beat-up offensive line and an abandonment of the game script when they were down 21-0 early in the game. The signs of a revamped rushing game are still there, but I’m still a bit skeptical of whether they’re truly a top-10 unit yet. There are good signs—they rank 11th in yards before contact per carry and t-fourth in 10+ yard rushes—but there are also discouraging signs, like their third-highest “stuffed” rate (rushes that earn 0 or fewer yards). Still, Jahmyr Gibbs is the ultimate equalizer, and he currently ranks fifth in rushing yards after contact (131). Week 1 (Titans): 68 rushing yards allowed, 4.9 YPC Week 2 (Packers): 63 rushing yards allowed, 3.5 YPC Again, it feels like we have very little information to go off of here. The Jets have only allowed 131 rushing yards thus far (fewest), but they’ve also faced the fewest rushing attempts, in just 32. The Packers may have the worst rushing attack in football right now, and the Titans actually ran the ball fairly effectively against the Jets (+0.11 EPA/rush, sixth-best in Week 1), but only rushed 14 times. So I’m more inclined to go off of last year’s numbers, which were pretty average: 21st in yards per carry allowed (4.4) 25th in rush EPA (-0.034) 17th in success rate (41.4%) That said, the Jets made some significant offseason moves to improve upon that unit, including trading for 360-pound defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat and signing veteran linebacker Demario Davis. Both have made a significant and noticeable difference. Player to watch: Sweat. Amongst interior defenders, Sweat ranks 19th with a 70.3 PFF run defense grade. That’ll be a serious test for Detroit’s up-and-down interior offensive line. Advantage: Draw. My gut tells me the Lions could get things going again with a healthy offensive line, but there’s just not enough data for me to feel any level of confidence there. Both the Jets and Lions look improved from last year, but there’s enough noise in the early data for me to be skeptical. Jets pass offense (8th) vs. Lions pass defense (19th) 2025 rankings: Jets pass offense (31st) vs. Lions pass defense (6th) Week 1 (Titans): 215 passing yards, 104.0 passer rating Week 2 (Packers): 218 passing yards, 90.2 passer rating The Jets were not just the worst passing offense in football for the 2025 season, it was one of the worst attacks in years. Unfortunately for Lions fans, I’m not sure how much we can look into last year’s data. The Jets made changes at offensive coordinator, quarterback, and added a handful of weapons this offseason, and it’s off to a somewhat promising start. It begins with Geno Smith, who is coming off a terrible year in Las Vegas, but has provided at least some stability in New York thus far. The Jets passing offense hasn’t been super explosive, but Smith has avoided the negative plays: no turnovers and just four sacks. So far, the Jets passing offense ranks: 15th in yards per attempt (7.1) 15th in passer rating (95.8) Ninth in dropback EPA (0.205) 12th in success rate (48.1%) The biggest key to the Jets’ success has been pass protection. They currently rank first in PFF pass blocking grade (77.4) and 13th in longest time to…

title: Lions vs. Jets preview: 3 key matchups
summary: Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions and Aaron Glenn’s New York Jets face off in Week 3 at Ford Field, both hungry to put their respective Week 2 losses in the rearview mirror. Glenn has the Jets playing more competitively to start the 2026 season after a rough first season. It is not hard to see how […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 11: Defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn of the Detroit Lions and head coach Dan Campbell look on prior to the game against the Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field on December 11, 2022 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dan Campbell’s Detroit Lions and Aaron Glenn’s New York Jets face off in Week 3 at Ford Field, both hungry to put their respective Week 2 losses in the rearview mirror. Glenn has the Jets playing more competitively to start the 2026 season after a rough first season. It is not hard to see how Jets are following the same blueprint as the Lions from the 2021-22 rebuild years. For that reason, Campbell knows this will be a physical matchup. “Our players know exactly what’s coming in here because the defensive coordinator was here for (four) years. Turn on the tape. … This is gonna be a knockout, 60-minute brawl.“ I agree. Which leads to the first key matchup. Dan Campbell vs. Aaron Glenn After spending four seasons at the Lions defensive coordinator on Campbell’s staff, Glenn knows exactly how the Lions operate. “I know how that program is run and I know that we have a challenge, we have a challenge just like every week.,” said Glenn when asked about the upcoming matchup . “But I can sit back and hear [Campbell] right now saying certain things, but it’ll be a good challenge for us, and we’ll be up for it, we’ll be ready.” The matchup between the head coaches in how they will use the years of experience with each other will be at the top of the list of factors I will be watching for. “There’s things that he knows we want to hang our hat on,” said Campbell. “I mean, that’s just gonna be there. And [there are] things that I know that he wants to hang his hat on. … But then there’ll be these other things. Because we know that, he knows that, there’ll be these wrinkles that get thrown in. It’ll be everything from a front to a pressure to a third down, you get a couple of these other looks that they haven’t put on tape yet.” Glenn has the Jets focused on turning games into slogs, ranking in the bottom five overall playing at one of the league’s slowest paces on offense in the NFL at 33.9 seconds per play while in a neutral game script. Conversely, the Lions operate as one of the top ten fastest-paced teams at 31.7 seconds per play in a neutral script. While the pace of play is a more conservative, defensive-minded approach incorporated by Glenn, I expect the Jets to take some calculated risks of aggression. Maybe some special teams aggression to try and steal a possession—something Glenn had a front row seat watching Campbell do in the early seasons of his tenure in Detroit. Blake Miller vs. David Bailey Rookie versus rookie. First-round pick versus first-round pick. It is Lions offensive tackle Blake Miller returning from his uncharacteristic missed game against the highly explosive edge rusher David Bailey. I think David Bailey vs. Blake Miller may be the single most important matchup this week in Lions vs. Jets. A lot of pressure on both rookies. https://t.co/0Yceu9kO5o — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) September 24, 2026 The rookie edge defender has gotten off to promising start with two sacks in his first two games, along with 11 QB pressures, per NFL NextGen Stats . However, when diving deeper into those numbers, the story looks a little different. Only three of Bailey’s 11 pressures were quick pressures i.e. pressures created in under 2.5 seconds. His average time to pressure, in fact, is 3.56 seconds and average time to sack is 5.30 seconds. With quarterback Jared Goff’s average time to throw at 2.80 seconds, Blake Miller is in a good position to be successful. Limit the quick pressures and it should be comfortable pocket for Goff to continue his impressive start. Christian Izien vs. Keyon Sadiq Injuries for both the Lions and the Jets bring on this key matchup. With Avonte Maddox out for the season , Christian Izien will be forced into a bigger role at safety. “I’m excited to see Christian Izien go out there and fly around at the safety spot this week,” said defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard. Similarly, the Jets starting tight end Mason Taylor has not practiced all week with a thumb injury. First-round pick Kenyon Sadiq takes center stage with an opportunity early in the season. Sadiq is an explosive and versatile chess piece who could be a matchup nightmare as his career unfolds. While only second on the team in routes run among tight ends, Sadiq leads the group in targets (6), receptions (5), and yards (38). He also scored his first NFL touchdown as a rushing attempt, reaching over 20mph on the 3-yard carry. KENYON SADIQ TD 🏈 O TE calouro dos Jets estreia na NFL com um touchdown corrido! pic.twitter.com/OgZjYcENGU — NFL BR Fantasy (@nflbrafantasy) September 13, 2026 It is a big week of Izien and the Lions defense. A strong performance would go a long way in reassuring that the past five quarters of Lions defense is not the version we’ll see the rest of the season. Three key matchups. Three opportunities. Dan Campbell has a chance to make it 3-0 against his former coordinators. Miller has a chance to build on his strong Week 1 performance. And the Izien has an excellent opportunity to right the ship of the defense. It’s going to be a brawl.

title: NFL crackdown on celebrations hits Detroit Lions, Amon-Ra St. Brown hard
summary: On Thursday, it was revealed that 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk received a $14,926 fine for his “juice” celebration of what appears to be a cracking-of-a-beer motion followed by drinking it. A few hours later, Adam Schefter revealed that Colts guard Matt Goncalves was fined $8,847 for imitating chugging a beer. Well, the Detroit Lions may […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 of the Detroit Lions celebrates with teammate running back Jahmyr Gibbs #0 after scoring a touchdown during the second half of an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and the Buffalo Billsat Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, USA, on Thursday, September 17, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images On Thursday, it was revealed that 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk received a $14,926 fine for his “juice” celebration of what appears to be a cracking-of-a-beer motion followed by drinking it . A few hours later, Adam Schefter revealed that Colts guard Matt Goncalves was fined $8,847 for imitating chugging a beer . Well, the Detroit Lions may have gotten the worst of the NFL’s recent crackdown on celebrations. In their Thursday night loss to the Buffalo Bills, Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown—along with Jameson Williams and Jahmyr Gibbs—appeared to pantomime smoking a blunt and passing it around between themselves after scoring a touchdown. And according to St. Brown, the NFL levied a fine for the celebration— one of four fines St. Brown apparently received for Thursday’s game . “It’s not good, man,” St. Brown said. “$14 (thousand and) something times four. You do the math.” St. Brown says he plans to appeal the fine. Here’s a brief video of the celebration, interspersed with St. Brown’s comment, as provided by the Detroit News’ Nolan Bianchi. #Lions WR Amon-Ra St. Brown said he got hit with four fines for a celebration where he appeared to mimic smoking a joint during last week’s game against the #Bills pic.twitter.com/J6iNokSAxH — Nolan Bianchi (@nolanbianchi) September 24, 2026 There is no specific mention in the NFL rulebook about whether the imitation of drug/alcohol use is considered unsportsmanlike conduct, but the fine letter for Juszcyk and Goncalves justified the fine with the following language: “Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste” The closest thing to a specific rule that was broken was this stipulation under unsportsmanlike conduct: Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, subset d: Any violent gesture, which shall include, but not be limited to, a throat slash, simulating firing or brandishing a gun, or using the “nose wipe” gesture, or an act that is sexually suggestive or offensive We’ll see if any of the three offenders win their appeals.

full_text: Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs celebrates a touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens with wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and the offensive line during the first half at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore, Md. on Monday, Sept. 22, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co If you look upon the Detroit Lions’ Thursday injury report for their Week 3 game against the New York Jets, it may look daunting. After all, four offensive linemen don the list, and Detroit can ill-afford any more injuries at the position. But upon closer examination, the news is mostly good for that unit. Let’s break down the entire injury report below. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . N o practice G Ben Bartch (foot) S Thomas Harper (ankle) Bartch and Harper missing a second straight practice is an ominous sign for both of their availability on Sunday vs. the Jets. In fact, it sounds more and more likely that Harper will miss the game based on how Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard spoke of getting Christian Izien ready to potentially start this week alongside Chuck Clark. “I’m excited to see Christian Izien and go out there and fly around at the safety spot this week,” Sheppard said. It’s unclear what Bartch’s prognosis is, nor is it clear whether this foot injury is related to the one that ended his 2025 season and limited him in training camp. Limited practice LG Christian Mahogany (hip) RT Blake Miller (knee) RG Tate Ratledge (elbow) No change for all three of the Lions’ starting offensive linemen on the injury report. However, it was suggested that both Mahogany and Miller may have played last week if the game was on Sunday instead of Thursday. Therefore, they likely seem on track to play again this week, barring any setbacks. Less is known about Ratledge’s injury, but the fact that he wasn’t downgraded to no practice on Thursday is a positive sign that this was not a sudden, serious injury that popped up during practice on Wednesday. For now, there’s no reason to believe that Detroit’s projected starting lineup—Penei Sewell, Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs, Tate Ratledge, and Blake Miller—will be disrupted this week. Full practice DT Alim McNeill (personal) — Upgraded from no practice on Wednesday EDGE Ahmed Hassanein (illness) — Upgraded from limited practice Wednesday LS Hogan Hatten (wrist) As expected, McNeill was back at practice on Thursday, and it doesn’t appear he’s in any danger of missing Sunday’s game. It’s the same positive outlook for Hatten. Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp reassured reporters on Thursday that Hatten is essentially unaffected by the wrist injury. “He snapped fine yesterday and he’ll play in the game. He looks good to me,” Fipp said. title: 6 takeaways from Detroit Lions coordinators: Kelvin Sheppard talks explosives
summary: On Thursday, the Detroit Lions coordinators met with the media for their weekly press conferences. It was a highly-anticipated day, particularly for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, who has come under plenty of fire after Detroit’s defense has allowed 71 points through two games. Here are my six takeaways from Thursday’s media sessions, two from each […]
full_text: Aug 2, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard addressed the media at Meijer Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Thursday, the Detroit Lions coordinators met with the media for their weekly press conferences. It was a highly-anticipated day, particularly for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, who has come under plenty of fire after Detroit’s defense has allowed 71 points through two games. Here are my six takeaways from Thursday’s media sessions, two from each coach. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Slow starts, game scripts The Lions have started each of their two games offensively with three-and-outs. It didn’t hurt them much against the Saints, but it was part of the reason Detroit fell into a quick 21-0 hole against the Bills. Petzing addressed the slow starts on Thursday. “I think you lock in on the plan, some of the first steps that come up in the game,” Petzing said of early-game solutions. “Making sure you feel real confident in what your job is, what we’re expecting on defense. Playing free, playing fast, I think is part of it. Getting the nerves out of the way pre-game so you can play loose. And calling the right plays at the right time.” Petzing said he does start games with a specific script, but wouldn’t say whether he needs to go back and adjust his strategy with those scripts moving forward. “Any time we don’t score a touchdown, I think you’re always going to second guess, ‘Oh, could I have done this? Should I have done that?’” Petzing said. “And I think it’s a balance because I think there are times where you look back at it and say, ‘Hey, I really liked what we called, and we didn’t have the execution I wanted, or something came up a little different.’ And then there’re other times you look at it and say, ‘I’m not sure that was the best call and maybe we needed to tweak that. Maybe I need to change my mindset here a little bit.’” Second-and-10 runs One minor complaint I had about Petzing and Detroit’s offense in the Bills game was the seemingly overreliance on rushing plays on second-and-10. It felt like Buffalo picked up on that tendency, and it resulted in a lot of negative plays late in the game when Detroit was attempting a comeback. Petzing defended those decisions, noting that getting into a third-and-manageable is very important in this league. And if the Lions just leaned into passing plays, they could end up facing third-down looks from the defense, which means increased pressure looks. Additionally, he made the point that in Detroit, they often operate like a four-down offense, so they often treat second down like first down. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard Done with the omitting explosives game Last year, Sheppard came under heat for a somewhat ridiculous assertion that Detroit played good run defense against the Los Angeles Rams when they allowed 159 yards on 29 carries. He argued that if you just took away three explosive runs, they played fine. Sheppard is changing his tune this year. Last year, the explosive plays were the problem, and that’s already reared its ugly head again this year. By the Lions’ measures, they’ve given up 23 explosive plays thus far through two games, and 75 percent of those were “self-induced.” But because it’s been such a consistent problem, they aren’t dismissing them. They’re hell-bent on fixing them. “I know before, guys, I stood up here and I said, ‘Alright, we played three quarters good, but in the fourth quarter you take that play out.’ Well, we’re no longer doing that this year because taking those plays out is the exact plays that’s been a demise to our defense,” Sheppard said. “And when I say that, coming out of half, I believe we had 77 pass yards total. And then the scramble play to a live aid that I think netted 40-something yards, kind of broke the dam. And led to them finishing with I think around 400 yards passing or something like that.” Sheppard said they looked at all 23 explosive plays, and had the players diagnose what—and why—things went wrong. “Tell me what you’re doing. Tell me what you’re supposed to be doing. Coaches, don’t say a word. Let’s let them talk because right now guys, there’s a gap. There’s a clear gap from meetings and practice.” But Sheppard took plenty of ownership, too. “We’ve got to do something different guys than we’ve been doing to make sure this gap is closed from meetings and practice to game day, Sheppard.” And I think that was one of the most transparent (meetings). There was a lot of honesty said out loud in that meeting, player to player, player to coach, coach to player. And we hashed out some things.“ Getting Christian Izien up to speed Communication is paramount to the Lions’ defense and that often starts with the Lions’ safeties. Unfortunately for Detroit, they look to be extremely shorthanded this week. Not only are Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch still on the Physically Unable to Perform list, but Avonte Maddox is out for the season with a foot injury, and Thomas Harper is currently sidelined with an ankle injury. That leaves Chuck Clark likely to be paired with Christian Izien, who has mostly been playing at nickel since training camp. When it became apparent that may be the reality the Lions were facing, Sheppard wasted no time in getting Izien up to speed. Starting Saturday, safeties coach Jim O’Neil started working with Izien to make sure they don’t take a step back on the backend. “It’s been the sole focus since I would say Saturday when we knew that was a reality and he’s been in here non-stop,” Sheppard said. “I told JO [Jim O’Neil] the other night, ‘Man, you still in there coaching?’ I mean, it’s just a revolving door in JO’s office right there.” Sheppard insists they won’t have to scale back their defense to accomodate for Izien, despite his relative inexperience at the position. Instead, he feels it’s his job to work with Izien to identify what he’s comfortable doing, and make sure the play calls are geared toward his strengths. “You got a new guy up here safety. ‘Izzy, come here. What calls do you like on this sheet? Tell me why. Don’t just tell me, ‘because,’ tell me why you like them,’” Sheppard said. “And that’s when you start to gain that level of understanding with the player. And then as the play caller, let’s put him in this position. ‘Here’s why, because you told me. You got me?’ All good. And that’s when we move forward.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp Hogan Hatten is fine, so stop calling Lions long snapper Hogan Hatten popped up on the injury report with a wrist injury on Wednesday. And despite him being listed as a full participant, Fipp said agents of seven different long snappers reached out to him Wednesday night. But he had to tell them all they weren’t interested. Obviously, the wrist is an important job for the long snapper, but Fipp assured everyone that there is no concern with Hatten or his snapping abilities right now. “He snapped fine yesterday and he’ll play in the game. He looks good to me,” Fipp said. Line drive kick still a work in progress With the new kickoff format, there is no better weapon than a kick that hits the ground within the landing zone (between the 20-yard line and the end zone). However, that type of kick is difficult, and Fipp noted how everyone around the league is still trying to get consistent at it, including Lions kicker Jake Bates. In the season opener, Bates tried that kick, only to land it about 12-yards short of the landing one, resulting in the Saints taking over at the 40-yard line. “Obviously it can be a tremendous weapon, obviously, if you can execute it 100% of the time,” Fipp said. “The challenge with it is everybody has some challenge with it. The teams that put the ball on the ground have also for the most part come short with the landing zone. And that’s a tough penalty because the ball goes to 40 and on average.” One interesting downside of…

After a disappointing initial season in New York, Glenn revamped his coaching staff and roster, and the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 14: Head Coach Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets looks on following the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at MetLife Stadium on August 14, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. […] AG checked all those boxes, and you’ve got to look through all the other stuff and really look at the substance behind it.” Offensive coordinato r: Frank Reich NFL coaching seasons : Entering 19th season Head coaching seasons : 6 seasons (Colts 2018-22, Panthers 2023) Offensive coordinator seasons : 5 years as OC (Chargers 2014-15, Eagles 2016-17, Jets 2026) Previous coaching positions : QB coach, WR coach, Offensive assistant Influences: Doug Pederson (RPO, aggression), Tony Dungy (Culture), Ken Whisenhunt (run game) Coached under: Pederson, Dungy, Mike McCoy, Whisenhunt, Jim Caldwell Coaching staff ties to Detroit : Seth Ryan (Passing game coordinator), Steve Heiden (OL coach), Shawn Jefferson (WR coach) Offensive scheme Passing game : Modern Pro-Spread (i.e. Pederson/Andy Reid style) Running scheme : Balanced; one-on-one inside-man-heavy Scouting notes : Traditional North-South offense Balanced Run/Pass split: 44% to 56% (8th highest run rate in NFL) Did have big variance dependent on opponent (i.e. 62/38 vs. Titans, but flipped to 38/62 vs. Packers) Personnel grouping also varied by opponent 11 personnel: 45% vs. Titans; 70% vs. Packers 12: 23% vs. Titans; 14% vs. Packers 13: 18% vs. Titans; 10% vs. Packers 22: 13% vs. Titans; 3% vs. Packers The personnel groups directly relate to success (on the ground vs. Titans) and game situation (Jets found little success on the ground vs. Packers, which is why they failed to run out the clock in the fourth quarter) Despite having the 8th highest run percentage in the NFL, their output is just 3.3 yards per carry (28th), and their EPA per run is -0.2 (also 28th) Biggest reason for rushing struggles: RBs only gain 0.76 yards before contact (24th) Solid Time-to-Pass (2.76 seconds – 13th) and sack rates (only four sacks allowed), but the OL has given up 33 pressures (28th) — QB Geno Smith has done well to escape pressure Dan Campbell on Jets’ QB Geno Smith: “He’s come in here and had some really good games against us, played really good football. And he is doing a good job of this whole thing about them possessing the football and finding completions, taking the shots when they’re there, just playing smart football. Man, he’s doing it. And he’s proving he will sit in the pocket and he’s looking for it. He’s fearless that way; he’s got that. But we cannot let him get out. I mean, if he makes throws in the pocket, then we’ve got to fight the next play. At least we gave ourselves a chance, but if we let him get out of there in the open field and run or find a throw downfield because he broke contain, that’s where that could be problematic.” Defensive coordinator: Brian Duker NFL coaching seasons : Entering his 11th season Defensive coordinator seasons : First Previous roles : Secondary coach (Dolphins, Lions), Defensive analyst (Ravens, 49ers), Intern (Browns) Influences: Aaron Glenn (scheme), Dan Campbell (culture), John Harbaugh (scheme) Coached under: Glenn, Campbell, Harbaugh, Wink Martindale, Anthony Weaver, Mike Macdonald, and Jim O’Neil (Lions safeties coach) Coaching staff ties to Detroit : Cameron Davis (Assistant DL/OLB coach) Defensive scheme Base : 3-4 Base, attacking front Coverage : Press-Man, balanced safety looks Scouting notes : Adaptive front More of a Ravens-style defense than what Glenn ran last year with the Jets — which was more Lions-esque Duker’s infuence/backgroud and Glenn adaptability/background show up here Main principles remain: Physicality, stop-the-run mentality, pressure/blitz on 3rd down Formation shifts in 2026: Less Base (down from 32% to 21%) and more nickel (up from 65% to 77%) Coverage shifts in 2026: Less man-cover (down from 33% to 25%) and more zone (up from 65% to 73%) Coverage philosophy shift: Less reliance on single high (Cover-1, -3); even split with 2-high shells Man coverage in 2026: Cover-0 (5%), Cover-1 (16%), Cover-2 man (4%) Zone coverage in 2026: Cover 2 (35%), Cover-3 (18%), Cover-4 (6%), Cover-6 (13%) Blitz rate in 2026: around 30% Yards allowed per game: 197 total (best in NFL) Yards allowed per play: 3.2 average (2nd) Jets defense in Base vs. run: -0.48 EPA (best in NFL) Jets defense in Subpackage vs. run: 0.13 EPA (19th) What does that mean? Deploy a lot of 11 personnel, keep them in nickel, run against nickel DL “get off” the snap: 0.71 seconds (best in NFL) Time to pressure: 2.69 seconds (21st) What does that mean: Jets DL is elite off the snap but struggles to shed blocks once engaged Sacks: Six (ninth) Pressures: 26 (13th) Dan Campbell on Jets’ defense: “I know enough to know that (Glenn) AG’s got a Rolodex of looks and pressures and he’s got it all and coverage disguises. So, we kind of got to be prepared for everything.”
author: Erik Schlitt

title: 5 Qs Lions vs. Jets preview: Big game from Amon-Ra St. Brown incoming?
summary: Reunited and it feels… nostalgic. This week, we had the pleasure of connecting with MacGregor Wells, the Deputy Manager for Gang Green Nation, to give us some insight into who these New York Jets are through two weeks. We learned how Jets fans are still very much in a “wait and see” moment with this […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - DECEMBER 18: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) during the National Football League game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions on December 18, 2022 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Reunited and it feels… nostalgic . This week, we had the pleasure of connecting with MacGregor Wells, the Deputy Manager for Gang Green Nation , to give us some insight into who these New York Jets are through two weeks. We learned how Jets fans are still very much in a “wait and see” moment with this football team, what Geno Smith needs to do in order to be successful during his second stint in Gotham, and what to make of these suffocating performances from the defense—and much more. 1. The New York Jets are off to about as good of a start as they could have anticipated. Led by Aaron Glenn, this defense ranks third in DVOA–first in run defense and sixth in pass defense. For all the mockery they faced at last year’s trade deadline, the Jets look like they’re a team on the rise. But after losing last week to the Green Bay Packers, with the questions surrounding Glenn’s game-management decisions, does it still feel like it appears to be from the outside looking in at this team? I think for the most part we’re in wait and see mode at this point in the season.The Jets defense has played well, but they have benefitted from the schedule, which started with a very bad Titans offense the Jets manhandled. Then we had a sloppy game in the rain against a Packers team with what looks like a bad offensive line dealing with multiple injuries. You can only play the teams on the schedule, and so far the Jets defense has done well, but I think the jury’s out on what this will look like against the better offenses in the NFL. The Jets secondary is of particular concern. I think over the course of the season we will see the Jets secondary get exploited. On offense the Jets have a good offensive line and some pretty good weapons in Breece Hall and Garrett Wilson, but so far that side of the ball remains a work in progress. They did well against a bad Titans team but struggled against the Packers. Are the Jets on the rise? I suppose, but coming off one of the worst teams I have ever seen last year, on the rise is expected; it would be difficult to be worse. 2. Geno Smith’s triumphant return to the team that drafted him 13 years ago is one helluva winding circle back to where it all started. Glenn moved on from Tanner Engstrand in January and hired veteran offensive mind Frank Reich to be the team’s third offensive coordinator in as many years. Smith’s lone season in Las Vegas was disastrous, finishing with a league-high 17 interceptions. It’s interesting to see Smith completing over 70% of his passes, sixth in completion percentage over expected, and 16th in EPA/dropback. How has Geno gotten off to such a sound start, what role has Reich served in that turnaround, and how optimistic are you in Smith playing the kind of football he needs to play when the other side of the ball is playing the way they are? Smith has always been an accurate quarterback with a strong arm. The issues with him haven’t been with his arm talent. The issues have always been his decision making and his ability to process what’s in front of him in a timely manner. He has always been prone to turnovers. While he has avoided turnovers thus far this year, I doubt he has changed this part of his game so late in his career. Ultimately if you don’t ask too much of Smith he can competently execute the offense. Give him enough time and he will deliver the ball accurately. The Jets have a pretty good offensive line so there should be a good number of games when Smith has plenty of time and he’ll competently execute the offense. However, there will be games when the offensive line allows pressure on Smith. Then he and the Jets offense will struggle. Sacks and turnovers will follow. Ask him to carry the team and Smith will likely implode. 3. New York’s stifling start on defense has a lot to do with their top draft pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, David Bailey. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, “Bailey has generated 11 pressures (23.4% pressure rate) and two sacks on 47 pass rushes, the third-most pressures by a rookie edge rusher through Week 2 in the Next Gen Stats era, trailing only Nick Bosa and Josh Hines-Allen (12 each in 2019).” His incredible athleticism is making all the difference right now, also according to Next Gen Stats: “Bailey is averaging a 0.75 second get-off time, the seventh-fastest among 92 edge rushers with at least 40 pass rushes. His 11 pressures are more than the rest of the Jets’ edge rushers combined (10).” With numbers like this Bailey has to be popping off the screen. Where is he primarily lining up on defense, what sort of versatility has he shown, and did the Jets just get the steal of last year’s draft? Bailey is primarily lining up on the edge. He is playing with his hand in the dirt at times and as a stand up pass rusher at other times. The Jets will occasionally drop him into coverage. I’m not sure that’s a great idea, other than as a rare gimmick to try to confuse the offense. Did the Jets get the steal of the draft? Oh, I don’t know. Two things here. First, I don’t think we can draw much in the way of conclusions based on two games. Second, Bailey was the #2 pick. At that slot it’s pretty difficult to be the steal of the draft. Great things are expected from #2 overall picks. To be the steal of the draft he’d have to outperform already sky high expectations. I like what I’ve seen for the most part from Bailey, but I would hesitate to already call him the steal of the draft. 4. The Jets’ defense has put up some incredibly eye-popping performances through two weeks. They held both the Titans and the Packers to less than 200 total yards in back-to-back weeks, and they’re tied for the fourth-best mark in EPA per play allowed (-0.25) and sack rate (8.5%). Which players, outside of Bailey, have been key to New York’s impressive defensive play to start the season? Have you noticed any new wrinkles to the defense, or any new emphases placed on this side of the ball? The Jets defense has played well so far, though, as discussed above, the schedule has probably had something to do with this. I would say the players who have stood out so far other than Bailey would be edge Kingsley Enagbare, who has surprised me with his stout overall play, defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat, who has done great work against the run, safety Dane Belton, who has been a sure tackler and fundamentally sound at his position, and second year cornerback Azareye’h Thomas, who has been sticky in coverage despite his speed limitations. The Jets are finding success by shutting down the run with strong defensive line play early, then putting pressure on the quarterback when he has to pass. This isn’t some revolutionary scheme, just sound fundamental defensive football so far. We’ll see how that holds up against better offenses. The secondary still appears to me to be vulnerable against better offenses. 5. The Jets opened as 7.5-point underdogs heading into Week 3 against a Lions team still licking their wounds after taking a beating the entire world saw courtesy of Josh Allen and Co. Since then the line has moved to the Lions being a 6.5-point favorite over at FanDuel Sportsbook . What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen at Ford Field this Sunday? One thing I want to see: the Jets getting first round pick Kenyon Sadiq more involved in the offense. They spent the 16th pick in the first round on a tight end. They need to get more production out of him. One thing I need to see: Breece Hall running more effectively. The Jets gave Hall a big bucks contract extension, presumably to be the bell cow back. Thus far this…
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Why Lions WR Isaac TeSlaa has limited targets, and when that will change
summary: Through two games, Detroit Lions receiver Isaac TeSlaa has just six targets and two catches—one being a garbage time conversion on fourth-and-18 while down 17 points with about two minutes left. Given how much draft capital the Lions have spent on the second-year receiver, some fans have expressed frustration with his lack of production. On […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Isaac Teslaa #18 of the Detroit Lions runs in action during a preseason game against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images Through two games, Detroit Lions receiver Isaac TeSlaa has just six targets and two catches—one being a garbage time conversion on fourth-and-18 while down 17 points with about two minutes left. Given how much draft capital the Lions have spent on the second-year receiver, some fans have expressed frustration with his lack of production. On Wednesday, Lions associate head coach and wide receivers coach Scottie Montgomery addressed TeSlaa’s lack of production so far. The main reasoning for it has little to do with TeSlaa himself and more to do with the fact that the Lions are just extremely deep when it comes to weapons in the passing game. TeSlaa is essentially fifth in line behind Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Sam LaPorta, and Jahmyr Gibbs. “Tes [TeSlaa], his opportunities are going to be limited just because of how we’re built as an offense, whether it be at tight end or it be at wideout, whether it be in the backfield, who we have a phenomenal player in the backfield,” Montgomery said. “So what he’s going to have to do is—all of his (opportunities) are going to be critical. They’re going to be fourth down, they’re going to be red zone, they’re going to be third downs.” Montgomery said teams have played Detroit’s offense a little differently than in previous years. The Lions are used to defenses shading coverages toward St. Brown, but the All-Pro receiver has surprisingly been put in a lot of one-on-one situations. There’s been very little need for Jared Goff to go beyond his first or second progressions thus far. But Montgomery expects that to eventually change—especially this week against the Jets and Aaron Glenn, who knows how dangerous St. Brown can be. That is when TeSlaa is going to have to show up. “We have to judge [TeSlaa] off of those plays until we get everything rolling to a point to where we are equally distributing because of the coverage and how they’re moving to Saint,” Montgomery said. “But at this point in time right now, it’s been really one of those situations where a lot of times our first in progression has been open, our second in progression has been open, and sometimes when you’re not first or second in the progression, you have to wait until you get going.” In the meantime, TeSlaa has been doing everything right away from the play. That involves doing the dirty work of blocking, being physical, and sometimes being so tight to the line that he’s essentially playing as another tight end. “Right now, he’s playing harder than damn-near anybody that we have on our offensive side of the ball,” Montgomery said. “He is mixing it up, he’s physical. And that’s what you have to do when you’re in that role. A lot of guys have never played in that role.” Montgomery believes as TeSlaa continues to gain this reputation as a dirty-work player that is an asset in the run game, they will be able to build plays off those tendencies. That’s when TeSlaa could become a serious weapon in a room full of weapons. “When you look at that, those situations the dirty work, all of those plays that no one else wants to make—and now because of that, we’re able to use those tendencies and create a bigger play for him in the game because some of the dirty work that he has,” Montgomery said. “And then all of a sudden, it’s that, ‘We’ve got to get him the ball more.’ So we look forward to those things happening.” TeSlaa was taken the the third round of the 2025 NFL Draft after Detroit traded two 2026 third-round picks to come up and get him. In his career, he has 18 catches for 265 yards and six touchdowns, although much of his production came after LaPorta went down with an injury last year. The production may not be there, but Montgomery believes they are still getting plenty of value out of him. “For what he’s able to do for us, he’s able to stretch the field, he can block in the box—those two deals don’t usually work together Outside receivers usually don’t have the ability to block (in) the box,” Montgomery said. “He gives us the ability now to take some of those shots off of Saint, use Saint in different situations. He can also clear down the middle of the field. He has short-area quickness in some of those tight spots where he’s a big body, he can make plays. We’ll start to see more of it as we go forward, but he has a tremendous value on this team.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Packers Week 3: Stats from Green Bay’s Loss to the Falcons
summary: As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers game this week, courtesy of SumerSports. Offense It will not surprise those of you who watched the game, but the Packers leaned heavily into the passing game against the Falcons. On the day, they finished with an […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we do every week in this space, we’re looking at some stats from the Green Bay Packers game this week, courtesy of SumerSports . Offense It will not surprise those of you who watched the game, but the Packers leaned heavily into the passing game against the Falcons. On the day, they finished with an 85.7% pass rate, a whopping 30.27% above the NFL average. Lest you think the numbers are skewed based on the game getting out of hand, they had a 79.2% pass rate in the 1st half. Drilling down one more level, they had an 80% pass rate in the 1st quarter. Did it work? Eh, not really, but the passing game was more effective than the running game. For the game, the passing game produced a +0.01 EPA per Play (42.6% Success Rate), compared to -0.33 EPA per Play (33.3% Success Rate) when running the ball. Love’s average time to throw of 2.46 seconds was slightly more than the 2.35 seconds he had coming into the game. The worst part on the pressure front is that the Falcons barely blitzed. Their Defensive Coordinator (Jeff Ulbrich) did a nice job mixing up looks, but the Falcons only blitzed on 16.67% of their snaps, 14.23% below the league average. Despite that low blitz rate, they pressured Love on 44.44% of his dropbacks and averaged 2.5 seconds to pressure. This game also saw the Packers lean heavier into 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) than we had seen previously. They were in 11 personnel on 81% of their snaps. That’s skewed a bit by playing catch-up in the second half, but they were in 11 personnel on 66.7% of their 1st half snaps, so they were rolling with more 3WR sets from the jump this week. As a reference, they were in 11 personnel on 47.8% of their snaps in Week 1 and 56% in Week 2. To round that out for this week, they were in 12 personnel on 15.9% and 13 personnel on 3.2%. They had their best performance in 11. Out of 11 personnel, they posted an EPA per Play of +0.13 (+0.06 in the 1st half). Their other two groupings were both in the negative. They were -0.55 EPA per Play out of 12 and -1.24 EPA per Play out of 13. In the run game, we once again saw them steering away from a zone-heavy system. They ran something in the zone family on 33.3% of their running plays. It seems counterintuitive given some of the smaller bodies they now employ up front, but they can’t get any movement on zone stuff. The only way they’ve been successful is by pulling those smaller bodies and smashing them into linebackers. They’ve built some fun pass stuff off of that, but the run game itself hasn’t done much of anything. The only positive EPA per Play they had in the run game was to the B gap, but that was on a single attempt. I do want to shout out J. Michael Sturdivant real quick. He had 3 catches for 22 yards (+1.11 EPA per Reception). Two of his receptions (+2.23 EPA per Reception) came on slants, which is something he showed nice skill on in the preseason. He’s a big, fast receiver with some suddenness on slants. If he can turn into something on the outside, that gives the Packers an option on the outside to be able to use Watson a little more in the slot. Also, big up to Matthew Golden. He had a 100-yard receiving day and caught his first regular-season TD. His EPA per Reception of +2.12 was the highest of any Packers WR on the day, and he also drew a big defensive pass interference penalty. He hasn’t been perfect, but Golden has shown some really nice things through 3 weeks. Defense If the offense looked a little ugly, you’re not gonna like the defense. They were in Man Coverage for 12% of their snaps and Zone for 88%. Here’s the breakdown of the types of zone they ran: Cover 3: 45% Cover 4: 27% Cover 2: 20% Cover 6: 8% Gannon continues to blitz above his pre-Packers reputation showed (32% blitz rate tonight), but they couldn’t consistently get home. They only got pressure on 20% of the Falcons’ dropbacks. Part of that was the quick release of Penix: he averaged 2.15 seconds to throw. The Packers had a missed tackle rate of 13.33% on the game, 0.06 above the NFL average. That may feel low, but you can only miss a tackle if you get close enough to make the tackle. Some of the big gains by Bijan Robinson felt less like missed tackles and more like poor tackling angles. (Although they also did miss their fair share of tackles.) Remember that Packers run gap chart I showed above? Here’s the Falcons’ chart. Avert your eyes, child. Looks like a lot more blue than the Packers chart. They had success against light boxes (+0.22 EPA per Play), heavy boxes (+0.23 EPA per Play) and even boxes (+0.38 EPA per Play). I believe they call that getting pushed around. Lukas Van Ness had another nice game. Due to the rush-heavy approach of the Falcons (they had a 62.1% run rate) and the quick release of Penix, LVN ended up with a low pressure rate (a mere 5%), but his average time to pressure was 2.34 seconds. If the defense was able to make Penix hold onto the ball for a tick longer, LVN could have had himself a very nice night. Albums listened to: Julien Baker – 2026 Tour EP ; Brother Bird – The Lodge in Miller County
author: Dusty Evely

title: Packers Snap Counts, Week 3: MarShawn Lloyd is RB3
summary: The Green Bay Packers made a couple of changes to their offensive and defensive lineups for Week 3, as the team is desperately trying to find their first win in regulation since Week 14 last year against the Chicago Bears. The loss to the Atlanta Falcons was gross, and I’m hoping to flush it from […]
full_text: (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers made a couple of changes to their offensive and defensive lineups for Week 3, as the team is desperately trying to find their first win in regulation since Week 14 last year against the Chicago Bears. The loss to the Atlanta Falcons was gross , and I’m hoping to flush it from my brain as quickly as possible. Here are the snap counts this week, so we can get it out of the way. Quarterback 63 snaps: Jordan Love 0: Tyrod Taylor Running Back 26: Chris Brooks 22: Kaleb Johnson 15: MarShawn Lloyd MarShawn Lloyd is officially the RB3 on the team. Last week, Lloyd split snaps perfectly (on non-penalties) with Kaleb Johnson, who didn’t play a single snap of offense in Week 1 for the Packers. Now, Lloyd is backing up Johnson as a ball-carrier, while Chris Brooks is still receiving the most snaps of any back in Green Bay. On the season, Brooks has 85 snaps of offense to Lloyd’s 59 and Johnson’s 36, but Johnson is making up ground on Lloyd. Receiver 51: Matthew Golden 51: Christian Watson 32: Skyy Moore 21: Bo Melton 20: J. Michael Sturdivant For the most part, Jayden Reed — who is likely to go on the injured reserve for a neck/back injury — was replaced by Skyy Moore, as expected. Moore played the backup slot role for the Packers all summer and before Reed’s injury. Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant both saw increased snaps from last week (when they played eight snaps combined), as Green Bay needed to rotate in fresh route-runners for an offense that dropped back nearly 60 times tonight. Tight End 49: Tucker Kraft 20: Jonnu Smith 7: Mark Redman 1: Josh Whyle Josh Whyle has played one snap the last two weeks, as 11 of his 12 snaps this season came in Week 1. There were a lot more three-receiver looks for the Packers in Week 3 than in Weeks 1 and 2, despite Jayden Reed’s injury, because of the game flow. While Green Bay was only down three points at the half, they went into point-chasing mode quickly, leading to the team having little to no use for blocking tight end Mark Redman. Offensive Line 63: Sean Rhyan 63: Jordan Morgan 63: Anthony Belton 63: Jager Burton 56: Jacob Monk 7: Donovan Jennings 0: John Williams 0: Travis Glover Jager Burton made his first career NFL start in Week 3, as the rookie replaced both left guard Aaron Banks (missed the game with an injury) and Donovan Jennings (apparently benched, despite the staff stating that they wanted continuity on the offensive line). Jennings did eventually come into the game, though, as right guard Jacob Monk left action with an undisclosed injury at the two-minute warning. Defensive Line 40: Karl Brooks 32 Javon Hargrave 31: Devonte Wyatt 27: Chris McClellan 26: Jonathan Ford Edge Defender 46: Lukas Van Ness 36: Dani Dennis-Sutton 26: Barryn Sorrell 23: Brenton Cox Jr. Rookie fourth-round pick Dani Dennis-Sutton has been the team’s fourth edge defender in the pecking order this season, but he leapfrogged both Barryn Sorrell and Brenton Cox Jr. in Week 3. It will be interesting to monitor if that will continue moving forward, or if this was just a one-off. Off-Ball Linebacker 66: Zaire Franklin 51: Edgerrin Cooper 15: Isaiah McDuffie 1: Ty’Ron Hopper 0: Nick Niemann Will linebacker Edgerrin Cooper was knocked out of the game with a head injury, was evaluated for a concussion and left for the locker room during the game. He did not return and was replaced by special teams captain Isaiah McDuffie. Cornerback 65: Keisean Nixon 65: Brandon Cisse 0: Carrington Valentine 0: Benjamin St-Juste 0: Kamal Hadden Safety 66: Evan Williams 66: Xavier McKinney 44: Javon Bullard 0: Kitan Oladapo The Packers mostly played nickel defense looks tonight, as you can see from Javon Bullard’s two-thirds usage. The team even played nickel on a crucial third-and-short look late in the game, when the Falcons threw three tight ends on the field. Atlanta rushed for a first down, which basically ended Green Bay’s chances of coming out of the game with a win.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Week 3 vs. the Falcons
summary: After a big fat doozy of a season opening loss, and a big fat doozy of a win last week, the Green Bay Packers have finally played their home opener, and it was, you guessed it: a big fat doozy of a game. On Thursday Night Football, the team laid a goose egg against the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a big fat doozy of a season opening loss, and a big fat doozy of a win last week, the Green Bay Packers have finally played their home opener, and it was, you guessed it: a big fat doozy of a game. On Thursday Night Football , the team laid a goose egg against the 0-2 Atlanta Falcons to kick off Week 3, and lost 35-14. Let’s get this show on the road. Winner: Brandon Cisse The rookie DB put together a nice little game for himself, despite the feeling of dread lingering throughout the entire stadium and my body. He had some great coverage which forced incompletions, and some good tackles either at the line of scrimmage, or at the point of catch, to prevent some big plays (don’t worry, big plays still happened). There wasn’t much to be unhappy with here, outside of a rookie mistake of an illegal contact foul, but I watched the game with my eyes closed, so I could be wrong. Either way, Cisse was a little bright spot during a very dark game. Winner: Matthew Golden Matthew Golden’s breakout season is off to a nice start. The 2nd year WR did a fantastic job adjusting in the first half and hauling in a 45 yard heave from Jordan Love. He also snagged his first regular season touchdown with an equally impressive catch. Bonus: he is an absolute magnet for DPI! Love goes DEEEP to Golden! @ATLvsGB on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rJKpsMBYXI — NFL (@NFL) September 25, 2026 GOLDEN! 📺: Prime Video pic.twitter.com/JvZsBwZfDm — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 25, 2026 Loser: Jordan Love The Packers QB is playing scared, and while I can’t exactly blame him, it’s time to get it together. He had some really bad throws Thursday night, both over and under thrown, and some which were just wildly off target. There was a hospital ball to Christian Watson. Love hesitated too much, and other times, he panicked. He looked completely lost against a very bad football team, and as a result, the offense couldn’t capitalize on some big plays by the defense. During the team’s second drive of the game, he seemed to get into a bit of a rhythm, and the drive ended in their first touchdown. But this…was about it! He looked really awful, but I’m not sure how much better anyone else would’ve looked under those same circumstances. Loser: MarShawn Lloyd My RB, my sweet little built-like-a-bowling-ball RB: you are blind. You could not find an opening if a sinkhole swallowed the field. Loser: The Offensive Line Exhibit A below. I’M GOING TO BED. Green Bay's offensive line is something special pic.twitter.com/Ya0txCv3xu — Underdog (@Underdog) September 25, 2026 The team heads into a desperately needed mini-bye week with a 1-2 record, and a lot to think about. Their next appearance comes on Sunday, October 4th, in Tampa Bay against the Buccaneers. The game will be at 1PM ET/12PM CT (that’s a threat).
author: Sam Kallien

title: Packers-Falcons Final Score: Green Bay fails to run the ball again in home-opening loss
summary: Thursday was as bad a showing as the Green Bay Packers have had all season, as the Atlanta Falcons came to Lambeau Field and upset the Packers 35-14 for Green Bay’s first home-opening loss since 2012. The team is now 1-7 over their last eight games, and boos were heard throughout the game — when […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Thursday was as bad a showing as the Green Bay Packers have had all season, as the Atlanta Falcons came to Lambeau Field and upset the Packers 35-14 for Green Bay’s first home-opening loss since 2012 . The team is now 1-7 over their last eight games, and boos were heard throughout the game — when Falcons fans weren’t chanting “A-T-L.” Packers fans were looking for one thing on offense tonight: Any signs of life for the running game. Green Bay ran the ball just eight times for 17 yards tonight, while quarterback Jordan Love threw the ball 53 times for head coach and play-caller Matt LaFleur (on top of taking a sack and scrambling once). Love was still in the game with a minute and change left on the clock, taking unnecessary hits in a game where the Packers were down three full touchdowns. Defensively, the Packers came in looking good. They led the NFL in yards per carry allowed through two weeks of football, despite having a poor showing in the red zone…until the Falcons countered Jonathan Gannon’s aggressive defense with outside zone runs that punished overpursuits. Thankfully, the Falcons never made the red zone going into Week 3…until they entered the red zone five times against Green Bay. Atlanta’s two stars on offense, running back Bijan Robinson and receiver Drake London, combined for 407 yards of total offense. It was clear who the Falcons were going to feed while quarterback Michael Penix Jr. made his first start since tearing his ACL last season — the Packers just couldn’t stop them. Special teams didn’t even go right for the Packers tonight, as they had a kick blocked. The occasional Matthew Golden and Christian Watson explosive play is fun to watch, but Love has played better football in his career — and Golden, Watson and tight end Tucker Kraft are dropping the ball — beyond the offensive line’s clear struggles. The offensive plan just isn’t working, assuming they have a plan. Something needs to change in Green Bay, or it’s going to be a long, gross year offensively. You can’t drop back 86 percent of the time in the NFL, like the Packers did tonight. Love won’t survive the season doing that. LaFleur might not, either.
