title: Saints vs. Raiders: Quarterback Matchup
summary: The Saints are set to finally host their home opener for the 2026 season against the Las Vegas Raiders in a matchup of two teams that have surprised the league through the first two weeks of the season. The Raiders have former Saints OC Klint Kubiak as their new head coach, and through the first […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) is sacked by Detroit Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Saints are set to finally host their home opener for the 2026 season against the Las Vegas Raiders in a matchup of two teams that have surprised the league through the first two weeks of the season. The Raiders have former Saints OC Klint Kubiak as their new head coach, and through the first two weeks of the season, Kubiak has the Raiders humming as a team. The Raiders had the first overall pick and selected Fernando Mendoza, but Mendoza has yet to make a start. Instead, it’s been Kirk Cousins leading the charge for the Raiders. Now, the Raiders have played against what may possibly be two of the worst teams in the NFL in the Dolphins and the Chargers, but the Raiders beat them, and Cousins played pretty well in both games. So far through two games, Cousins has completed 67.8% of his passes for 413 yards, 6 TDs, and 3 interceptions. He has also been sacked twice so far this season. Cousins is very familiar with playing against the Saints and in the Dome, but this experience may be a little different. Being at home, the defense will want to pressure Cousins up the middle, and having a true home-field advantage will help with slowing down the offensive linemen from getting off the ball, especially on the edges. Keep in mind, Cousins is a 15-year veteran, so fooling him will not be something that is easily accomplished. Blitzing for the sake of blitzing should not be the focus here. Instead, change what he sees post-snap and make the pressure feel like it’s always coming at him through simulated looks. If the rush can start making him hesitate, he will hold the ball and also start to force passes into tight windows, which could lead to increasing that already elevated interception number that he has. Tyler Shough is coming into his first game as the captain of this team and is also coming off one of the biggest road victories this team has had in nearly half a decade. The Dome will be ready to celebrate the new face of the team, and deservedly so. Shough is finding his groove. Shough is currently leading the NFL in several categories: passing yards with 662, completions with 62, 20-yard completions with 11, and passing yards per game with 331. He is also second in attempts with 90. Through two games, Shough has 4 TDs and 2 INTs. The great thing about this is that both interceptions came in the Week 1 game against the Lions, and he was able to finish the game against the Ravens with 0 turnovers. Shough has to stay on this path and continue to limit the turnovers. He will have a tough challenge this week, as starting LT Kelvin Banks Jr. will be out with a high ankle sprain, and the Raiders will feature Maxx Crosby, one of the league’s best pass rushers. So, protection will be at a premium. The Saints will also have to get a run game going to support Shough, keep the linebackers and safeties off balance, and utilize the play-action game as an actual threat. Shough will also have to identify the coverage. The Raiders will feature a 3-4 base defense that will mix up which four defenders will rush. Three keys to keep Shough rolling as one of the best QBs in the league for this game can be simplified to the three Ps: protection, patience, and play action. This is a matchup of a very experienced veteran who is mentoring a future starter and a young, rising QB who is showcasing a little bit of superstar potential. Who will be the one who can come out on top in this matchup? Can the Saints force the veteran to the bench and push Kubiak to put in the young rookie because they need a spark? That is very unlikely, especially on the road, but that was a situation Tyler Shough found himself in during the middle part of last season against the Rams. Sunday will be a very fun game. Two teams that no one really had high expectations for will face off, and the Saints walk into this matchup with the edge at the QB position. Who do you think will have the better game? What do you think the Saints should do to help elevate Shough and slow down Cousins?
author: Anthony Parker

title: Matt Nagy is charge of ‘lane change’ for NY Giants’ offense
summary: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh calls the team’s necessary offensive stylistic change, with Jameis Winston replacing Jaxson Dart at quarterback, a “lane change.” The man primarily responsible for implementing that lane change is offensive coordinator Matt Nagy. He knows what the Giants are getting into with Winston, a 12-year veteran quarterback whose play […]
full_text: Jameis Winston | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh calls the team’s necessary offensive stylistic change, with Jameis Winston replacing Jaxson Dart at quarterback, a “lane change.” The man primarily responsible for implementing that lane change is offensive coordinator Matt Nagy . He knows what the Giants are getting into with Winston, a 12-year veteran quarterback whose play can swing wildly from positive to negative. In Big Blue View parlance, Winston might be considered a walking “Kwillie.” “We know who he is,” Nagy said. “We talked all training camp about protecting the football. There is a lot of that feast or famine with him. We’ve joked over time about the 30 touchdowns and 30 picks, but now here it is.” That is a reference to Winston’s confounding 2019 season with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. That year, Winston threw for an incredible 5,109 yards with 33 touchdowns. He also threw 30 interceptions. That made Winston the only quarterback in NFL history to go 30-30 in touchdown passes and interceptions. “Respecting that football and ball security is paramount, this type of team that we have. So, he knows that,” Nagy said of Winston. “And again, he’s as true of a pro as you’ll be around, preparation-wise and how he handles this. So, you just play his game, be who he is, and then we’ve got to help him as a staff, too.” “We know who he is.” — Matt Nagy on Jameis Winston ‘Ultimate trust’ in Winston The Giants know they can’t survive with the 11 of 27 for 111 yards and an interception performance Winston had Monday in relief of Dart becoming a regular thing. Nagy believes they can help Winston with a game plan tailored to the things that suit his skill set. “Probably the biggest thing is – one of the things with this offense when we first got started is we wanted to be able to be prepared to have multiple styles of offense,” Nagy said. “And so, if something like this does happen, it doesn’t put you in a hole where you just — it changes everything. Obviously, Jaxson (Dart) is a dual-threat quarterback. That’s one of his strengths. It’s what he does well. And so, when you lose that part of it and what he does well, that’s part of the playbook. That’s stating the obvious. “But at the same point in time, we look at it with Jameis that here’s a guy that’s played a lot of football games in his career. We have ultimate trust in him. And so, unlike the game when it happens on play seven, where you have most of your game designed around Jaxson, now we get a chance to design around Jameis’ strengths and what he does.” ‘Reps are huge’ Nagy was asked about the difficulty — for both coach and backup quarterback — of navigating a situation where the starter is injured so early in a game. “The first part is that there’s a part of the playbook that we do lose any way you look at it,” Nagy said. “And I’m sure this is for most teams, when you have the strength of your quarterback, a lot of that is directed towards what they do well. So, if there’s areas of his game that, when you lose him, you lose that part of the playbook. But it’s not a massive number to where you can’t run an offense. I want to be clear with that. “The other part of this, too, is your reps are so valuable throughout the week, and I think I said it last week to you all, but the walkthrough reps are huge. And we have our volume of plays is – there’s a lot of plays that we run throughout the week, and Jameis has to do it mentally. And so, Jaxson himself is trying to get timing down with some of these skill receivers, running backs, wideouts, tight ends, etc. Now you’re thrown into the mix seven plays in and running these plays that you didn’t run all week. You did mentally, but you didn’t timing-wise. There’s a lot involved there.” Nagy said the Giants did try to adapt some things on the fly. The issue there, though, becomes not running things the way they were practiced. “I’ll give you an example. If there’s a motion and a shift in a play, we either eliminated it or we used one motion, not two. That’s just an example,” Nagy said. “If there’s something on the play where we could make it easier for him [Winston] to play faster and have less decisions, we wanted to do that. So, you try to adapt in the game. But now, again, we get to have a full week of prep, and he gets to get out here and get throws on time, which helps.” As Nagy acknowledged, the quarterback run is not something that can be a regular part of the plan with Winston. There will also be some differences in the types of throws Winston prefers to what Dart is best at. “There might be a couple concepts where you’re able to do some different things to his strengths,” Nagy said. “For us as coaches, I think it’s very important that you know that Jameis knows what we do offensively. Thank God he’s been here for all the OTAs and training camp. So, calling a play, understanding why a play is in, where to go, his eyes going to where our eyes go, is good. “But then he also has his strengths on certain routes that he throws, and maybe he does it slightly better than Jaxson, maybe he doesn’t. But we need to make sure that we’re putting that stuff in to where Jameis feels comfortable, and that’s what I think we’re doing.” Will the Giants’ “lane change” land them in the slow lane or the fast lane? We will see what that looks like on Sunday vs. the Tennessee Titans.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Giants vs. Titans: How will New York handle Brian Daboll’s offense?
summary: The New York Giants are regrouping for a Week 3 matchup against the 0-2 Tennessee Titans. New York lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season, a brutal gut-punch. The Giants are 2.5-point favorites, with the Over/Under at 39.5 points. The Giants welcome back former head coach Brian Daboll. It is the Titans’ first road […]
full_text: Brian Daboll | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are regrouping for a Week 3 matchup against the 0-2 Tennessee Titans. New York lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season, a brutal gut-punch. The Giants are 2.5-point favorites, with the Over/Under at 39.5 points. The Giants welcome back former head coach Brian Daboll. It is the Titans’ first road game of the 2026 season. Tennessee is rebuilding in Robert Saleh’s first season as head coach, but does have its quarterback of the foreseeable future and a few young offensive weapons. Let’s look at how the Giants’ defense matches up with Tennessee’s offense. Brian Daboll’s offense Daboll took Carmen Bricillo, Shea Tierney, and Cade Knox to Nashville to coach under Saleh. Daboll inherited quarterback Cam Ward, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft. Ward looked much more comfortable in the Titans’ 24-20 last-second loss against the Philadelphia Eagles. Daboll’s squad mustered only 10 points in their Week 1 loss to the Jets. The Titans have used 11 personnel at a 71% rate through two games — as expected after signing Wan’Dale Robinson to a four-year, $70-million contract. Ward has operated under center at a 37% rate; under Daboll last season, Dart was under center only 20% of the time. The Titans’ offense has yet to eclipse 300 yards in a game this season. They’re 10 of 25 on third down ( 40% conversion rate ), and they have three touchdowns through two games; Ward has two touchdowns on the ground, and he threw a touchdown pass to Elic Ayomanor in Week 1. Ayomanor dropped a touchdown in Week 2, but the throw was off-target. Ward is 32 of 53 ( 61.5% ) through the air for 323 yards ( 6.2 YPA ) with just one touchdown and no interceptions. Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears split rushing work, but rookie Nicholas Singleton dressed after being a healthy scratch in Week 1. Pollard has rushed 21 times for 99 yards ( 4.7 YPC ) with six missed tackles forced and a 3.05 yards-after-contact number, while catching two passes for zero yards. Spears sprung a long catch in Week 2 and has secured four passes for 41 yards through two games. He averaged 5.3 yards per carry with just ten rushes for 53 yards, and an impressive 3.90 yards after contact. Tennessee’s receiving corps consists of three young receivers: Ayomanor, Chimere Dike, and first-round pick Carnell Tate. Robinson operates the slot, and Calvin Ridley is still a Titan. Ridley has played 62% of the snaps this season. Tennessee used more 12 personnel against the Eagles, leading to more Daniel Bellinger, who is the second tight end behind Gunnar Helm. Ayomanor leads the Titans in receiving yards; he’s caught three of six targets for 80 yards and one receiving touchdown. Tate has seen 11 targets and secured seven for 65 yards. Robinson has caught six of seven for 47 yards, and Helm has secured all six of his targets for 41 yards. The Titans’ offensive line has former Giants’ center Austin Schlottmann anchoring the unit; Pro Football Focus has graded him well in pass protection, but poorly in run blocking, which is consistent across the Titans’ front, who dealt with two solid defensive fronts with the Eagles and Jets. Dan Moore Jr. and JC Latham will have their hands full with the dangerous Giants’ pass rush on the edges, while Peter Skoronski and Fernando Carmona — the latter has surrendered four pressures on the season already — will be starting at guard for Bricillo. The Giants can win the matchup of the trenches. Giants’ game plan Dart wasn’t the only significant loss in Week 2. Brian Burns had his ankle rolled up on with six minutes left in the 28-6 game. The Giants will be without their star edge defender, which will force Dennard Wilson to change how he uses his personnel. Kayvon Thibodeaux is in for an increased role without Burns. He’s played 59 snaps so far this season to Burns’ 91 and Abdul Carter’s 108. Chauncey Golston may receive more snaps on the edge, as well as Arvell Reese in certain packages. Tae Banks remains questionable for the game; if he can not dress, Colton Hood will receive the spot opposite Greg Newsome II. The Giants should dress Jason Pinnock in this game as insurance behind Tyler Nubin, who was attacked by McVay’s offense in Week 2. The Giants faced a Rams team that used 13 personnel on over half of their snaps — that won’t be the case against Brian Daboll’s offense. Giants’ nickel cornerback, Dru Phillips, played on just 48% of snaps against the Rams, after playing on in 83% against Dallas. Expect to see less base personnel and more nickel packages against a Titans team that has run 11 personnel at a 71% rate. Daboll has used 12 personnel at an 18% rate. The 17% blitz rate from Week 2 is going to increase in Week 3. Cam Ward has been blitzed at a 31% rate overall and a 38% rate on third down. I expect to see more five-man rushes from the Giants. Wilson should dictate via aggression against the young quarterback. There is an option to expand Reese’s role as a blitzer, too. Reese has 11 pass rush snaps this season; possible use of him on the edge in certain situations versus 11 personnel could be something for the Giants to explore. New York could use a lot of Cover-3, middle-of-the-field-closed with both strong/weak-side buzz rotation against 3×1 sets. Final thoughts I expect the Giants, although injured, will handle business against the Titans. I believe we’ve seen the worst of Jameis Winston, and he’ll help stabilize the offense, which will likely be in 12 and 22 personnel often. I also expect Wilson to have more freedom and comfort to get creative against Ward and Daboll’s offense. I have the Giants winning, 20-13.
author: Nick Falato

title: Giants vs. Titans: Can the Giants’ offense rebound on a short week?
summary: It was a long flight home to the Meadowlands for the New York Giants after their Monday nightmare against the Los Angeles Rams. That flight turned into a long and trying Tuesday as the Giants learned that starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the remainder of the season. In doing so, the keys to […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback Jameis Winston throws a pass. | Getty Images It was a long flight home to the Meadowlands for the New York Giants after their Monday nightmare against the Los Angeles Rams. That flight turned into a long and trying Tuesday as the Giants learned that starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the remainder of the season. In doing so, the keys to the Giants’ offense were passed to backup quarterback Jameis Winston . Winston’s first test will come against the Tennessee Titans and a collection of former faces. This game had been circled for a while, largely because of all the storylines surrounding it. Brian Daboll , cornerback Cor’Dale Flott , wide receiver Wan’Dale Robinson , center Austin Schlottman , and tight end Daniel Bellinger are all familiar familiar with Winston, as well as many of their offensive linemen, tight ends, and running backs. Robert Saleh will be calling the Titans’ defense, but he has plenty of resources from whom he can seek insight. The Titans were expected to be a relatively easy win after the Giants steamrolled the Dallas Cowboys. Now, the Giants are only slim favorites at home. How will the offense respond in Winston’s first test? Jameis Winston at QB The Giants had to adapt to a new reality early on in their loss to the Rams, when Dart was lost for the game to a knee injury. It didn’t go well and Winston appeared rattled when he came on the field for the Giants against the Rams. While his job as the veteran backup is to be a steady presence in troubled times, he did not appear comfortable at all on Monday night. Winston appeared to distrust his protection, not see the defense well, nor throw the ball well. For as bad as Winston looked after coming onto the field following Dart’s injury, there is the silver lining that the Titans can’t be sure just what the Giants’ offense will look like with a pure pocket passer under center. They can be sure that Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely will still be centerpieces, but they can’t know just what form the offense will take. Winston is a different type of quarterback from Dart. The two share charisma and competitiveness, as well as a baseball background and impressive arm talent, however they’re very different athletes. That’s going to change how the Giants structure and call their offense. The quarterback run game that kept defenses honest is gone, as is the threat of a scramble once things break down. However, Winston is also a much more experienced quarterback who has seen just about every type of defense the NFL has to offer, and is willing to attack them all. That can get him into trouble, but it can also be an asset if the Giants embrace it. It’s worth remembering that the Winston-led Giants never trailed in regulation against the Lions and he was solid against the Green Bay Packers, and that was with a more flawed coaching staff and a worse offensive roster. Winston has the arm strength to push the ball down the field and the Giants have enough pieces to take advantage of mistakes in coverage when they happen — assuming Winston can control his characteristic aggression long enough for them to manifest. The possibility of explosive passing plays could also loosen things up for the run game, which we know John Harbaugh wants to rely upon. The Giants have very limited time in which to shift gears from Dart to Winston, but the fact that the Titans can’t know exactly what the Giants will do is an advantage they should seize. How will the Titans defend Jameis? The Giants aren’t the only ones who have to shift gears after the injury to Dart. The Titans now have a very different quarterback to defend, with different challenges. Conventional wisdom suggests that the Titans will focus on Harbaugh and Greg Roman’s desire to be a run-first team. It would follow that they would focus on stacking the box and force Winston to beat them through the air. However, Saleh is (yet another) member of the Fangio tree. He prefers to rotate between Cover 4 and Cover 3 looks, and San Francisco ran among the highest rates of those coverages in the NFL. Saleh’s defense was also among the League leaders in nickel usage. The Titans obviously don’t have the same defensive personnel as the 49er’s, nor do they have anything like San Francisco’s offense. However, Saleh’s overall philosophy has been pretty consistent over the years. The Fangio style of defense is designed to both prevent explosive plays and confuse quarterbacks with late rotations. The Titans won’t have to worry about the Giants’ quarterback run game with Winston under center, nor will they have to pay particular attention to spying a mobile quarterback. The Giants should be alert to the possibility that rather than try to go against their defensive philosophy to sell out to defend the run, they’ll instead try to force Jameis Winston to be patient and frustrate him. Winston has a bad history of throwing the ball to the team wearing the wrong color jerseys, and safety Amani Hooker intercepted Jalen Hurts twice last week (nearly returning one for a touchdown). The Giants could look to be a more explosive passing offense with Winston, moving away from the surgical attack they used with Dart to emphasize Winston’s arm strength and aggressiveness. Playing coverage would keep a lid on the Giants’ offense and potentially take away Winston’s biggest asset, while also providing the defense with opportunities to take the ball away. Inside, the Titans would be counting on defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to both pressure Winston into making a mistake as well as disrupting runs behind the line of scrimmage. Their linebackers played relatively well against the Philadelphia Eagles last week, and could frustrate the Giants’ underneath passing game. Attacking Saleh’s defense How the Giants attack the Titans’ defense will likely be decided over the first drive or two and there will likely be a “feeling out” period for both of these teams. The Giants are shifting gears in an offense that’s still new. There’s little tape on the Giants’ offense and basically none on the Giants’ offense with Winston. On the flip side, the Titans are only playing their third game in a new defense. While Saleh’s general scheme and philosophy, there’s still only limited tape on how it’s being applied to the Titans’ roster. The easy answer is that the Giants should counter-punch however the Titans opt to defend them. If the Titans try to lock down the run, the Giants should take the dare to beat them through the air. Conversely, if the Titans play coverage, the Giants should play to their running strengths and use an intermediate passing attack to supplement the run and attack the voids underneath the deep coverage zones. That may be frustrating for Winston, but keeping the offense moving would (hopefully) mitigate that until opportunities for explosive plays open up. The Giants’ offense wants to be based on running the ball, however they do have an unconventionally built roster. The Giants are heavy on running backs and tight ends, but light on receivers. If the Giants play a more conventional passing offense, they’ll be able to use their personnel to disguise their intentions. Isaiah Likely and Theo Johnson are both athletic tight ends who can stress the seams of Saleh’s Cover 3 shells, while all of the Giants’ running backs are able to catch the ball. Likewise, Nabers, Darnell Mooney , and Likely are all able to pick up yards after catch on screens or quick passes to the flats. The Giants’ lives were made significantly more difficult on offense after the injury to Dart. That, however, doesn’t mean that it’s time to pack it in. They still have weapons and pieces that can allow them to continue to win. The job of Harbaugh, his coaching staff, and Winston is now to steady the ship and rally the team with a win at home.

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as Jameis Winston gets set to take the helm for the Giants this weekend. John Harbaugh keeps Giants believing in team meeting | New York Daily News Safety Jevon Holland said the meeting “was great” from the players’ perspective and that Harbaugh had set the tone before the season by putting the message “win and learn” on a whiteboard before their first game of the season against the Dallas Cowboys.. “He does a great job of extracting a lesson out of whatever the situation is,” Holland said at his locker. “Whether it’s a win, a loss. But now the Giants’ offense is in the hands of Winston, who signed a two-year, $13 million extension on Sept. 6. Winston is comfortable operating out of the shotgun, which offensive coordinator Matt Nagy — with his ties to Kansas City and Andy Reid — can accommodate. This is where Nabers enters the fray. He has been slow to launch through two games, which is understandable given his recovery from a torn ACL. But elite receivers can make backup QBs look like starters. The Giants will need Nabers to have that effect. And Winston did provide a spark last season, so perhaps he finds that groove again. How Jameis Winston embraces leading Giants to Ws, not just eating them | The Record Jameis Winston has never lost confidence in the quarterback he believed he could be. The dream of being one of the best in the NFL and one day winning a Super Bowl has been deferred for a while now, and Winston accepted his role with the New York Giants for what it was. Giants would be foolish to make desperate QB trade in wake of Jaxson Dart injury | The Athletic Draft picks are a precious commodity, especially for a Giants team that is still building. They’re already without their fourth- and seventh-round picks in next year’s draft as a result of previous trades, although they have an additional sixth-rounder from the Daniel Faalele trade with the Jaguars in August. None of those options should excite fans. And that’s why losing a starting quarterback is such a devastating blow. There isn’t a surplus of quality quarterbacks available, especially during the season. The time to fortify the roster is during the offseason. The Giants did that by showing their belief in Winston with the extension. Now is the time to see it through, not get desperate and burn a valuable draft pick. Jaxson Dart’s injury explained: Could he return this year? We asked a doctor | NJ.com “I’ve seen a few people come back around four months, so it’s possible but unlikely,” Dr. Clint Soppe, an orthopedic surgeon at Cedars-Sinai Orthopedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, regarding Dart playing in the postseason. “It depends on the type of tear and exactly what’s going on…Most MCL tears, if they’re just isolated tears, those can be treated without surgery, and they heal on their own. But then I think when they got the MRI and found out there’s a more significant meniscus tear, that’s when everything changed.” Darius Slayton was ‘ not really ’ surprised by New York Giants release | USAToday.com “I mean kind of just based on the way camp was going and kind of the situation that they had over there it wasn’t really that much of a surprise to me but you know ultimately it is what it is that led to me being here today and I’m happy about it,” said Slayton. “I definitely feel healthy and I feel like you know I’m kind of back.” From Big Blue View Jaxson Dart placed on IR; 2 other Giants’ stars miss practice Giants will ride with Jameis Winston at quarterback, as they should Life after Jaxson Dart: How can the NY Giants adapt to losing their QB? title: Brian Daboll on Jaxson Dart: He’ll be back ‘stronger than ever’
summary: The New York Giants suffered a “gut punch”, to quote John Harbaugh, when starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the 2026 season to a knee injury. It’s a big deal for Harbaugh. Not only is Dart his starting quarterback and a galvanizing captain, Dart’s presence — his upside, passion for football, and charisma — […]
full_text: ﻿Former New York Giants head coach Brian Daboll with the Tennessee Titans | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants suffered a “gut punch”, to quote John Harbaugh, when starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the 2026 season to a knee injury. It’s a big deal for Harbaugh. Not only is Dart his starting quarterback and a galvanizing captain, Dart’s presence — his upside, passion for football, and charisma — was one of the biggest reasons Harbaugh agreed to be to be the Giants’ new head coach. But in many ways, Dart was the parting gift from Harbaugh’s predecessor. That’s because while Dart may be The Guy for Harbaugh and the Giants, he was drafted by the man against whom his team will be playing this week. Former Giants head coach Brian Daboll is now the Tennessee Titans offensive coordinator, but he was the one pounding the table for Dart in the lead-up to the 2025 NFL Draft. Daboll is, obviously, upset that Dart is lost for the year. Dart was “his guy” during the draft process and he was probably the most excited person in the Giants’ organization to move up and draft Dart at 25th overall. “It’s always tough. I have a very good relationship with him,” Daboll said on Thursday. “Obviously he’s devastated with what happened. Prayers to him, his family, great people.” Since the 2025 draft, we’ve learned that Daboll was the driving force behind the Giants drafting Jaxson Dart, and Daboll was probably Dart’s biggest fan. “You guys are convicted in him. You believe in him. We did the process,” general manager Joe Schoen said as the Giants consummated the trade up for Dart . “He checked all the boxes. Let’s f—— roll the dice, roll the dice.” “Good goin’ buddy!” Schoen exclaimed, grabbing Daboll’s hand in a big handshake. Brian Daboll loves aggressive quarterbacks and big personalities, and Dart has both. We saw his affection for Dart in real time over the summer, and again as Dart took his first snaps against the Los Angeles Chargers. Nobody expected the Giants to win that game, let alone with a rookie quarterback in his first start. Yet Daboll’s faith in Dart was vindicated with the Giants’ first win of the season. Roughly year later, Daboll was new team was preparing to face the quarterback for whom he lobbied. At least up until Monday night, when an injury changed the entire complexion of this game. “We’re in a competitive industry, but we’re in a human industry too,” Daboll said. “And you build a lot of good relationships wherever you’re at with players, with coaches, staff members. And it was a tough one to see.” Other than perhaps Lane Kiffin, there was nobody outside the Giants organization (and his own family) for whom the news was harder. “I got a lot of respect for him, a lot of love for him,” Daboll finished. “And I know he’ll come back stronger than ever.” Giants fans may be done with Daboll, and he’s now working to add insult to injury for Dart and his teammates, but on this they agree on Dart himself.

title: NY Giants will ride with Jameis Winston at quarterback, as they should
summary: In the hours since learning that Jaxson Dart will miss the rest of the season with a knee injury, New York Giants fans have named just about every quarterback under the sun as a potential replacement. From JJ McCarthy to Tom Brady, fans have thrown out the name of just about every quarterback they could […]
full_text: Jameis Winston | Getty Images In the hours since learning that Jaxson Dart will miss the rest of the season with a knee injury, New York Giants fans have named just about every quarterback under the sun as a potential replacement. From JJ McCarthy to Tom Brady, fans have thrown out the name of just about every quarterback they could think of as a guy the Giants should go get. There are reports that the Giants could be hoping to sign veteran backup Jimmy Garoppolo . Regardless of all of that speculation, and whether or not they sign Garoppolo or someone like everybody’s favorite emergency third quarterback — Josh Johnson — there is a central truth: Jameis Winston is now the Giants’ starting quarterback. That is going to be the case on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. Unless he gets injured or unexpectedly proves so ineffective that the Giants have no choice but to trade for someone else to be fair to the rest of the locker room, Winston is probably the quarterback for the next 15 games. The Giants have confidence in Winston. “The team loves Jameis. We voted him captain, so I think that says plenty,” safety Jevon Holland told me on Wednesday. “Jameis is going to do a phenomenal job when he steps in there. He’s been leading us in multiple ways already, so it’s not uncommon. It’s not like a new voice or anything like that, so I think it will fit swimmingly.” Winston had a ragged performance on Monday in relief of Dart, going just 11 of 27 for 111 yards and an interception. He was well off-target on a number of throws. “I have to execute better and I am going to execute better,” Winston said on Wednesday. The Giants’ offense, of course, has been built around Dart’s strengths, not Winston’s. That will change beginning this week against the Titans. “A big part of it is building a game plan now for Jameis. He’ll be the starter. So, build the game plan for Jameis to suit his skill set,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “The game plan this last week was built for Jaxson, obviously. So, this will be an opportunity to do that, and that’s exactly what we’ll do. We’ll build around all the things that he does well that are in the offense, which is – there’s plenty in the offense. And then, of course, how to attack Tennessee and their defense and what they do.” Dart and Winston are, of course, vastly different quarterbacks. The designed quarterback run game and scrambling ability are in Dart’s arsenal. They are not in Winston’s. The types of passes the two quarterbacks might prefer could also differ. Harbaugh said the Giants do not have to build an entirely new offense. “I don’t think it’s too big, because all this stuff is in the offense,” Harbaugh said. “All those plays are plays that we have, that we’ve been practicing and running. It’s just kind of more like a shift maybe over a little bit as opposed to a new – maybe a lane change as opposed to changing direction or anything like that, more of a lane change.” Of course, the Giants need more than just two quarterbacks — Winston and Jake Haener — on the roster. There are, though, varying levels of what the Giants could do. I am going to put them in three buckets. Practice squad QBs/free agents Garoppolo is, of course, a free agent. He is the most accomplished of the players the Giants could bring in, and would be a viable short-term starting option once up to speed if Winston were hurt or playing poorly. Other free agent possibilities: Guys who are currently available include: Bailey Zappe Jake Browning Nick Mullens Browning played pretty well for the Bengals in 2023, pretty badly for the Bengals in 2025. Practice squad possibilities: Will Levis — New York Jets Joe Milton — Dallas Cowboys Josh Johnson — Bengals Hendon Hooker — Titans Max Brosmer — Vikiongs Milton is, of course, the candidate du jour in the fan base. The 26-year-old has completed 37 of 53 passes (69.8%) for 424 yards, with two touchdowns and two interceptions in five games over two seasons for the New England Patriots and Cowboys. Milton would, of course, be an upside The problem there is that he is a young player who a) hasn’t been tested in critical situations and b) would likely take longer than a more experienced quarterback to assimilate into the Giants’ system. That’s a problem in the middle of the season when there isn’t a lot of time for coaches to spend teaching him the offense. Trades J.J. McCarthy (Vikings), Justin Fields (Kansas City Chiefs), Mac Jones (San Francisco 49ers), Mitchell Trubisky (Titans) are among the names you hear bandied about in proposed trades. A few points about trades. Why would anyone deal a quarterback now? In two weeks, we have seen Dart, Caleb Williams (and Tyler Bagent), Jayden Daniels, and Kyler Murray get hurt. Michael Penix is making his season-debut Thursday night. Why would any team that believes it has even a small chance to make the playoffs deal quarterback depth now? To be honest, until any team knows it is out of the race that is GM malpractice at the rate quarterbacks are getting injured. Why would the Giants surrender draft capital? Please don’t tell me you think trading Kayvon Thibodeaux for someone like Fields is a smart move. To get a quarterback via trade, the Giants would have to surrender draft capital. Why would they be willing to do that? They are still building for the future, and the plan would still be to have Dart lead that future. What sense does it make to trade away draft capital that could help Dart, and the team as a whole, in the future to chase one or two more victories now? The best course, in my view, is to ride with Winston. He received a two-year, $13 million extension because the franchise believes in him. So, now they need to prove it by not making a panic move and selling out future help for possible short-term satisfaction. Cull the practice squads and free agency for the best help you can get. If this season goes off the rails because of quarterback play, so be it. A word about J.J. McCarthy When it comes to trading for a quarterback, the 23-year-old McCarthy is the hot name. Reality is this: The Giants’ organization passed on McCarthy in the 2024 NFL Draft, likely because it didn’t believe McCarthy would succeed in New York. GM Joe Schoen and the front office are not going to be advocating for a McCarthy trade now. The only way it even gets considered is if Harbaugh loves McCarthy and bangs the table for one. The only way Harbaugh does that is if he believes McCarthy has more upside than Dart. Off what we have seen from both of them, that idea is ludicrous. The nuclear option I keep seeing the opinion that if the Giants’ season turns into a train wreck, and they end up with the opportunity to draft Arch Manning, Dante Moore, Trinidad Chambliss or another top 10-worthy quarterback they should do it. My view is that idea is nonsense. One knee injury and two games missed because of a concussion doesn’t mean it is time to give up on the idea that Dart can and will be a top-tier NFL quarterback. Drafting over Dart, and starting over, is foolishness. What I could sign off on is the idea of drafting a young player in the middle rounds and trying to develop him as a viable backup. That doesn’t always work, but investing a fourth- or fifth-round pick is not that big of a gamble. I don’t know who the first one to point this out was, but I did see it online and it is correct. Matthew Stafford, who is heading to the Hall of Fame, was limited by injuries to just 13 games over his first two seasons. That was way back in 2009 and 2010, and he’s done OK since then. What you do if you have a top 10, or especially a top 5, pick, is maximize it. You help Dart. If you are in position to select the best player in the class, Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith, you do that. Otherwise, you package picks to move down and collect as much talent as you can over the first three or four rounds of a draft that is said to be dripping with talent.

title: NFL Week 3 picks, predictions: Can Giants win without Jaxson Dart?
summary: The season has changed for the New York Giants with the loss of Jaxson Dart. Can they begin version 2.0 of their 2026 season with a victory? See how Big Blue View writers answered that question, and how they picked all of the Week 3 NFL action below. Chris Pflum This is a game the […]
full_text: Jameis Winston handing the ball to Cam Skattebo. | Getty Images The season has changed for the New York Giants with the loss of Jaxson Dart. Can they begin version 2.0 of their 2026 season with a victory? See how Big Blue View writers answered that question, and how they picked all of the Week 3 NFL action below. Chris Pflum This is a game the Giants should win. Or at least they should if Jameis Winston is worth the money he got in his extension, and the coaching staff is as good as we think. But there’s a lot of unknowns that are giving me pause. How healthy are Andrew Thomas, Malik Nabers, and Deonte Banks? Can Winston rally the team back from the gut punch of losing Dart in a short week? How quickly can the coaching staff shift gears to reorient the scheme for Winston’s skill set? On the flip side, are the Titans better than we thought they were? Or are the Eagles worse? Ultimately, I’m sticking with my pre-season pick of the Giants this week. But now I’m leaning on the Giants’ experienced coaching staff. John Harbaugh and Matt Nagy have been here before, just last year. Meanwhile, Brian Callahan and Dennard Wilson know Cam Ward better than anyone in the NFL. I’m going to trust that leadership to see the Giants through this week while they figure out their way forward. I suspect this is going to be a sloppy game, and I don’t feel great about the Giants, but I’m sticking with my pick. Pick: Giants Tony DelGenio It’s anybody’s guess how the Giants will respond to the loss of Jaxson Dart for the season. If Monday night was any indication, we’ve got a problem, but in-game adjustments when playing one of the best teams in the NFL isn’t a fair test. We do have two examples from 2025, when Dart missed games against Green Bay and Detroit after Dart was sidelined with a concussion. Jameis Winston played well enough for the Giants to win both games, but the defense and possibly a bad pass route by Jalin Hyatt ruined any chance for a win. The question is whether this time, knowing Dart is gone for the season, John Harbaugh and the assistant coaches will be able to sufficiently motivate the team to carry on and take tangible steps toward contention in 2028. This is a unique game because so many ex-Giants are playing or coaching for Tennessee. Whether this gives one team an advantage or not, I don’t know. What I do know is that Cam Ward is still trying to figure things out, that he was greatly affected by pressure against the Eagles (though not against the Jets the previous week), and that he has mostly been throwing short passes. Unfortunately without Brian Burns, pressure is going to have to come from other places. I’d love to see Dennard Wilson get creative with stunts, simulated pressures, etc., to try to keep Ward off balance. Most likely, Brian Daboll will lean on the run game with Tony Pollard, who has four consecutive 1,000 yards seasons, the last two as a Titan. When the Giants are on offense, the Titans are stout up front with Jeffery Simmons and John Franklin-Myers in the middle and Jermaine Johnson and Jacob Martin on the edge, all of whom have more pressures than any Giant. To me, the game will hinge on whether the Giants’ OL can bounce back from their dismal showing in Los Angeles and creates lanes for Cam Skattebo and time for Winston. Without Dart, this game is more a coin flip than it originally seemed, but I’ll guess that the troops rally and come away with a win. Pick: Giants James Hickey Rahm Emanuel famously said, “You never want a serious crisis to go to waste. And what I mean by that is it’s an opportunity to do things that you think you could not do before.” Over the last decade plus for the New York Football Giants, there seems to be just one crisis after another. The next three weeks present opportunities. The first is Jameis Winston, the lovable teammate and media personality who must now take over at quarterback. Winston needs to stay away from the big mistake. The 12-year veteran should only be expected to be a game manager who gives the Giants a chance to win. But the biggest burden— and honestly the most disappointing part of the season so far— falls on the defensive line and more specifically the edge rushers. Quite simply, they are paid to sack the quarterback and Abdul Carter, Brian Burns and Kayvon Thibodeaux have not made enough of an impact to live up to their buildup the last two years. Tennessee has a lot of familiar faces coming back to MetLife, led by Brian Daboll, who undoubtedly will be extra motivated to win this week. But a young team playing its first game on the road looking for its first win? Look for the Giants to get a lead early and run the ball effectively as they did in their opening week matchup against Dallas. Pick: Giants 24, Titans 10 David Hartman How quickly things can change in the NFL. For the Giants, the euphoria of a huge Week 1 win over the rival Cowboys in prime time quickly gave way to the stomach punch of not only losing to the Rams on Monday night in Week 2, but more importantly losing Jaxson Dart to a knee injury for the remainder of the regular season. It’s been a tough week for the Giants and their fans. Why can’t we have nice things? Talk about a roller coaster… Now the team – players, coaches, and the rest – must quickly regroup, and the good news is that a home date with the Titans, albeit on a short week, is a fairly soft landing. Tennessee (0-2) gave the Eagles all they wanted last week at home, before predictably losing late, so they aren’t a total pushover. Still, this is a game New York should win, even without Dart, Brian Burns, Paulson Adeebo, and whoever else can’t suit up. I think John Harbaugh will have his team fired up and ready to play, but will that be enough? Jameis Winston is going to need to play better (and smarter) than he did on Monday night, and hopefully a week of practicing with the 1’s will help. We’ve seen him play well in the past. As for the Titans, Brian Daboll’s offense hasn’t been great and doesn’t have personnel that should scare Big Blue. Look for Cam Ward to make more mistakes than Winston. The Giants’ defense needs to control this game, and I think they will, even without Burns. I’ll take the G-Men to take care of business at home. For at least one week, the emotional pendulum will swing back. Pick: Giants Valentine’s View Winning football games got a lot more difficult for the Giants this week with the news about Dart. How much more difficult? Well, perhaps one way to conceptualize it is to look at the point spread. The Giants were 6.5-point favorites as of Monday morning. Now, they are 2.5-point favorites . That is a massive swing in the betting world. Throw in the reality that it appears edge defender Brian Burns won’t play Sunday, and that complicates matters even more for the Giants. Still, I think this is a game where the Giants play with emotion and with determination to prove that their season is not lost. I think this is a game where the guiding hand of John Harbaugh should have a steadying impact. I also think the Giants are fortunate to be playing an 0-2 team that isn’t very good, even if the Titans did push the Philadelphia Eagles to the final minute in Week 2. I’m concerned about a lot of things with this Giants team. The quarterback play. The lack of explosive plays on offense. The defense as a whole, especially if the pass rush doesn’t impact games. I think, though, that they have enough to win on Sunday. Pick: Giants Giants fans: Make your pick in the SB Nation app! title: Fantasy Football 2026: Week 3 preview — Start/sit and more
summary: Welcome to Week 3! Week 2 saw a return to normalcy, in terms of scoring. After a whopping 90 offensive TDs were tallied in an insane Week 1, that number dropped by about a third, to 61 in Week 2. Fantasy scores came crashing down as a result. And now with three high-end starting quarterbacks […]
full_text: ARSB! | Getty Images Welcome to Week 3! Week 2 saw a return to normalcy, in terms of scoring. After a whopping 90 offensive TDs were tallied in an insane Week 1, that number dropped by about a third, to 61 in Week 2. Fantasy scores came crashing down as a result. And now with three high-end starting quarterbacks going down last week (Jayden Daniels, Caleb Williams, and Jaxson Dart), plus a slew of other injuries, fantasy managers are facing challenges up and down their lineups. If you’re new to fantasy football, welcome to paradise. Speaking of paradise, I’m still away on vacation so you’re getting another abbreviated column this week. Sorry about that. But if you could see where I’m sitting while I’m writing this…well…Sorry about that too. Let’s just say it beats the views at home. Stats of the Week : The Bears scored 56 fewer points in Week 2 than they did in Week 1. If I had a research and stats department at my disposal, they’d tell me if that’s the biggest week-to-week scoring drop in NFL history. It probably isn’t, but it’s huge. The Colts have lost nine straight games, and Daniel Jones is now 1-16 as a starter in primetime. The Seahawks have won 12 straight games. Patrick Mahomes has never lost a regular season game in OT (8-0). The Falcons are one of four teams since the merger with zero red zone possessions in their first two games of a season. Michael Penix, Jr. to the rescue? I have my doubts. OK, Week 3, here we go! Bye Weeks: NONE Week 3 Rides, Fades and Sleepers For those who are familiar with this column, you know the drill. For everyone else: The Rides, Fades, and Sleepers is an analysis of players that I think are primed for an especially strong or poor performance, often as compared to consensus expectations. This isn’t a straight-up Start/Sit exercise. As a general rule, start your studs. I’ll rarely list the most obvious names at a position as “Rides” because those players are almost always expected to have strong performances. You don’t need me or anyone else telling you to start Amon-Ra St. Brown . While this analysis is intended for season-long play, it works for DFS formats too. Half PPR scoring and Expert Consensus Rankings (ECR) are used for the column. Each week, I’m picking a Ride, Fade ,and Sleeper of the Week . The rules: The Ride of the Week can’t be a truly elite option, the Fade can’t be someone who nobody is starting anyway, and the Sleeper must be an actual sleeper, from down in the rankings. This week, since the column is short, I’m doing two of each. Last week, my Rides, Fades, and Sleepers did pretty well, for the most part. Injuries wrecked a few of my Ride calls, but what can you do? You can check my work here . And you can see my Week 3 Waiver Wire column here. Rides of the Week: Justin Herbert (@BUF). If you’ve been riding with Herbert as your QB1, there’s a good chance you’re 0-2. He’s been a highly disappointing player on the league’s most disappointing team through two weeks. And now he’s got to head to Buffalo to face one of the AFC’s power teams. Maybe leaving home will help. This is a contrarian pick, but lost in Josh Allen’s heroics is how vulnerable Buffalo’s defense has been – or at least, how much pressure has been put on them by Allen’s massive scoring output. They’ve allowed the second most TD passes (six), third most passing yards, and fifth most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to opposing QBs, and they don’t have an INT. It’s now or never for Herbert and Co. He’s ranked outside the Top-12 quarterbacks this week and I think he’s going to come through with a QB1 finish in Buffalo. Devonta Smith (@CHI).Chicago’s defense played much better in Week 2, but bad weather and a backup QB on the other side had a lot to do with it. Smith and Jalen Hurts were very much on the same page against Washington last week, and now they get another suspect secondary to attack. With Dallas Goedert out, and Saquon Barkley at less than 100%, Smith should be even more of a volume hog and red zone threat. He’s a smash start this week. Fades of the Week: Terry McLaurin (vs. SEA). Through two weeks, Settle’s suffocating defense has allowed just 126 yards to opposing wideouts, and, needless to say, the fewest FPPG. Marcus Mariota is competent, but no matter how you slice it, this is a bad spot for McLaurin, who’s off to another slow start. He’s likely to remain stuck in the mud for at least one more week. Baker Mayfield (vs. MIN). Mayfield – the QB5 two seasons ago — was a sneaky pick this season as a low-end QB1, high-end QB2. Well, after the Chargers, the Bucs are the second biggest disappointment through two weeks. Losing to Deshaun Watson and the Browns at home? YIKES. If you’re platooning Mayfield with someone else in a 1-QB league, this is probably a good week to go with the other end of the platoon. The Vikings have allowed just two TD passes through two weeks, are great at getting after the QB and forcing turnovers, and just held the Bears to three points. I’m sure Baker is smarting after losing to the team that drafted and then gave up on him, but he and the 0-2 Bucs are struggling, and I don’t like this spot for righting the ship. Sleepers of the Week: Geno Smith (@DET) and Sam Darnold / Drew Lock (@WAS). OK, laugh all you want about Lock/Smith. But hear me out. If you’re in a Superflex format, and you just lost one of your QBs to injury, here are two teams with QB matchups that should make you salivate. The Commanders have been dreadful against opposing QBs for much of this decade and so far, 2026 is more of the same. They’ve allowed the most TD passers (seven) and second most FPPG to the position. Only one defense has allowed more FPPG to opposing quarterback. Guess who that is? Yup, it’s the toothless Lions’ defense, and in a game where the Jets will almost surely be playing catch up, Geno should have some success. A lot of lower-end QBs are playing poorly – I’m not even listing guys like Aaron Rodgers or Cam Ward as fades at this point. You could do a lot worse than these two as your second QB, or even your QB1 if you’re really in a bind. Other Rides and Sleepers : Going beyond the obvious elite options at each position (and for the record, Patrick Mahomes has returned to elite option status and especially this week at Miami), here are a few more Rides for me this week: QB: B. Purdy (vs. ARI), J. Goff (vs. NYG), Jor. Love (vs. ATL), and if you need more sleepers beyond the two I already mentioned, B. Young (@CLE), and C.J. Stroud (@IND, especially if Nico Collins returns). Young is probably no longer a sleeper after his torrid start. Desperate? What’s more fun than the J. Winston (vs. TEN) experience? D. Watson (vs. CAR) needs at least one more good week before I can even consider typing his name as a sleeper. I should install software that prohibits such a thing. RB: A. Jeanty (@NO), O. Hampton (@BUF), D. Montgomery (@IND, and yes, I’m nervous about him too but HOU has to have this game and I think he’s finding the end zone at least once this week), C. Skattebo (vs. TEN), C. Hubbard (@CLE, and especially with J. Brooks headed to IR), and J. Warren (vs. CIN). If you need to dig deep, K. Monangai (vs. PHI), T. Pollard (@NYG), and K. Black (vs. ARI). WR: C. Olave (vs. LV), G. Wilson (@DET), C. Watson (vs. ATL), J. Waddle (vs. LAR), R. Rice (vs. MIA), Z. Flowers (@DAL, if he plays), and J. Coker (@CLE). If you need to go deep, D. Samuel, Sr. (vs. ARI), A. Mitchell (@DET), D. Wicks (@CHI), D. Boston (vs. CAR), and R. Bateman (@DAL). TE: T. Kraft (vs. ATL), T. Kelce (@MIA), G. Kittle (vs. ARI), and D. Schultz (@IND), and if you need someone from down in the rankings, J. Ferguson (v. BAL), O. Gadsden II (@BUF), A.J. Barner (@WAS), and T. Ferguson (@DEN). Other Fades (limited to players who a lot of people might consider starting this week): QB: J. Burrow (@PIT – I’m not expecting anyone to sit him, but the Steelers have allowed the fewest FPPG to opposing QBs through two games, and just one TD pass, and this game…

summary: The Jets fell to 1-1 in Week 2 as the Green Bay Packers rallied from 10 points down in the fourth quarter to force overtime. The Packers were able to outplay the Jets in all three phases of the game in the final 10 minutes of regulation and overtime. Blame for the loss does not […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) carries the ball against the New York Jets during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Jets fell to 1-1 in Week 2 as the Green Bay Packers rallied from 10 points down in the fourth quarter to force overtime. The Packers were able to outplay the Jets in all three phases of the game in the final 10 minutes of regulation and overtime. Blame for the loss does not entirely fall on the Jets’ defense. In fact, Green Bay’s tying field goal that forced overtime was set up by a long punt return that immediately put the Packers into field goal range. The Jets’ defense did well to hold up and force a field goal. The unit also stood up after the Jets were stopped on a fourth down near midfield near the end of regulation. So this video should not be viewed as an overall condemnation of the game the defense played. But in case you were interested in the plays the Packers executed down the stretch against the Jets defense to win it, here is a video breakdown I produced.

title: Eagles-Bears Film Preview: Vic Fangio vs. Ben Johnson
summary: The Bears’ first two games could hardly have looked more different. They scored 59 points and ran all over the Panthers, then scored three points in a rain-soaked loss to the Vikings. The quarterback situation adds another layer of uncertainty, so this preview is tough to write! Caleb Williams has a hamstring injury, Tyson Bagent […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - AUGUST 28: Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio looks on during the pre season game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Cincinnati Bengals on August 28th, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Bears’ first two games could hardly have looked more different. They scored 59 points and ran all over the Panthers, then scored three points in a rain-soaked loss to the Vikings. The quarterback situation adds another layer of uncertainty, so this preview is tough to write! Caleb Williams has a hamstring injury, Tyson Bagent is in concussion protocol, so Case Keenum took the first-team practice reps on Wednesday. I’m going to assume Keenum is starting, so I won’t talk much about quarterback in this one. The Bears ran for 281 yards against the Eagles last November, and Ben Johnson has built another offense that can make life very difficult if the run game gets going. Fangio and his defense will remember that afternoon. Pass Game Williams is special. He’s not consistently good, but his highs are special. I know that is hardly a groundbreaking statement, but it matters when evaluating the Bears because he can make a well-defended play look badly defended in about two seconds. He is outstanding on the move, keeps looking downfield while escaping pressure and has the arm to find a receiver long after the original concept should have ended. The Panthers game showed the frightening version of this offense. The Vikings game showed the other side. Flores was causing problems before Williams got hurt. Minnesota constantly threatened pressure, disrupted the timing of the passing game, and forced the Bears into uncomfortable downs. Williams can evade a free rusher better than almost anyone, but that does not mean the offense can live indefinitely with defenders arriving before its intermediate routes develop. If he plays on Monday, the hamstring also raises an obvious question about how freely he can escape. If he does not, the Eagles are facing a fundamentally different kind of quarterback. Ben Johnson has said he does not anticipate dramatically changing the game plan based on the starter. I believe him in terms of the structure of the offense, but no coach can replace Williams’ movement and creativity. Keenum is experienced and should be able to run the system, but the Eagles will be much less concerned about him turning a broken play into a 25-yard gain. Bagent is more willing to take chances and push the ball if he clears protocol, although that can create opportunities for the defense too. What surprised me while watching the first two games was how straightforward the Bears’ starting point has been. I expected more of the varied, puller-heavy run game associated with Johnson’s time in Detroit and perhaps more constant motion. Instead, the Bears have repeatedly lined up under center, run outside zone, and built passes from that same presentation. The lack of variety in the core run concept should not be confused with a lack of imagination. Johnson changes the formations, personnel, and accompanying routes so that the defense keeps seeing familiar movement with a different answer attached. One of my favorite examples has a receiver moving through the C-gap. It looks like the sort of insert action that could bring an extra blocker into the run fit. Instead, the receiver continues upfield and becomes part of a three-level stretch in the passing game. A defender trained by the previous runs to react to movement through that gap now has to decide whether to fit the run, pick up the route, or pass it to someone else. Johnson makes you cover every blade of grass, and he is particularly good at creating that moment of indecision. 3) No surprise, but they marry the run and pass game together very well. That's why they love running from under center. This is one of the coolest plays I've seen this season. Like the Rams, they frequently use a C-gap insert blocker in the run game. This time, they use a WR… pic.twitter.com/RlzUNwRjO1 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 This Cole Kmet leak is beautiful, too. The Bears show outside zone to the left while bringing a tight end across the formation to block back the other way. They use that movement in their actual running game, which is why the fake is convincing. This time, Cole Kmet slips out into space. It is easy to describe as a play-action pass; the impressive part is how closely the pass resembles a run the defense has already had to respect. One false step from a linebacker or safety is enough. This is Ben Johnson’s secret. The run and pass game are as well connected as anyone’s offense. 4) This is as good as it gets. They fake outside zone to the left after using this motion with the TE coming across the formation and blocking back the other way (which they do a lot in the run game) and they have Cole Kmet on the TE leak route. It's beautiful design and… pic.twitter.com/9UVcLcOSJ2 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 The receiving group gives Johnson several ways to finish those designs. Rome Odunze can win downfield, and Luther Burden III can turn a quick completion into more. Kmet and Colston Loveland threaten the middle of the field, which is exactly where a defense can become vulnerable if its second-level defenders are responding to outside zone. Kalif Raymond has been heavily involved, which is a little surprising, given he hasn’t had much success. The Bears also want more than quick throws. Their intermediate routes often develop quite deep, and they will send receivers vertically to create space underneath and across the field. I would be wary of playing passively and assuming a backup quarterback cannot hurt the Eagles. Give Johnson enough time, and he will find a way to get somebody open. Conversely, if the Eagles can make the quarterback throw before the deeper over or vertical route develops, the offense becomes far less threatening. That was a significant part of the Vikings’ success. 7) It might be different this week without Caleb, but the Bears want to throw the ball down the field. I think if you play passively, Ben Johnson will find a way to get receivers open. Their intermediate routes are often deep, and if you can get after them with pressure, you can… pic.twitter.com/x6RPcGWKws — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 This brings us to protection, which I think is one of the most interesting parts of the matchup. The Bears’ line can move people in the running game. Darnell Wright is an outstanding right tackle, Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson give them quality at guard, and they showed against the Panthers how well they can work together on zone runs. But I thought center Garrett Bradbury looked vulnerable when the Panthers and Vikings stressed him with stunts and twists. The Vikings, in particular, made the Bears communicate against changing pressure looks, and there were snaps where the protection never looked comfortable. Fangio is not Flores. I can’t imagine the Eagles spending the entire night showing six defenders at the line and sending pressure at Minnesota’s rate. I do think this is a good week to mix in stunts and simulated pressures, though. Make Bradbury identify the rush, make the line pass defenders off, and see whether a four-man rush can create a problem after the Bears have accounted for the wrong threats. That fits Fangio far better than asking him to abandon his normal approach and blitz constantly. 5) I do think that center Garrett Bradbury is a weakness right now with the Bears' line. The Vikings put pressure and succeeded, as did the Panthers on this rep. Fangio doesn't often send more than 4 rushers, but he might have to mix it up a bit this week. I'll be interested to… pic.twitter.com/JZpJ2mtnH0 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 The Eagles should also watch who the Bears leave in protection.…

title: Eagles News: DeVonta Smith is one of the NFL’s highest-graded receivers so far
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! To no surprise, Smitty is off to a strong start. Did anyone actually question if he could be WR1? That never shouldn’t been in doubt, if it even was at all. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: DeVonta Smith #6 of the Philadelphia Eagles walks through the tunnel against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! To no surprise, Smitty is off to a strong start. Did anyone actually question if he could be WR1? That never shouldn’t been in doubt, if it even was at all. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL wide receiver rankings: Jaxon Smith-Njigba leads top 32 – PFF DeVonta Smith, Philadelphia Eagles. Smith has benefited from the departure of A.J. Brown this offseason, averaging 2.30 yards per route run and ranking fourth at the position with a 91.4 PFF receiving grade. Now the No. 1 target in Philadelphia, he has a strong chance to put together the best season of his career. Eagles vs. Bears Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 3 enemy – BGN 4 – What’s the biggest matchup in the Bears’ favor and the biggest matchup against their favor? Well, I think the easiest one is the biggest disadvantage, and that will be the Eagles offensive line vs. the Bears defensive line. I understand Landon Dickerson is out, and the Eagles offensive line isn’t quite what it used to be, but it’s still a strong unit, and the Bears defensive line just isn’t. If the Philly OL can’t control the line of scrimmage, that would be rather surprising. I think the biggest advantage for them is the fact that the Eagles are struggling to stop the run right now, and the Bears block it extremely well. Maybe it’s a cliché, but I think this game is going to come down to controlling the line of scrimmage. Both teams have strong offensive lines and have a chance to control the line when they have the ball. I think the Bears need to really have long drives and keep their defense off the field. Can they do it without Caleb Williams? We will see on Monday night. Eagles mailbag: OL talk galore: Regrets? Trades? Reason for hope? – PhillyVoice Question from @jjapostolico (via Bluesky): Do Jurgens’ and Dickerson’s health make them less viable than the young guys like Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin? Dickerson has been a great player for the last half decade for the Eagles. He was a first-round talent who they got in Round 2 because he had major injury concerns. I think that when they drafted him they knew he wasn’t going to have some sort of 12-year career, and they got a bunch of Pro Bowl seasons out of him. But it does feel like the end is near, and we could kind of see it in training camp, even before he performed poorly Week 1 against the Commanders. The younger guys are more viable options than him at this point. Jurgens has kind of gotten lumped in with Dickerson because he had injury issues all last season and both guys went to Colombia for stem cell treatments during the offseason. But to me, Jurgens looked fine in training camp, at least compared to Dickerson. In Week 1, Jurgens had a couple of penalties in the first quarter, but I thought he played well enough otherwise. Obviously, he had a terrible game Week 2 against Simmons after he was forced into a new role. But I’m not yet ready to say that he’s a candidate for replacement in the starting lineup. Week 3 NFL game preview: Chicago Bears vs. Philadelphia Eagles – Windy City Gridiron The first primetime game for the 2026 Chicago Bears has lost much of its luster since the team will most likely be starting its third quarterback on Monday night. The Bears welcome the Philadelphia Eagles to Soldier Field in what should have been a great matchup of historical franchises with young quarterbacks dueling it out. But the NFL is a fickle thing. Bears head coach Ben Johnson has to navigate his first game without his QB1 or QB2. And the Eagles, coming in 2-0 but not looking dominant, have a lot to prove. Beyond wanting to flush the memories of Black Friday last season, when the Bears completely dominated them. The Eagles want to make a statement that they’re back to being true contenders and that their new offense is working well. Even with a third QB, it should be an interesting game. Let’s get into the opponent then. One thing we’ve learned about the Eagles at every position group through two weeks: Offense edition – PHLY Eagles Tight end: Howie Roseman’s view of the position needs to evolve. I wonder, if given truth serum as he often likes to say, if the tight end position is the group Howie Roseman would most like a mulligan on from this offseason. For as much credit as Roseman should get for rebuilding the Eagles receiving corps in a post-A.J. Brown world, there are as many if not more questions about whether his additions at tight end are sufficient for the offense Mannion wants to run. At the start of the offseason, Roseman said he needed to change the way he viewed the position to better reflect the value of versatility on the perimeter rather than prioritizing capable pass-catching options, something that has accelerated league-wide even further this season. According to TruMedia, the Rams, Bills, Bears, and Ravens have all run more plays out of 13 personnel through two weeks than any team did this time last season. The Rams and Bills in particular have double the snaps with three tight ends on the field this year than last year’s leader (the Arizona Cardinals with 20 snaps). Watching these teams, it’s not hard to understand why they’ve shifted toward getting heavier personnel sets on the field. It often forces modern defenses set up to play with five defensive backs to instead play out of their base personnel groupings with one fewer and gives the offense an advantage on outside-zone runs in particular because of the improved blocking on the outside. And for teams like the Rams and Bills, the versatility of their tight-end rooms allows them to still throw out of those looks without sacrificing too much of a threat downfield. According to TruMedia, the Bills have generated four explosive plays out of 13-personnel this season, more than a handful of offenses have managed overall this season. At least through two weeks, the Eagles tight end room seems behind the curve. Eli Stowers projected as a receiving-only tight end even before a disappointing summer ended with a quad strain that landed him on injured reserve. Johnny Mundt’s addition gave them the option to put two trusted blocking options on the field to start the season, but Mundt’s even struggled at times in understandably difficult matchups with bigger defensive linemen. With Dallas Goedert sidelined and Zach Ertz stepping into his role, the room is not tailor-made for this outside zone-based system Mannion wants to run. It may be one of Roseman’s biggest misses this offseason, especially considering the questions about Stowers’ usage will likely extend beyond just his rookie season. Why Jalen Hurts got emotional pulling up to Nissan Stadium in Nashville Sunday – NBCSP Hurts, in his weekly chat with the Eagles beat writers after practice, grew emotional sharing a story about the Eagles’ team bus pulling up to Nissan Stadium in Nashville Sunday before the Eagles-Titans game and how a giant photo of long-time Titans quarterback Steve McNair on the side of the stadium caught his attention. “It was a really good feeling and a bit emotional feeling, you know, pulling up to the stadium and seeing Steve McNair on the wallpaper outside,” Hurts said. “He’s the only one that I’ve looked up to … I got to meet, you know, M.J. (Michael Jordan) and, you know, build relationships with him and Tom Brady and all these other guys. Steve McNair is the only one that I’ve truly looked up to and watched and been enamored by and never got to meet him. So I think that was special for that reason. I was reminded of that when we pulled up to the stadium and it kind of hit me there.” The…
