full_text: Today during the press conference, all the 49ers said something similar about the Arizona Cardinals’ defense. They all mentioned two things: how Arizona swarms to the ball and how much they’re shifting/rotating their looks. Of course, you have to take everything players say to the media with a hypertension-inducing-sized grain of salt. It’s a game within the game. Still, I went ahead and read up on what DC Nick Rallis has been doing with the Cardinals. The first article linked gave a nice, clear breakdown on how they’ve been deploying Cover 6. The scheme’s sheer complexity can work against it, especially considering that Arizona’s starting CBs are hurt right now. I’m curious to see how Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy will try to exploit that. The Cardinals Are Suddenly Leaning on the NFL’s Most Confusing Defense “Cover 6 is a combination of Cover 2 on one side of the field with the other half playing Cover 4. It operates with two high safeties and has one boundary corner rolling deep to ultimately create three deep zones while the opposite corner stays in the flat…Rallis isn’t inherently aggressive in nature. The Cardinals ranked near the middle of the table in blitz percentage last season while Week 1 saw him send pressure on just 20% of plays, which ranked second to last on Sunday. By no means is he Brian Flores, but he opts for confusion post-snap, and that’s where the heavy Cover 6 comes into play….Defenders can show vastly different alignments before the play and by splitting the field into two entirely different looks post-snap, progressions are much harder to successfully move through. The data backs that up, too. According to Sumer Sports, Cover 6 had the highest interception rate of any coverage last season….Perhaps the biggest issue lies within its strengths. It’s tough for an offense to diagnose Cover 6, but it’s equally tough on the defenders running it. The amount of football IQ, communication and recognition it takes to successfully implement Cover 6 is high. One of the biggest complaints around Rallis’ defensive units is the amount of missed assignments, where communication breaks down and guys are left open…From an x’s and o’s standpoint, Cover 6 has weaknesses in the flats and the “hole” between the boundary corner and safety. Deep ball success isn’t often against Cover 6, though running a seam/streak and post pattern attacking the Cover 2 side can create problems as well.” 49ers Week 2 Trench Grades: Unexpected optimism (paywall) “This was a big day for Nick Bosa almost getting home. Also a big day for Osa-Keion White stunts. That’s going to be a big theme going forward, and those stunt pairings will be interesting to track….I’m increasingly liking what I’m seeing from Gracen Halton. Even in the run game, when he’s one-on-one and initially gets displaced, he’s often able to anchor and use an immense amount of torque to shed blockers. His low center of gravity is a clear benefit there. He needs to work on how to run stunts as the pick player, but he’s got speed to get through as a looper.” Raheem Morris, Klay Kubiak, Brock Purdy share updates ahead of 49ers-Cardinals “In general, has [Gracen Halton] surprised you? Watching the tape at Oklahoma, I think a lot of people didn’t realize he played as well against the run. “I think I said this before, but his movement was not the surprise. He had great movement and things like that in Oklahoma. His natural ability to move around and kind of stunt and do some things like that. We thought we would get like this guy that can really help out in the pass rush. We knew that right away. But, when he got here, really shocked us with his ability to use his hands and played well in the run game and be able to be stout and do some real cool things there. I forget when we kind of got that revelation. I think it was sometime in camp, we put the pads on for sure, but his ability to go out there and play the run for us is really good as well. We’re excited about that with him going forward.” NFL fines 49ers’ Kyle Juszczyk for imitating ‘chugging a beer’ “Niners coach Kyle Shanahan informed Juszczyk of the fine during practice Wednesday afternoon. At the time, Juszczyk said he thought perhaps it was a prank. “I thought maybe he was just messing with me, but it’s real,” Juszczyk said. “My hearing is on Tuesday and hopefully something changes.” Fred Warner opens up about the 49ers’ run defense struggles “If you can limit big runs and find a way to get one stop per series, it all but shuts down the running game for that drive. The 49ers have done just that. The Niners have allowed only three carries of 10+ yards through two games, tying for the second-fewest in the NFL. Their 11 stuffs rank 14th, but average is good enough when you consider how well they’ve defended the pass. Players like Nick Bosa, Fred Warner, and Upton Stout have single-handedly ruined drives. It may not be a sustainable way to win against the run, but it’s worked so far, and the way that each of those three has won, there’s no evidence to suggest it will stop. It won’t get any easier, as the loss of West and James Thompson Jr. means the Niners will lean on a couple of other players who were not on the roster heading into Week 1. Naquan Jones and McKinnley Jackson’s conditioning will be tested. They’ll need to play, simply because there are no other bodies after Osa Odighizuwa and Gracen Halton. Morris’s five-man fronts in Week 2 consisted of all defensive linemen. Perhaps he goes back to the Week 1 version, where he used Jaden Dugger on the EDGE.” 49ers star Nick Bosa lands on injury report with calf issue before Week 3 game “Bosa did not practice Wednesday, but it was a scheduled rest day and not injury related. This one is different. Bosa sustained a torn ACL in the 49ers’ third game last season, and he was back in time for the regular-season opener two weeks ago in Australia. He has been managing his knee condition since the opening of training camp, and now he is dealing with an unspecified calf injury, too.” Who gets the best locker in the San Francisco 49ers’ locker room? It’s complicated (paywall) “The north wall might be the worst place to be. It’s certainly the loudest. That’s because there’s a regulation-height basketball hoop (the room has 20-foot ceilings) directly across from those lockers with a 3-point contest — with multiple balls in use — going on at all times. Conduct an interview at that end of the locker room and you risk having your recording device knocked from your hand or not being able to decipher key words because they coincided with a ball clanking against the rim or a shout of joy/despair over a made/missed shot…..Though the area around it might not be a desirable neighborhood for a locker, the hoop has some gravity. Players tend to stop by for a shot — or two, or 75 — while strolling by on the way to the showers, which are in the northwest corner. The locker room lost one of its best shooters when wide receiver Jauan Jennings left for the Minnesota Vikings in free agency this offseason. Greenlaw is also known for his 3-point ability, while the offensive linemen — including guard Dominick Puni, whose locker is directly across from the hoop — are better than one might expect.”
author: Yinon Raviv

title: Nick Bosa was added to the 49ers’ injury report with a calf issue
summary: The San Francisco 49ers injury report is out for Thursday. Dre Greenlaw, Christian McCaffrey, and Trent Williams returned after missing Wednesday’s session due to Veterans Day. Romello Height (hand) and Mike Evans (hip) missed the second day in a row. Evans was reportedly working on the side of the field. Despite it being his first […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers injury report is out for Thursday. Dre Greenlaw, Christian McCaffrey, and Trent Williams returned after missing Wednesday’s session due to Veterans Day. Romello Height (hand) and Mike Evans (hip) missed the second day in a row. Evans was reportedly working on the side of the field. Despite it being his first year with the 49ers, Evans qualifies as one of the players who could go a full week without practice and still suit up on Sunday. That was the case before San Francisco suffered multiple injuries at wide receiver. The one change that might ring the alarms is Nick Bosa, who missed Wednesday with his typical day off. However, Bosa had an injury designation for Thursday. Bosa did not participate due to a calf injury. He had previously had a knee injury, but that’s been the case since the Niners’ first injury report. Kyle Shanahan will have more information about Bosa’s injury on Friday. You’d like to think the team is being cautious with its best player. They’ve done something similar with Evans early in the season, and Shanahan has alluded to a potential management plan for Bosa this week, especially coming off a season-ending knee injury.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Kyle Juszczyk appeals bizarre fine for TD celebration
summary: 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk was subjected to a bizarre piece of league discipline this week as he was fined for his touchdown celebration in San Francisco’s blowout win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 2. The NFL hit Juszczyk with a $14,926 fine for what the league claimed to be a “beer-chugging” celebration following his […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Kyle Juszczyk #44 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after his receiving touchdown against the Miami Dolphins in the third quarter of a game at Levi's Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk was subjected to a bizarre piece of league discipline this week as he was fined for his touchdown celebration in San Francisco’s blowout win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 2. The NFL hit Juszczyk with a $14,926 fine for what the league claimed to be a “beer-chugging” celebration following his receiving score in the third quarter, which put the 49ers up 28-6. In a letter to Juszczyk, the league said: “Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste.” The punishment makes little sense, given “Juice” is Juszczyk’s nickname and he has celebrated in that fashion — mimicking drinking from a juice carton — for many years. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported the news and said that he received a text from Juszczyk that read: “And I don’t even drink beer!” He can’t be stopped!! This is before practice! Are you kidding me @JuiceCheck44 🧃 pic.twitter.com/AOgHnOFDuo — George Kittle (@gkittle46) September 24, 2026 That assertion was backed up tight end George Kittle, who replied to Schefter’s post on X (formerly Twitter): “Can confirm he doesn’t really drink beer but is a good guy.” And Juszczyk is not about to just accept the punishment, with Schefter adding that Juszczyk has already appealed against the fine. The veteran Juszczyk, now in his 14th season in the league and 10th with San Francisco, is unlikely to lose any sleep over the fine. But it’s a matter of principle as the league office has clearly misunderstood Juszczyk’s long-time celebration. Hopefully, common sense prevails when the NFL looks at his appeal.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: John Lynch uses the 49ers’ history as a reason to keep Mac Jones
summary: San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch has been consistent in his approach to wanting a quality backup for his starter. So far, the backup has always had experience. Jimmy Garoppolo, Sam Darnold, Josh Dobbs, Josh Johnson, and now Mac Jones. Kurtis Rourke lacks that, which might be one of the driving factors for Lynch […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch has been consistent in his approach to wanting a quality backup for his starter. So far, the backup has always had experience. Jimmy Garoppolo, Sam Darnold, Josh Dobbs, Josh Johnson, and now Mac Jones. Kurtis Rourke lacks that, which might be one of the driving factors for Lynch to be stingy when it comes to dealing Jones. During an appearance on KNBR Thursday , Lynch didn’t want to address whether he’s received any calls about Jones in light of the recent quarterback injuries. Lynch said, “I’m going to leave that alone.” There has been no shortage of injuries at the most important position in all sports over the past two weeks: Sam Darnold (glute) Caleb Williams (hamstring) Jayden Daniels (dislocated elbow) Jaxson Dart (MCL sprain) The Falcons are getting Michael Penix Jr. back from an injury. Their starter, Tua Tagovailoa, had an oblique injury. We’re early enough in the season that every team thinks they have a chance. In Atlanta and New York’s case, each has a first-year head coach with no prior ties to the current quarterbacks. Despite what’s happening around the NFL in 2026, Lynch referenced the 49ers quarterback room from the late 1980s and early ’90s: “What I will tell you is I think a lot of people see all of that and say, ‘Okay, there’s opportunity.’ It also tells you we’re very fortunate to have a guy like Brock, franchise quarterback. But then to have a guy like Mac, in the event, there’s no more important position in football. They’re all important, but I think we know, as your quarterback goes, so goes your team. And so, I think it’s a really special situation to have Brock [Purdy] here, to have Mac here, and then to have a guy we’re really excited about with Kurtis Rourke. And I think back to Bill Walsh, and maybe he was onto something when he had Joe Montana, but he also brought Steve Young in here, and had Steve Bono behind them. So, it’s a good position to be in a position of strength at, and it provides opportunities in a number of ways. The most important way being you’re well insulated in the event something were ever to happen.” It’s easy to say that you’d trade away Jones when you’re not in Lynch’s seat. There are no repercussions for those of us on the outside. He’s also coming off a season where the backup started nearly half the season. That doesn’t mean Lynch won’t be influenced over the next month and a half by offers that may be too good to turn down. With Jones headed to free agency, the question is what pick it would take for the 49ers to part ways with their backup. The 2027 NFL Draft is projected to be the best of the decade in terms of quality and depth. A third-round pick would be a no-brainer. A fourth-round pick might do the trick, especially if Brock Purdy continues to play at an MVP level. The 49ers don’t have to make any moves, but are also in a position to capitalize on a desperate team.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Fred Warner opens up about the 49ers’ run defense struggles
summary: Two weeks into the season, the San Francisco 49ers’ rushing defense sits 17th in success rate and 12th in EPA per rush. Both the Rams and Dolphins have stretches where they got whatever they wanted to on the ground. Injuries have zapped the Niners’ depth. Part of the reason Los Angeles and Miami moved the […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Two weeks into the season, the San Francisco 49ers’ rushing defense sits 17th in success rate and 12th in EPA per rush. Both the Rams and Dolphins have stretches where they got whatever they wanted to on the ground. Injuries have zapped the Niners’ depth. Part of the reason Los Angeles and Miami moved the ball was due to the players the 49ers put on the field. Raheem Morris probably felt good about where the team was at with Sam Okuayinonu and Alfred Collins. Sam O is an underrated defender, while Collins, paired with CJ West, looked to build on their rookie campaigns. Collins was recovering from a torn labrum that required offseason surgery. It kept him out of the first block of training camp practices. Then, right before the season, a torn patellar tendon cost Collins his season. Okuayinonu broke his foot the day before. Those injuries led to the 49ers needing to scramble. Khalid Kareem went from the Falcons’ practice squad to a defensive-line contributor. When your depth is depleted, the plan to use Romello Height goes out the window. Now, he’s an every-down player instead of a designated pass rusher. All-Pro linebacker Fred Warner explained some of the early-season struggles against the run: “I think the run game right now, you’ve got to remember, it’s a new system. New things, techniques, schemes are being put into place. It’s a new group, guys kind of meshing together trying to figure out where does everybody fit. I think the thing that has helped a ton is the style of play, but it’s something that will continue to get better as we go on.” We’re a couple of weeks away from Mykel Williams being eligible to return from the PUP list. The domino effect of that is you don’t have to play Kareem, Ogbo Okoronkwo’s snaps become limited, and Keion White can be used exclusively inside — not to mention Height can play on obvious passing downs. Warner continued: “I’m not sitting here saying I’m complacent with it at all. Selfishly, I want us to be dominant in all areas, especially in the run game. But the No. 1 thing the offenses want to do is create explosives. They want to get the run game going to get guys biting up to ultimately take shots down the field. So everything got to be complementary. It’s something that we’re looking at and something we’re looking to get better in all areas.” If you can limit big runs and find a way to get one stop per series, it all but shuts down the running game for that drive. The 49ers have done just that. The Niners have allowed only three carries of 10+ yards through two games, tying for the second-fewest in the NFL. Their 11 stuffs rank 14th, but average is good enough when you consider how well they’ve defended the pass. Players like Nick Bosa, Fred Warner, and Upton Stout have single-handedly ruined drives. It may not be a sustainable way to win against the run, but it’s worked so far, and the way that each of those three has won, there’s no evidence to suggest it will stop. It won’t get any easier, as the loss of West and James Thompson Jr. means the Niners will lean on a couple of other players who were not on the roster heading into Week 1. Naquan Jones and McKinnley Jackson’s conditioning will be tested. They’ll need to play, simply because there are no other bodies after Osa Odighizuwa and Gracen Halton. Morris’s five-man fronts in Week 2 consisted of all defensive linemen. Perhaps he goes back to the Week 1 version, where he used Jaden Dugger on the EDGE. We know Raheem will adapt to his personnel. He’s shown that through two weeks. The best weapon on the 49ers’ defense is on the other side of the ball, with the offense scoring at an absurd clip and forcing opponents to keep pace.
author: Kyle Posey

title: John Lynch on Brock Purdy: We’re just entering his prime
summary: It’s been a strong start to the season for San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy, who has thrown for 492 yards, five touchdowns, and an interception, while completing over 80 percent of his passes. Purdy, who is coming off a season where he played just nine games, had one of the best statistical games of […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers looks to throw a pass against the Miami Dolphins in the third quarter of a game at Levi's Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s been a strong start to the season for San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy, who has thrown for 492 yards, five touchdowns, and an interception, while completing over 80 percent of his passes. Purdy, who is coming off a season where he played just nine games, had one of the best statistical games of his career on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. He completed 20 of 22 passes for 287 yards and two touchdowns, while adding a third on the ground in the 35-13 win. For years, Purdy has had his fair share of supporters and detractors, with the discourse mainly revolving around where he ranks among his peers. But as his surrounding environment has continued to change, Purdy has consistently gotten better, with turnovers really being his only blemish. Now in Year 5 at age 26, are we starting to get in Brock Purdy’s prime? “Yeah, I think we are just entering it,” John Lynch said on KNBR’s Murph and Mac on Thursday morning. “When you really go back and look at it, Brock’s been pretty damn good from the first time that he got on the field here. He’s been efficient. This is a league where you have to go do it week in and week out. I saw another jump this training camp. The place I see it, I think he’s just playing extremely aggressive football and he always has, but I think he’s ripping the ball. He’s throwing with conviction all the time. Raheem [Morris] came in here, he calls him The Layer King because of his ability to layer the ball over linebackers. “So probably, people are more accustomed to touch passes with Brock. I think what you’ve seen, think of the ball that he threw to Demarcus [Robinson] in Australia down under. It was down under, but it was over the top, and man, he let that thing go, he did it with such conviction. He’s really throwing the ball, playing with great confidence, great conviction. So, do you see other steps? I have, but he’s been pretty damn good since he’s been here. You just look at the body of work.” After a solid game against the Los Angeles Rams following an early interception, Purdy was the catalyst of the offense in Week 2, as he missed just two throws, with one of them being a drop. “The game he played against the Miami Dolphins was darn near flawless,” Lynch added. “We do a game review up top, from young scouts to high-ranking executives, everybody ranks, and the grades he got were just sick. You go back and review them because we want to have a hard standard, and those grades were right. He played that well. And that means his teammates are playing that well. Our offensive line’s protection has been phenomenal here in the first two weeks. “But Brock is the first to know that you got to go do it every week, but it’s really exciting to see him play this type of football. The one thing, we create a standard like that, now you got to go do it each week, and he knows that and he looks forward to that opportunity.” Many of Purdy’s detractors have pointed out his arm strength and size versus some of the league’s best quarterbacks. But the 49ers signal-caller has always been an elite anticipator. And, speaking on the Built 4 More podcast, Purdy broke down the value and importance of processing and anticipating, and why it’s made him such a good quarterback. “My quarterback coach, Brian Griese, the last couple years, he and I talked about that,” Purdy said. “He played 11 years, his dad’s Bob Griese. But we got talking about how really it’s 60/40. You can see about 60 percent of the time, and the other 40 percent you really can’t. I mean, it doesn’t matter how big you are. I’m already shorter in stature, but he goes, that’s why it’s so important when it comes down to knowing coverages, knowing scheme, where our players are supposed to be, how many steps they’re breaking, and where the ball should be over a certain backer. All those things, man, it matters.” We’ve often seen quarterbacks get hyped with combine performances and pro day throws, but Purdy doesn’t believe that’s the most accurate representation of a game setting. “And that’s why guys, you know, if you go to a combine and all those things, you’re just throwing on air, and yeah, you look all good with a strong arm and fast, jumping, all that stuff. But when it comes down to 11-on-11 and you got guys that are a foot taller than you and you can’t see, it comes down to the processing. “Like before the play, I know that this safety is probably going to rotate down. It’s going to be one high, and I got one hitch, no more than that, to rip it where Deebo’s supposed to be, like just inside the hash. And there’s a backer that’s also got a 40-inch vert that I got to put it [over].” That has been one of Purdy’s best skills as a quarterback, and he’s continued to sharpen his skill set as he grows in the NFL. Entering Year 5 and only 26 years old, the best is yet to come for the 49ers signal-caller.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Robert Saleh reveals 49ers missed out on a top RB target in 2025 NFL Draft
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have regularly been connected to the running back position in the NFL Draft, and they picked up another rookie this offseason, taking Kaelon Black in the third round. That pick was quite controversial at the time, as Black was expected to go much later on Day 3 and there hadn’t been […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 21: Cam Skattebo #44 of the New York Giants runs with the ball against Quentin Lake #37 of the Los Angeles Rams during the second quarter of the game at SoFi Stadium on September 21, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have regularly been connected to the running back position in the NFL Draft, and they picked up another rookie this offseason, taking Kaelon Black in the third round. That pick was quite controversial at the time, as Black was expected to go much later on Day 3 and there hadn’t been a running back picked since Jadarian Price went at No. 32 overall. But head coach Kyle Shanahan revealed Black was the team’s No. 2 running back in the draft, and the rookie has gotten off to a fast start to the 2026 season. It marked the fifth time in six years that the 49ers had drafted a running back. Only two of those five are on the active roster: Black and 2025 fifth-round pick Jordan James. James was the latest selection of the five picks, as the 49ers took him in the fifth round. He missed much of his rookie season with a finger injury, and has played in just four games so far in the NFL, carrying the ball four times for 15 yards. James was considered a solid Day 3 prospect in last year’s draft, but there was another running back the 49ers actually had their eyes on going into the draft: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo. Skattebo, who went to Arizona State, was taken by the Giants with the No. 105 overall pick at the top of the fourth round. At the time, there was buzz that the 49ers were interested in the running back, and that he was a target for them at No. 113 overall. Well, former defensive coordinator Robert Saleh confirmed the interest earlier this week, noting that Kyle Shanahan ‘loved’ Skattebo and that the 49ers would’ve taken him if he hadn’t been picked. “He’s like the old school, 2010s man hit-stick,” Saleh said of Skattebo this week. “Lower your shoulder, run people over, plays his ass off, lots of energy… We actually were about to draft him in San Francisco [last year]. Kyle loved him, and he ended up getting taken right before we were picking. I think we ended up with C.J. West, who was a pretty damn good player too. But he’s a sparkplug.” Skattebo has quickly ascended to being the Giants starter at running back, rushing for 410 yards and five touchdowns, while catching 24 passes for 207 yards in eight games last year before a season-ending injury. So far this season, he’s rushed for 117 yards and one touchdown in two games. While there are a ton of similar hypotheticals in the NFL, Skattebo would’ve definitely been an interesting fit for the 49ers, and you could see the appeal. He’s a hard-nosed runner with a high motor who has also shown an affinity for pass-catching so far. Instead of Skattebo, the 49ers took CJ West at No. 113 after taking Upton Stout at No. 100. They proceeded to take a running back in the fifth round with Jordan James instead.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

(Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buccaneers released their second injury report of the week Thursday as they continue preparations for Sunday’s matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. Tampa Bay rookie outside linebacker Rueben Bain Jr. remained sidelined with a groin injury, marking his second consecutive missed practice. Bain suffered the injury during last week’s loss to Cleveland. There was better news for the Bucs elsewhere on defense. Josiah Trotter (shoulder) and Anthony Nelson (shin) returned to practice Thursday after both were non-participants to begin the week. title: Titans vs. Giants predictions: Take advantage of a beat-up team
summary: It is time for the Tennessee Titans to get the first win of their season. The New York Giants will be without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart after he suffered a season-ending knee injury on Monday night. They could also be without star EDGE rusher Brian Burns. The Titans need to capitalize. Jameis Winston will get […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans throws a pass against the New York Jets during the second half of the game at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is time for the Tennessee Titans to get the first win of their season. The New York Giants will be without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart after he suffered a season-ending knee injury on Monday night. They could also be without star EDGE rusher Brian Burns. The Titans need to capitalize. Jameis Winston will get the start for the Giants. Winston is not a bad quarterback, but he does have the propensity to give the ball to the other team. The Titans picked off Jalen Hurts twice last week. If they can do that again, they will have a really good shot. On offense, they need to build off last week’s momentum. The key there will be the ability to stay balanced. Against the Eagles, they had 29 rushes and 20 passes. They can only do that if they don’t fall behind early and if they stay ahead of the chains. Cam Ward needs to continue the progress we saw from Week 1 to Week 2. He hasn’t turned the ball over in either of the first two games. Limiting his throws is the best path forward for now. There will come a time when they have to lean on him to win games. The hope is that he is better equipped to do that as he continues to become comfortable in Brian Daboll’s offense. This is a game the Titans really need to win. They get the benefit of facing a backup quarterback. Winston is a pretty good player, but there is a reason Dart was the starter. They have a tough 3-game stretch coming after this, with games at the Baltimore Ravens, at home against the Houston Texans, and at the Indianapolis Colts. Go take advantage of a beat-up Giants team. summary: The Tennessee Titans have a winnable game versus the New York Giants in Week 3. The Titans played a competitive game against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2. Meanwhile the Giants lost several starters to injury, including quarterback Jaxson Dart. We’ve identified three Titans who could lead Tennessee to victory in Week 3. WR Carnell […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Carnell Tate #14 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans have a winnable game versus the New York Giants in Week 3. The Titans played a competitive game against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2. Meanwhile the Giants lost several starters to injury, including quarterback Jaxson Dart. We’ve identified three Titans who could lead Tennessee to victory in Week 3. WR Carnell Tate Rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate has produced just seven receptions for 65 yards through two games. The fourth overall pick has started slower than anyone anticipated. Both Cam Ward and Tate have been responsible for missed opportunities. The Giants’ secondary was torched by Davante Adams on MNF. Tate and the Titans’ passing attack should have opportunities to generate explosive plays on Sunday. It’s time for the rookie wideout to have his breakout game. RB Tony Pollard Tony Pollard ran the football rather effectively versus the Eagles in Week 2. He rushed for 64 yards via 14 carries, averaging 4.6 yards per attempt. He could have scored a touchdown if Ward didn’t scramble for two scores. Pollard is averaging 4.7 yards per carry. The Titans’ offensive line has been better than expected or advertised. With Jaxson Dart missing Week 3, hopefully the Titans will control the football for longer as they currently rank 32nd in time of possession. Pollard could have a big day. DT Jeffery Simmons Superstar defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was dominant versus the Eagles in Week 2. He currently leads the NFL in pressures. He’s playing like the Pro Bowl-caliber player he is in Robert Saleh’s new system. The Giants have a rookie guard in Francis Mauigoa and a struggling center in John-Michael Schmitz. With Jameis Winston at quarterback, Simmons is definitely capable of forcing him into a mistake or two. He should be his usual reliable self.

title: This chart proves Titans OT JC Latham is better than you think
summary: Tennessee Titans offensive tackle JC Latham is a player who always seems to draw controversial opinions. Some Titans fans believe he’s growing into a franchise right tackle. Others claim he needs replacing ASAP, or needs to switch positions inside to guard. Latham is arguably the Titans’ most polarizing player. In Sunday’s nailbiting Week 2 loss […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: JC Latham #55 of the Tennessee Titans runs out prior to an NFL football game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tennessee Titans offensive tackle JC Latham is a player who always seems to draw controversial opinions. Some Titans fans believe he’s growing into a franchise right tackle. Others claim he needs replacing ASAP, or needs to switch positions inside to guard. Latham is arguably the Titans’ most polarizing player. In Sunday’s nailbiting Week 2 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, he gave up an ill-timed sack on a questionable bootleg play-call on 1st-and-goal late in the fourth quarter. Latham does have a tendency to make glaring mistakes, drawing criticism he doesn’t always deserve. The honest account is that Latham is a very good, ascending blocker. His 1-2 mistakes per weekend tend to be glaring, with some Titans fans forming overreactionary takes. A recent pass-blocking chart from Pro Football Focus highlights how good Latham has actually been for the Titans through two weeks. The former Alabama standout has the highest “island rate” of any offensive tackle in the NFL, meaning he’s faced more one-on-one matchups than any other OT. Despite that, Latham has won the fifth-most matchups of any tackle when left on an island. JC Latham's ranks this season among OT Island Rate: Highest Island Pass Block Win Rate: 5th Highest pic.twitter.com/AJu8rIXMPI — PFF (@PFF) September 23, 2026 This means the Titans trust Latham to win one-on-one matchups. The results indicate he’s repaying their faith by doing just that at a very effective clip. Latham is still a 23-year-old blocker on the third year of his rookie contract. He’s undeniably an above-average right tackle with room to get better. PFF has credited Latham with allowing just three pressures and zero sacks this season, though he definitely deserved blame for that Jalen Carter sack. He’s faced some good pass rushers on the Jets and Eagles such as David Bailey, Jalyx Hunt, and Nolan Smith. Most of the time, Lahtam is providing Titans QB Cam Ward with clean pockets. Titans fans need to confront the truth about Latham.

title: Commanders GM Adam Peters provides Jayden Daniels injury update
summary: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels has traveled around the country seeing specialists for how to best treat a left elbow dislocation that occurred at the end of the first half of a Week 2 loss at Dallas.   Daniels got back late on Thursday and the team was still sitting down to decide on the best […]
full_text: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels has traveled around the country seeing specialists for how to best treat a left elbow dislocation that occurred at the end of the first half of a Week 2 loss at Dallas . Daniels got back late on Thursday and the team was still sitting down to decide on the best course of action moving forward. General manager Adam Peters didn’t have definitive answers about Daniels’ rehab process, but he did say that surgery is not on the table and that the team isn’t currently discussing injured reserve with Daniels. That should be considered a positive for the Commanders, creating a prospect that Daniels might not miss much time. “He just got back late last night and the guys are meeting with him this morning,” Peters said Friday morning during his weekly appearance with the The Junkies on 106.7-FM The Fan in Washington . “We met with doctors all over the country and were really thorough. And we got a lot of good opinions. And now it’s a matter of thinking about what’s the best course of action. “As of right now surgery is not on the table and we haven’t discussed (injured reserve). It’s just a matter of how we’re going to get him back on the field. That’s still to be determined.” Peters said the Commanders will lean on medical personnel to makes final decisions about the best course of action. Not placing him on IR would suggest some confidence he can return faster than the four weeks he’d be out with that designation. Washington’s GM hedged that first answer a little bit later in the interview, making sure his previous comments were related this moment. “At this time,” Peters said. “I don’t want to make any proclamations, but those aren’t things we’ve discussed and landed on yet. He just got back. We haven’t even sat down and talked about what we’re doing moving forward.” Peters also said it was a “longshot” for linebacker Frankie Luvu (groin), tight end Chig Okonkwo (hamstring) and guard Sam Cosmi (concussion) to play against the Seahawks.

title: Washington Commanders vs Seattle Seahawks Week 3: Five Questions with Field Gulls
summary: It’s week 3 of the NFL season, and the 0-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 2-0 Seattle Seahawks team at home in Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD this Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET. Despite losing starting QB Sam Darnold to a glute injury on the first drive of the first game, the Seahawks have […]
full_text: In a home game at Northwest Stadium on Nov. 2, quarterback Jayden Daniels scores the only Commanders touchdown in the 38-14 week nine loss against the Seattle Seahawks. | Marcus Relacion/The Washington Informer It’s week 3 of the NFL season, and the 0-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 2-0 Seattle Seahawks team at home in Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD this Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET. Despite losing starting QB Sam Darnold to a glute injury on the first drive of the first game, the Seahawks have managed to beat the Patriots 13-10 in week 1 and beat the Cardinals 31-7 in week 2. It is unclear if Darnold will return to play in week 3, but he has practiced this week. On offense, the Seahawks are coached by OC Brian Fleury, former TEs coach and run-game coordinator of the 49ers from 2022 to 2025. A TEs coach has good insight into both the blocking and pass-catching aspects of offense due to TEs being heavily involved in both duties. The fact that Fleury was also the run-game coordinator for the 49ers means he should be well suited to understanding and coaching all aspects of the Shanahan offense (note that Cowboys OC Klayton Adams was formerly a TEs coach for the Colts and OL coach for the Cardinals who designed their prolific run game before moving to Dallas). So far, the Seahawks offense has stayed true to its Shanahan roots , with heavy use of under center, play action passing, and an outside-zone run game. Perhaps to simplify the passing game for a backup QB, the Seahawks have been targeting WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba with an absurd 44% share of targets (last year he led the NFL with a 35.8% target share). It makes sense to simplify things for your backup QB by scheming him to just throw it to his best player. On defense, the Seahawks are still coached by head coach Mike Macdonald, former DC of the Ravens, and DC Aden Durde, former defensive line coach of the Cowboys. Perhaps unsurprising given that their DC is a former DL coach, the Seahawks defense is anchored around the excellent play of their defensive line. Last year, the Seahawks were able to achieve the 6th-best QB pressure rate despite the 7th-lowest blitz rate, meaning they were able to get pressure rushing four most of the time, and leave more players back in coverage to stop passing plays and explosive plays. The result is a defense that allows the NFL’s fewest passing yards and 9th-fewest rushing yards through two games this year. I asked John Gilbert of Field Gulls five questions to better understand the state of the Seahawks and what to look for in this game. 1) The Seahawks defense has held their opponents to 10 or fewer points in the last two games. How much of this is personnel, how much is scheme, and what is special about Mike Macdonald’s scheme and playcalling? Holding both 2026 opponents they have faced to 10 or fewer points really seems to be a continuation of how the Seattle defense finished the 2025 season, which was by holding five of the last nine teams played to 10 or fewer points. Of the games in which the other team has managed to put more than ten points on the board against this defense since Thanksgiving, they were quarterbacked by Philip Rivers (16), Matthew Stafford (37 & 27) and Drake Maye (13), and any team with a quarterback that isn’t in the tier of those named has struggled against the defense. As for what makes Macdonald’s defense so successful, it’s not one thing in particular. The players are good, but Macdonald makes them better by putting them in a position to succeed by understanding the tendencies of the opponent, while simultaneously giving his players the freedom to operate as needed for success. For example, former undrafted free agent linebacker Drake Thomas changed the defensive front Macdonald had called on a key second and one near midfield early in the game against the Cardinals. Similarly, on the fourth down that effectively clinched the NFC Championship for the Seahawks, DeMarcus Lawrence recognized what the Rams were trying to do and broke off his assignment to prevent Stafford having an easy completion to Kyren Williams for either a first down or score. It’s a rare combination of a scheme that confuses opponents, with players who perform at a high level within the system and have the skills and football IQ to operate with a higher level of freedom, and the experience necessary in the system to play fast without having to think to analyze how to react. 2) On the other side of the ball, how has the Seahawks offense looked? Is it different under new OC Brian Fleury and what changes with Drew Lock vs Sam Darnold at QB? The season opener did not start off well for anyone hoping for the offense would be as explosive as it was last season, as the team was shutout by the Patriots until after halftime. Certainly a part of that is likely due to the fact that Sam Darnold’s injury meant Drew Lock taking over, as well as some rust overall as the starters had not played during the preseason. The fact that the backup is in at quarterback means the jury is largely still out as far as a lot of the questions that surrounded the offense heading into the season. With that said, through the first two games one of the consistent threads that has continued through from 2025 has been the continued usage of two and three tight end packages. Specifically, during the 2025 season the Seahawks used 12- or 13-personnel on a little more than a third of their offensive snaps, while so far in 2026 the usage has been even higher. A big piece of that, of course, is likely that they were up big and running the ball a lot against the Cardinals in the second half of Week 2, so it remains to be seen how much they’ll rely on their tight end heavy packages in more competitive contests. In addition, Fleury has tweaked how the Seattle offense uses motion through the first two games, and that has made things more difficult for opponents to figure out what’s coming. One clear change made by Seahawks OC Brian Fleury is removing a tell from last season. Seattle motioned on 32% of runs and 85% of passes in the Super Bowl. A clear sign a pass was coming. Seattle has motioned on 60.0% of runs and 55.6% of passes this season. No clear pattern. pic.twitter.com/knMhlNhnwz — Brian Nemhauser (@hawkblogger) September 21, 2026 3) What is your overall opinion of Seahawks GM John Schneider and has it evolved since the hiring of Mike Macdonald? Did you ever think he should have been sent packing along with Pete Carroll for a completely fresh start? After coming out of the gates on an absolute scorcher and drafting multiple Hall of Fame caliber players to start his career as a general manager, things went off the rails for several years. From 2017 through 2021 the results of the team’s drafting was not on par with what is necessary for sustained success in the NFL, and that certainly contributed to Carroll’s demise. A big piece of the issues from 2018 on appear to have been reworking the draft board and an over reliance on looking for “maturity” in the wake of the Malik McDowell debacle of 2017. Beginning in 2018 the Seahawks draft classes were consistently among the oldest in the NFL, while many of their biggest hits to come out of those drafts were players like DK Metcalf who were among the younger members of their respective draft class. Where the wheels truly came off, though, was when the Seahawks made a conscious decision to effectively punt on the 2021 draft as a result of the anticipated uncertainty of the COVID season. Seattle made only three selections in the 2021 draft after trading a first and a third for Jamal Adams, a fifth for Gabe Jackson and a seventh for Carlos Dunlap. Of course, the draft is about uncertainty, and the Loser’s Curse is a concept developed decades ago regarding the uncertainty of the draft. That all said, since 2022 Schneider has been back on a heater, and the quality of the roster shows. Even after the departure in free agency of Kenneth Walker, Coby Bryant, Boye…

title: Commanders vs. Seahawks Thursday injury report: Javon Kinlaw returns
summary: The Commanders got a little piece of good news in a sea of bad injury luck on Thursday, as defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw returned to practice in a limited capacity. That’s a win for Washington, as Kinlaw’s off to a solid start this season. He’s dealing with back and shoulder issues, according to the Commanders […]
full_text: The Commanders got a little piece of good news in a sea of bad injury luck on Thursday, as defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw returned to practice in a limited capacity. That’s a win for Washington, as Kinlaw’s off to a solid start this season. He’s dealing with back and shoulder issues, according to the Commanders participation report. They’re still working without some important players, with linebacker Frankie Luvu (groin), tight end Chig Okonkwo (hamstring), right guard Sam Cosmi (concussion), safety Nick Cross (illness) and, of course, quarterback Jayden Daniels (elbow). Those are some important folks listed above, so the Commanders depth will be tested in some key areas on Sunday against Seattle if they aren’t deemed ready to play. There are also six players limited in some capacity, including linebacker Leo Chenal and defensive lineman Charles Omenihu, key members of the defensive front seven. full_text: The Commanders sure didn’t want to start 0-2, but that’s where they find themselves heading into a Week 3 contest with the Seattle Seahawks that doubles as their home opener. Washington must get right without starting quarterback Jayden Daniels, who suffered a left elbow dislocation during a Week 2 loss to the Dallas Cowboys . Marcus Mariota’s now running the show , with plenty of experience to rely on in this tough situation. The Seahawks defense is a formidable foe, but the home crowd should have a positive impact on a team that desperately needs it. This is an important contest, especially with the team headed to London in Week 4 . How can Washington come out on top? No, seriously. We’re asking you. We’ll hit five key questions for you to answer in this reverse Q+A using the article comments below. As we always do, we’ll pull the best answers to each question and put them in the main part of the article on Friday morning. Let’s get to it: Question 1: How can Marcus Mariota lead the Commanders to victory? What will it be important for him to do to get a win? Question 2: After the way Rachaad White played versus Dallas, would you consider using him as the feature back and putting Jacory Croskey-Merritt into more of a backup role? Question 3: The Commanders secondary is a mess, especially without Nick Cross available. Would you make any personnel switches in the defensive backfield at this point? Question 4: What’s your level of concern with Jayden Daniels’ ability to stay healthy on a consistent basis? Does this injury change your mind on whether to offer him a long-term extension? Question 5: The Commanders are off to a tough start. In what scenario could you see owner Josh Harris letting Dan Quinn go during the season?

title: Tyler’s Take: What can be done with Mike Sainristil
summary: To say Mike Sainristil has been a massive disappointment throughout the first two games of the 2026 season is an understatement. As things are presently looking, Sainristil is going down as yet another wasted top-60 draft pick for Commanders general manager Adam Peters. I was bullish on Sainristil coming into the season. I felt the […]
full_text: To say Mike Sainristil has been a massive disappointment throughout the first two games of the 2026 season is an understatement. As things are presently looking, Sainristil is going down as yet another wasted top-60 draft pick for Commanders general manager Adam Peters. I was bullish on Sainristil coming into the season. I felt the cornerback had a solid rookie season on a below-average defense and he was thrust into a scheme in 2025 that didn’t fit his skillset — coupled with a coordinator who was fired midseason and injuries all around him. I was wrong to go out on a limb and defend him during the offseason and preseason, and I will be the first to admit that a change NEEDS to happen. So, what could that change be? Leave him where he is and hope he improves To me, this is the definition of insanity. CLEARLY the young man is broken and I don’t know if there is an immediate fix for him in his current role. Coaches, players and fans seem to be fed up with him, and more bad play will just dig him deeper into the hole he’s already in. Cornerbacks in the NFL are required to have a short memory, but the way Mikey is trending, he’ll have Alzheimer’s by the time he’s 27. Free Safety Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones currently has no free safety and it’s becoming a major problem. Jeremy Reaves looks lost and had been frequently targeted by Philadelphia and Dallas in the middle of the field. Quan Martin has also seen some time as a deep safety, but he hasn’t looked much better than Reaves. Mikey tends to play a lot better with his eyes towards the quarterback. He struggles mightily when put in hip-trail where he’s usually chasing a bigger receiver or when Washington runs match-up man. As a free safety, he can read and diagnose plays from a distance and use his athleticism to break on the ball once it leaves the quarterback’s hand. He has plus ball-skills, so this may help generate more turnovers. The downside here, is his angles and tackling have been a liability, so that would need to be immediately cleaned up. However, he showed as a rookie he’s not afraid to stick his head in there and mix things up. Wide Receiver This may be a bit far-fetched, but Sainristil was a receiver coming into Michigan before being moved to cornerback after his redshirt-sophomore season. He does own 37 career collegiate receptions for 539 yards and five touchdowns as a Wolverine. It would take a year of seasoning to get him up to speed as a slot receiver, but with Diggs signed for just one year, and Terry McLaurin likely on his way out after this season, maybe he can find a spot on the roster with a new head coach in 2027 after taking 2026 to learn some of the nuances of the position in the NFL. Bench him This might be the best option. Maybe taking some time to ride the pine and hopefully get his mental state right will help him. Let’s not forget, he’s seen significant starting time since his rookie year, so this could be a humbling experience designed to first break him down before building him back up. This move would need to result in Commanders coaches being able to admit they were wrong, something head coach Dan Quinn and company have not shown in the past. However, if they can get over their egos and do what’s best for the team, it actually may turn out to be what’s also best for the player. As Commanders analyst Brian Mitchell so eloquently put it — “We can’t sit up here and be mad at the player if the coach keep putting him back on the field.” Trade him There is probably not much of a trade market for a guy who is ranked dead last by two different analytics services and in the bottom five by another. But, every coach thinks they can fix what’s wrong with someone and it only takes one team to view his upside as intriguing enough to pull the trigger. Sure, he’s not going to net Washington much in return, but getting him off the team, which may be a distraction at the moment, and giving him a fresh start elsewhere may be best for both parties. If you were head coach Dan Quinn, what would you choose to do with the diminutive corner? Please discuss in the comments section.

title: What advanced stats tell us about Commanders loss to Cowboys — Stats and Snaps
summary: The Commanders were always going to go as far as Jayden Daniels took them this season. On the final play of the first half, Daniels dislocated the same elbow as he did last season. At the time of this story’s Thursday publication, the prognosis is unknown. He could miss anywhere from three weeks to the […]
full_text: The Commanders were always going to go as far as Jayden Daniels took them this season. On the final play of the first half, Daniels dislocated the same elbow as he did last season. At the time of this story’s Thursday publication, the prognosis is unknown. He could miss anywhere from three weeks to the rest of the season. The speed of Daniels’ recovery and return to play will likely set the limit on the Commanders’ season outlook. That is all up in the air right now. While Daniels’ injury was a disaster and the play on both sides of the ball left plenty of room for improvement, it wasn’t all bad. On the positive side, Washington’s offense ranked second in the league in rushing average in Week 2 at 5.7 yards per attempt, while the run defense held the Cowboys to just 3.1 yards/attempt, tied for 8 th lowest in the league. The Commanders’ rushing attack generated four explosive runs (>10 yds), putting them in a 4-way tie for 4 th in the league. The defense held Dallas to just one explosive run, putting them in a 5-way tie for last place (in a good way). On the not so positive side, the Commanders averaged just 5.9 net yards per pass attempt on offense (rank 20 th ); while the defense allowed Dak Prescott to average 8.1 net yards per attempt (rank 5 th ). Washington’s pass defense conceded four explosive plays (completions > 20 yds), which put them in a seven-way tie for 9 th most in Week 2. Meanwhile, the offense made three of their own, which put them in a four-way tie for 16 th place. As of Week 3, the Commanders are hovering at league average in offensive efficiency (weighted EPA/play) and have sunk to a little below average in defensive efficiency: Graphic courtesy of RBSDM.com Can Daronte Jones make the adjustments needed on defense to keep the team competitive while Marcus Mariota buys them time at QB? It will be a challenge. But there were some glimmers of hope in Week 2, including solid play from Mariota and standout performances by RB Rachaad White, RT Josh Conerly Jr, OLB K’Lavon Chaisson, and DT Javon Kinlaw, as well as flashes from a few others, including rookie WR Antonio Williams, veteran WR Dyami Brown, LT Brandon Coleman and CB Amik Robertson. Now, let’s take a look at how the Commanders’ individual players fared in the Week 2 road loss to the Dallas Cowboys. Technicalities: Last season, I began listing advanced stats from both Pro Football Focus (PFF) and Pro Football Reference (PFR) to give readers alternative perspectives and to raise awareness of the variability of advanced stats between observers. This has resulted in some cluttering of the narrative and left readers wondering what to believe when the two stats services give varying accounts. Starting this week, I will make an effort to reduce the clutter by emphasizing consensus of stats which can differ as a result of judgement calls (e.g coverage yardage, broken tackles) and by picking a preferred source in cases where advanced stats from different sources are scored differently, making them not comparable (e.g. pressure counts, yards before contact). As always, official NFL stats trump those from PFF and PFR, right or wrong. OFFENSE Prior to his game-ending injury on the last play of the first half, Jayden Daniels played an efficient game at QB, completing 11-of-17 passes (64.7%, ADOT 11.1 yds ) for 96 yds and 1 TD, with 1 throw-away and 1 dropped by the receiver. He also ran 7 times (6 scrambles) for 79 yds (9.9 Y/A) with a long of 20. Jayden’s 70.7 total QBR ranked 14 th among starting QBs in Week 2. Marcus Mariota’s passing game in the second half was even more efficient than the injured starter he replaced. The Commanders backup QB completed 11-of-16 passes (68.8%, ADOT 12.4 yds) for 111 yds and 1 TD, with no throw aways or drops. Mariota was less of a threat on the ground, with just 1 carry for 3 yds. His effort earned an impressive 84.0 total QBR. Yardage before contact and broken tackle figures were sourced from Pro Football Reference. After a tenuous start in Week 1, Rachaad White stepped it up against Dallas, leading Commanders’ backs with 43 yards and 4 first downs on 7 carries (6.1 Y/A), with 2 broken tackles. White’s 85.7% rushing success rate was the second highest among RBs in Week 2 after Derrick Henry (87.5%, min 5 att.). White averaged 3.4 yards before contact/attempt, which is better than the 90 th percentile based on 2025 season stats. White also led the team with 6 receptions (100% rec rate), and was third in receiving total at 40 yds. He was the Commanders’ second most productive receiver at a respectable 1.74 Y/RR. Jacory Croskey-Merritt had the same total yardage as White, but it took him 12 carries to get there. His rushing average (3.6 Y/A) was the lowest among the RBs. Running behind the same blockers as White, Bill averaged just 2.0 YBC/att, a little below the 2025 NFL average. Bill caught his only passing target for a 5-yard reception. Kaytron Allen had 5 rushing attempts for 24 yards (4.8 Y/A). Terry McLaurin caught 2 of 9 targets (22.2%) for 50 yds at an ADOT of 13.7 yds, with 1 drop. He was the Commanders’ third most productive receiver at 1.47 Y/RR. However, he had the lowest receiving success rate at just 22.2%. Terry was also flagged for a questionable 9 yard offensive pass interference penalty in the first quarter. Stefon Diggs picked up where he left off in the fourth quarter in Philadelphia. Playing primarily in the slot, he caught 5-of-6 targets (83.3%) for 47 yds at an ADOT of 12.0 yds, and was 2-for-2 on contested targets. He was the Commanders’ most productive receiver at 2.04 Y/RR. His 83.3% receiving success rate might lead the team in many games, but was only fifth best on Sunday. Antonio Williams played a nearly equal mix of snaps in the slot and out wide. He caught 3-of-3 targets for 24 yds at an ADOT of 5.3 yds. Through his first 2 NFL games, he is 7-for-7 for 88 yds and a TD, with a 100% receiving success rate. Williams also attempted 1 pass for an incompletion. Dyami Brown caught 4-of-6 targets (66.6%) for 21 yds at an ADOT of 3.2 yds, with 1 drop. He seemed to be robbed of a 35 yd TD reception by a bad call by the officials: If this isn’t a touchdown in the NFL anymore I don’t know what is bro!!! pic.twitter.com/fjuqLhmE9F — Cornelius Davidson (@CorneliusDGNTV) September 20, 2026 Had that TD been credited to him, he would have been the Commanders’ leading receiver. Brown lost a fumble, forced by Jaishawn Barham, in the third quarter. He also completed 1 pass for 0 yds. Treylon Burks did not catch his lone target. Jaylin Lane was not targeted. Despite getting the fewest snaps, Colson Yankoff led the tight end group in receiving yardage for the first time in his pro career, as the result of catching his lone target for a 14 yard reception. Ben Sinnott was not far behind at 1-for-1 for 6 yards. Sinnott also led the team in snaps at fullback. None of the tight ends earned a PFF run blocking grade above 60, which is a little unusual (Yankoff 59.7, Bates 58.0, Sinnott 54.0). Pressure counts and run-blocking grades were sourced from Pro Football Focus. Brandon Coleman left the game early with a finger injury. In 37 pressure opportunities (pass reps minus spikes and no-plays) he allowed three QB hurries. His 8.1% pressure rate in pass protection is a bottom quartile figure for starting OTs based on 2025 season stats. His 95.8 run blocking grade, on the other hand, led all NFL offensive linemen in Week 2 (min 20 blocking snaps). Coleman was penalized five yards for being ineligible downfield. Chris Paul allowed 0 pressures in 42 opportunities. His 48.2 run-blocking grade was the second lowest on the team at any position. Nick Allegretti allowed 1 hurry and 1 QB hit in pass protection. His 4.8% pressure rate is a bottom quartile figure for starting centers. His 46.7 run-blocking grade was the lowest on the team. full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 20: Stefon Diggs #3 of the Washington Commanders looks on prior to a game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 24 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Antonio Williams Impressive Start [The play described in this excerpt is the same one shown in video on the tweet embedded below] There were multiple strong reports on Williams throughout the offseason and in training camp, but you never really know how a rookie is going to do until you see them in a game. So how has he fared in his first two games? Williams has totaled seven catches on seven targets for 88 yards and a touchdown. Five of his seven catches have picked up first downs. Those stats are the second best of any receiver on the team, behind only Stefon Diggs. But stats only tell part of the story, so let’s dive into the film. We’ll start first with some plays from his NFL debut against the Eagles. We saw a lot of what Williams is about on his first career catch. On this play, Williams lines up in a stacked set with Jaylin Lane to the left of the formation. The pair execute a switch release. Lane lines up outside of Williams, but he releases inside and works over the middle, while Williams releases outside and works vertical. Williams gets matched up against Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean and he beats him with a very nice route. As he releases outside, Williams widens his route from his starting point in the seam out to the top of the numbers. By widening like this, he gives himself the ability to be a legitimate threat to cut in any direction with space both outside and inside available to him. He’s always cutting back inside due to the route, but DeJean doesn’t know that. So as he gets to the top of the route, Williams does a nice job squaring up and making DeJean believe he could legitimately be breaking either way. Because of that threat, DeJean looks to get physical and tries to stay on top of the route, but Williams makes too sharp of a cut, stopping quickly on the 10 yard line and cutting back inside. He uses DeJean’s physical style against him, fighting through the contact and using a throw-by technique to push DeJean beyond him, creating more space to work with inside. DeJean takes a few extra steps to slow down, by which point Williams is already by him. Quarterback Jayden Daniels does a nice job progressing through his reads and getting all the way back to Williams, who he finds over the middle for a nice gain and nearly a touchdown. But it wasn’t just one route that Wiliams ran well in that opener against the Eagles. Even when he wasn’t getting the ball, he was giving defenders trouble with his route running. If Antonio Williams continues on his current path, it won’t be long before he establishes himself as one of the Commanders top receivers. I broke down his encouraging start: https://t.co/3bt0fR7M6L pic.twitter.com/9Kt4CJcSrS — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) September 24, 2026 Download the SB Nation app Commanders fans, take command of game day! Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Chat live during every game Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . ESPN Commanders reject notion they abandoned Daniels: “Stuff is nonsense” Daniels’ injury happened on the last play of the first half, which led to confusion by the players about what they could do or how long they could linger. Though the camera showed them walking past Daniels, almost all waited on the sideline and watched from there. A number of them then returned to Daniels’ side after trainers had popped his dislocated elbow back into place. But Washington coach Dan Quinn said, “When the half is over, the referees are saying, ‘Man, I can’t delay the half. They can’t stay on the field.’ The players were like, ‘No, we want to stay.’ “So it’s just the opposite of that. They were gutted. They love this guy. So halftime was hard and emotional in that space.” “We stayed on the field and once they got it situated and did what they had to do we checked on him,” Coleman said. “Dan told most [players] to go into the locker room. But it’s tough to go in when you see something like that. You see the whole starting line out there, a bunch of receivers, some defensive guys.” A number of players indeed were seen standing around Daniels — as Coleman said there were offensive linemen, defensive linemen, defensive backs, receivers and running backs. Linebackers were seen exiting as well as Daniels’ cart drove away. Coleman and fellow lineman Josh Conerly Jr., were among the last two to leave, along with Quinn and backup quarterbacks Marcus Mariota and Athan Kaliakmanis. “We know we had to get back in the locker room,” receiver Terry McLaurin said after the game, “but no one wanted to leave. That’s our brother.” “All that stuff is ridiculous,” Sinnott said. “As far as the love and brotherhood we have for Jayden, it’s really strong.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE From The Athletic: The clip shown on the Fox broadcast missed several aspects of what transpired, Washington players said Wednesday. For starters, Quinn followed the official’s instructions and told players to get back to the locker room. In the locker room after the game at AT&T Stadium, players were clearly distraught. “It’s bulls— what people are saying,” Coleman said. “Jay’s our guy. He’s been our guy. There was no malice behind that. My thought process was, ‘(The medical staff has) got to go.’ I saw the injury happen. I saw what happened, and I just wanted to give them space to do what they have to do. It’s no good for 30 guys to stand right there looking over when they’re trying to get an elbow back in.” To read more of this article from The Athletic, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Washington Spent All Offseason Preaching Takeaways. Two Games In, That Message Hasn’t Paid Off As of this past Sunday, Washington has not forced a single turnover through two regular-season games. This was a major offseason focus and remains a constant practice focus because the team was near the bottom of the league in takeaways a season ago and entered this year looking to correct that. Edge rusher Odafe Oweh believes it’s just a matter of time: “It’s going to get loose soon. It’s bound to stop. If we keep forcing the issue, keep punching the ball out, it’s going to get loose.” Oweh’s point rests on the reasoning that the Commanders haven’t abandoned the mindset because the results haven’t followed. The defense believes continuing to attack the ball will eventually produce the much-needed takeaways. Of course, forcing turnovers contains an element of randomness, but creating repeated opportunities to force them does not. title: NFL Week 3 betting guide: Analysis and top plays for Sunday's games
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 3 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game-winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 3.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week  | Solak's plays  | Walder's props 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 Kansas City Chiefs at Miami Dolphins (-10.5, 46.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Hard Rock Stadium, Miami Gardens, Fla.

 

 I tend to stay away from double-digit spreads in this league (especially for road favorites). That can be bad business given the talent level and coaching we get on Sundays. But looking at the matchup and scheme advantages with Kansas City, I'm in on Andy Reid's team. I'll give you my quick notes for both clubs, along with some player props.

 

 When the Chiefs have the ball: The offseason addition of Kenneth Walker III has given the Chiefs a true difference-maker with dual-threat traits in the backfield. Walker has rushed for at least 117 yards -- with at least 23 carries -- in both games this season, and in a Week 2 win over the Indianapolis Colts he caught six of 10 targets for 61 yards. We can expect Walker to get his touches on the ground against a Miami defense giving up 112.5 rushing yards per game (18th in the NFL), which allows Reid's unit to control offensive tempo.

 In the pass game, I see clear matchup advantages for the Chiefs. The Dolphins are giving up an average of 8.6 YPA (30th in the NFL), and they play man coverage at a rate of 58.9% (fourth most). Look for Reid to set up his receivers for catch-and-run throws from Patrick Mahomes , with Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce working multiple levels of the field against a Miami secondary that lacks high-end talent.

 When Miami has the ball: The Dolphins have struggled to build offensive rhythm and lack an identity, having failed to score more than 13 points in each of their first two games. Running back De'Von Achane has rushed for a total of 110 yards this season, and we aren't seeing his elite pass-catching ability (he has only 49 yards receiving). Quarterback Malik Willis has shown flashes, but his accuracy has been inconsistent (completing 58% of his passes), and he has thrown only one touchdown pass.

 Now, Miami does have some young talent in the pass game with Malik Washington , Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell , but the Dolphins lack a proven No. 1 who can win critical game situations at a high rate. They average only 183.5 passing yards per game, and now get a multiple Chiefs defense -- one that leans on late movement and schemed pressure. This Kansas City defense is giving up 90 yards rushing per game and only 5.5 YPA. Miami will need to find a way to create positive game flow while producing some explosive plays to stay in this one.

 

 Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

 Rashee Rice receiving yards OVER 47.5 (-114) 

 Rice, who caught four of six targets for 83 yards in the Week 2 win over the Colts, could have early opportunities against the Dolphins' single-high man coverages. Rice can turn an underneath throw into an explosive gain.

 Travis Kelce receptions OVER 4.5 receptions (-114) 

 Kelce's play speed looked different last week against the Colts, both in the route stem and after the catch. Kelce caught nine of 11 targets in that game, using his high-end coverage awareness to find open grass. He should be a priority target again for Mahomes on Sunday.

 Tyquan Thornton anytime TD (+475) 

 I'm thinking of a shot-play throw here to Thornton on Sunday. Thornton caught all four of his targets for 86 yards last week against the Colts, so look for Reid to set up him on a deep-ball concept in Miami.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Baltimore Ravens -3.5 (-105) vs. Dallas Cowboys 

 Injuries are important to watch heading into this game. Not one of WR Zay Flowers , OT Ronnie Stanley or OLB Trey Hendrickson practiced Wednesday for the Ravens. Still, head coach Jesse Minter said after practice that he feels "like we will have a good shot with a lot of guys this week."

 

 Assuming the Ravens are relatively close to full strength, I like their matchup against Dallas quite a bit. The Cowboys' back seven has struggled tremendously through two weeks of the Christian Parker era on defense; it's a challenging defensive scheme, and they are generally lacking for team speed. Their light edge rushers can be targeted in the run game. Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has excelled at two things so far: attacking the edge in the running game, and generating YAC opportunities for Flowers. Baltimore might steamroll the Cowboys.

 I'm a little worried about the travel and field in Brazil, which can introduce some chaos. The Cowboys' offense can also score in bunches. But the Ravens are a better pressure team, thanks to the play of Hendrickson and Minter's willingness to send pressures on key downs. I like them to get enough stops in what should be a high-scoring affair.

 I'd take this up to -4 (-110), but only if we get positive injury news throughout the week.

 Zay Flowers 90+ receiving yards (+154) 

 I have all of the Flowers overs and alts for similar reasons listed above. Flowers was red hot in Week 1, with five catches for 150 yards and a score on six targets in just the first half against Indianapolis. Now he gets a Cowboys secondary that might be without starting CB Cobie Durant and S P.J. Locke , both of whom defensive coordinator Brian Schottenheimer said are likely to sit out multiple weeks, and fellow safety Malik Hooker , who fractured his forearm in Week 1, sat out Week 2 and did not practice Wednesday. The Cowboys' secondary is already bleeding talent.

 This also is a bust-riddled group that has already dealt with communication changes (rookie third-round LB Jaishawn Barham wore the green dot in Week 2) because of linebacker injuries. With Flowers' speed and positional versatility, the Ravens should be able to funnel him easy targets in space at will.

 Of course, Flowers might not go this week; he's dealing with a hamstring injury, and the field in Brazil is reportedly imperfect. But if he does go, I want to have his numbers from early in the week before they get steamed.

 Houston Texans -2.5 (-118) at Indianapolis Colts 

 Two 0-2 division rivals seemingly with their seasons already on the line -- intense stuff for Week 3. I admired the Colts' pluck in their game against the Chiefs, but the Texans' defense is made of far stiffer stuff. Houston has won the last five games between the teams, though QB  Daniel Jones was hurt for the most recent matchup.

 

 The Colts have relied heavily on big-play receiver Alec Pierce to generate explosive plays against DeMeco Ryans' aggressive defense. Last season against the Texans across two games, Pierce had eight catches, 210 yards and three touchdowns. Pierce hurt his heel against the Chiefs and is on injured reserve, which puts all the more pressure on Josh Downs , Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell at receiver. It's hard to imagine the Colts finding the same big plays that the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals have against this Texans secondary.

 I'm happy to buy the Texans now before the number hits -3, even though Nico Collins (hamstring) did not practice Wednesday. The reporting around the injury…

This ship will right itself. -- Walder 

 Viewers rating (out of 10): 8.4. This is an important game between two 1-1 AFC contenders. The Jaguars just came off a game in which interior pressure ruined them; now they get to block DTs  Milton Williams and Christian Barmore . If New England keeps ending drives early, Lawrence should get enough chances to cover three points. Read more . -- Maldonaldo

 Chargers (0-2) at Bills (2-0)

 What we're hearing on the Chargers: The Chargers' usual platitude-laden QB, Justin Herbert , broke character this week after Los Angeles fell to 0-2. He cut off a reporter's second question about vocal leadership with a fierce response. "I'm going to stop you right there and say that it's very present," he said. "I don't think anyone is panicked or worried because that's not going to be the sentiment. It's moving on to the next play and understanding that we're close; we've made mistakes -- how do we fix it?" -- Kris Rhim 

 What we're hearing on the Bills: WR DJ Moore ( shoulder ) returned to practice in a limited capacity this week, and he and coach Joe Brady spoke optimistically about his chances of being available Sunday. But Brady cautions against correlating offensive aggressiveness directly to Moore's downfield talents: "The average depth of target is never important to me. A long incompletion doesn't do much either." -- Nick Suss
