title: Mike LaFleur's coaching roots fast track to NFL
summary: The Shanahan-LaFleur dynamic spreads to Arizona, where new head coach Mike has taken the reins in the desert.
full_text:
TEMPE, Arizona -- Mike LaFleur's career is about to come full circle on Sunday.

 Twelve years ago, as a 27-year-old, LaFleur's first NFL season was spent on the banks of Lake Erie as an offensive intern for the Cleveland Browns under the direction of a young, up-and-coming offensive coordinator named Kyle Shanahan.

 Until then, LaFleur had spent his coaching career at small colleges such Division III Elmhurst, Division II J Joseph's and Division I FCS Davidson, watching his older brother, Matt, make the jump to the NFL in 2008 and engrain himself with a group of young, nascent coaches who would go on to become friends and a coaching "crew," as one of them described it, that currently holds six of the league's 32 head-coaching jobs.

 In Week 1, that "crew", which includes Rams head coach Sean McVay, Tennessee Titans head coach Robert Saleh, Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur and Shanahan, the San Francisco 49ers head coach, watched as Mike LaFleur walked the sidelines as a head coach for the first time, getting a win in his debut. And on Sunday, they'll all have an eye on his first game as a head coach against his NFL sherpa, Shanahan, when the Cardinals visit the 49ers (4:05 p.m. ET, Fox). Mike LaFleur was Shanahan's pass game coordinator and wide receivers coach from 2017 to 2020.

 The sentimentality of the moment Sunday has lost its shine after LaFleur faced Shanahan six times during three seasons as the Rams' offensive coordinator, but this one will, eventually, mean something.

 "When you're in the moment, you're in the moment, you're not thinking about that stuff," LaFleur said. "I'm excited to see him before the game, obviously, say what's up, but then it's on and that's how they're going to feel and that's how we feel.

 "And I'm sure when all is said and done next February and we get to see each other in the offseason, we'll talk about it. But I mean, this is the Niners versus the Cardinals."

 In LaFleur, who followed Shanahan from Cleveland to the Atlanta Falcons and then to the 49ers -- seven straight seasons in all -- Shanahan saw someone who was "as good as any of those other guys" that Shanahan had on his staff.

 That's saying something coming from Shanahan.

 Seven of his former assistants, starting from his time as the Houston Texans' offensive coordinator in 2008 to his time as the 49ers head coach, have gone on to become NFL head coaches. And it's quite a group: McVay, Matt LaFleur, Saleh, Hafley, former Dolphins head coach and current Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, Houston Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans and, now, Mike LaFleur.

 "I've had a couple of these guys and Mike's right there with all those dudes in terms of he's very smart, he knows the game," Shanahan said. "There's lots of coaches who can do some good stuff, but you always know guys in your building who see it a little bit better than most people, and Mike's one of those guys."

 

 

 MIKE'S THE BABY of the group of Shanahan disciples at 39 years old, and after he got hired, the love showered on him felt like big brothers bragging about their little sibling.

 "I think he's one of the real good guys in this league," Hafley said. "He's going to treat people the right way."

 "Mikey's going to be a successful head coach because of his ability to communicate with his players, communicate with everyone in the building," Saleh said. "He's got a clear vision, and he can articulate it the right way."

 They're spread out across divisions and conferences but still keep tabs on each other. Hackett and Matt LaFleur FaceTime regularly. Mike and Matt talk often. And they see each other throughout the season. 

 "It's a cool, close-knit circle in the National Football League where if you're fortunate enough to be here long enough, you can work with some really talented people," McDaniel said.

 And after LaFleur's Week 1 over the Chargers, the texts flooded in.

 "I was really happy for Mike," McVay said. "He's obviously one of my closest friends and I love Mike. He's meant a lot to me and my family, his family has. I thought it was an awesome day for the Cardinals. I thought they looked really good in all three phases. I got a chance to watch that whole game.

 "It's unique because they're in the division, but it overrides because it's like family. Being able to see mom and dad and how nervous they were in the stands. ...Mom was excited to see it, even when they were in four-minute mode and had control when they showed them on the TV, and seeing Lauren and the kids. It was cool. They looked awesome."

 Hackett couldn't help but smile thinking about everyone attached to each other becoming a head coach at some point in their careers, him included in 2022 with the Denver Broncos for a season.

 "It's awesome," Hackett said. "I mean, all of us. I'm so happy for anybody that gets that opportunity. I mean, the reality of it is you never know what's going to happen."

 Yet, his friends recognize why LaFleur has a shot to be a success. "I think the biggest thing for Mike," said Ryans, who was on the 49ers staff with LaFleur from 2017 to 2020, "is him being able to learn under Kyle for however many years he was there."

 

 

 ON THE DAY LaFleur was introduced as the Cardinals' head coach, Washington Commanders head coach Dan Quinn, who hired LaFleur in Atlanta in 2015, sent him a quick text message. He followed up with a call later that night to tell LaFleur how "pumped I am for him" and that he'd be there for LaFleur to bounce ideas off or if something comes across his desk that he didn't know how to handle or wasn't prepared for as a first-time head coach.

 Then, about six weeks later, at the NFL's annual meetings in Phoenix, Quinn got to tell LaFleur in person how proud he was of his latest protégé becoming a head coach. In 2015, when Quinn was hired as the Atlanta Falcons' head coach, he built a staff that included LaFleur as an offensive assistant, his brother as quarterbacks coach, Shanahan as offensive coordinator and McDaniel as another offensive assistant.

 All four have gone on to be head coaches. "I would say I hope during the time that we were together, there's something that was significant in their development to be where they're at and be authentic in that way," Quinn told ESPN. "And I'm hopeful that I showed that and demonstrated that in some way to them and that they're able to hit into that same space.

 "But, man, I'm incredibly proud of them."

 Commanders reporter John Keim, Dolphins reporter Marcel Louis-Jaques, 49ers reporter Nick Wagoner, Titans reporter Turron Davenport, Rams reporter Sarah Barshop and Chargers reporter Kris Rhim contributed to this report.

title: NFL Week 3 uniforms: Colts to wear 'Anvil Strike,' Bills debut 'Nickel City'
summary: Here's a look at what each NFL team is wearing in Week 3, led by the new NFL Rivalries look from the Indianapolis Colts.
full_text:
Tuesday marked the first day of fall. The blue skies across the country will turn to gray with the colder months approaching. But to spot a more immediate gray shade, look no further than NFL uniforms in Week 3 -- namely, the Indianapolis Colts and Buffalo Bills . 

 

 Indianapolis will debut its Rivalries uniform against the Houston Texans . Nicknamed "Anvil Strike," they are inspired by the steel of an anvil and the jersey's "dark anthracite" color is one that "embodies the grit and intensity of Colts football." The all-gray threads are complete with a metallic blue helmet. For the first time in team history, the Colts' horseshoe is included on one of their uniforms -- a silver version appears on the sleeve. Other uniform elements are classic blue numbers and "For The Shoe" on the inside collar. The Colts are the first team to debut the latest batch of Rivalries uniforms this season. 

 Buffalo is similarly wearing all-gray when it faces the Los Angeles Chargers at home. The "Nickel City" uniforms are a tribute to the "strength, grit and authenticity" of Western New York. The all-gray design is directly inspired by the Buffalo Nickel , a coin minted from 1913 to 1938. A metallic royal blue "charge" helmet tops the look. The helmet's design is meant to bring a charging buffalo to life with the horn, eye and charge streak displayed in red. 

 The Denver Broncos will wear their midnight navy alternate look on "Sunday Night Football" against the Los Angeles Rams . Denver first introduced the look ahead of the 2024 season and is 2-0 in the all-navy combination . Last year, the Broncos paired their summit white helmet with the threads, but they'll go with a navy-colored lid this time around.

 In the throwback space, the Jacksonville Jaguars are rocking their classic prowler design . First unveiled in 2024, the teal uniforms include a prowling jaguar on the sleeves and a black helmet with the franchises' original primary logo on it. The numbers boast a custom font in white with a black and gold trim. A similar three-color accent runs down the white pants in a teal stripe with gold and black trim.

title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why you should use 49ers, Chiefs in Week 3
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and picks for Week 3 including the 49ers and Chiefs.
full_text:
Welcome to 2026 ESPN NFL Survivor ! The rules are simple: Pick one NFL team each week to win its game. If that team wins (or ties), you advance to the next week. If that team loses, you are out. Survive all 18 weeks and you can take home a share of the $25,000 grand prize. The catch is that each team can be chosen only once.

 While the rules are simple, the game theory is not. Depending on the size of your group or what platform you play on, the optimal selections could change drastically. Smaller groups will likely end well before Week 18, so optimizing win probability each week is paramount. However, the larger the group, the more you need to focus on saving strong teams for later. ESPN's game requires just one team each week, so that will be the strategic focus of this column, though we will touch on the big contests at Circa and Splash Sports.

 

 For the second straight week, the most-selected team in ESPN Survivor lost as an 8.5-point favorite. In Week 1, the Chargers knocked out 21% of entries, falling to the Cardinals. In Week 2, it was the Buccaneers' turn, blowing a 10-point lead at home against the Cleveland Browns to eliminate 27% of the field. That wasn't the only Week 2 upset, as the Chargers lost again as 6.5-point favorites, while the Baltimore Ravens were stunned by the New Orleans Saints as 8.5-point favorites.

 As a result, 68% of the original entries are already out just two weeks into the season. The Chargers are responsible for 33% of those eliminations, while the Buccaneers are responsible for another 23%.

 This week, the major decision concerns the Kansas City Chiefs , who are going to be the most-selected team so far (currently 35%). Even though they are on the road, they are the largest betting favorites as they face the Miami Dolphins . Plus, they are widely available, having been used by only 9% of entries.

 The second-biggest favorites are the San Francisco 49ers , who are available to only 59% of the ESPN Survivor field after hammering Miami last week. They are the only other team besides the Chiefs laying more than a touchdown, but with three of their next five games coming against the  Washington Commanders , Atlanta Falcons  and Ravens, they will be a staple of this column.

 

 I was planning on making the New York Giants my top choice on Monday morning, but after injuries to Jaxson Dart and others on Monday night, they are a much more difficult click. The Green Bay Packers also were going to be one of my top picks before Sunday's games, but they looked sluggish in an overtime win against the New York Jets and picked up more injuries. The Philadelphia Eagles are a consideration if Case Keenum starts for the Chicago Bears , but they have less win equity than other teams while having strong future value, so I will pass. And as bad as the Pittsburgh Steelers offense has looked, I am not ready to fade them as a divisional home underdog against the Cincinnati Bengals .

 For contests that require multiple picks this week, the Carolina Panthers are a fun but risky pick. Despite last week's win, the Browns still grade out as the third-worst team in the NFL according to ESPN Analytics, and the Panthers aren't projected to be more than a 54% favorite again until Week 18 according to our two models.

 All that said, my top two picks for ESPN will be the two biggest favorites, the 49ers and the Chiefs. 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 The Road to 18-0 

 
 Week 1: Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Browns) -- Win 
 Week 2: San Francisco 49ers (vs. Dolphins) -- Win 
 Week 3: Kansas City Chiefs (at Dolphins)  
 

 

 1.   San Francisco 49ers (vs. Cardinals ) 

 If you still have the 49ers available, the best question is when to deploy them. Considering that both our models have this as the most-lopsided game this week and the easiest game remaining for the 49ers, and they will likely be less than 10% owned, this is as good a week as any. They are a stronger pick in ESPN and Circa than they are in the two main Splash contests.

 
 Chance to win: 89% (ESPN Analytics), 91% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: 49ers -8.5 (-485 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fourth 
 ESPN Selection: 7% 
 

 2. Kansas City Chiefs (at Dolphins ) 

 

 The Chiefs will be the heavy chalk, but deservingly so as they are the biggest betting favorites while also having less future value than any of the other big favorites. Plus, for those of you in contests that have double-pick weeks, most of the Chiefs' hardest matchups fall in those slots, making them even less valuable down the road. They will likely be my most-selected team on both major Splash contests.

 
 Chance to win: 84% (ESPN Analytics), 87% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Chiefs -11.5 (-850 moneyline) 
 Future value: Ninth 
 ESPN Selection: 35% 
 

 3. Detroit Lions (vs. Jets ) 

 Out of the three teams favored by around a touchdown, I lean towards the Lions, especially on ESPN. While the Lions have eight games after this week where our models have them as at least a 60% favorite right now, they don't have the high-end ceiling of the  Seattle Seahawks and Buffalo Bills  with no games higher than a 79% win probability. Detroit is a very valuable team to hold on Splash, since most of their easiest games fall in double-pick weeks, but if you've burned the 49ers already and want to fade the Chiefs, the Lions are a fine pivot.

 
 Chance to win: 75% (ESPN Analytics), 75% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Lions -6.5 (-305 moneyline) 
 Future value: Eighth 
 ESPN Selection: 10% 
 

 4. New Orleans Saints (vs. Raiders ) 

 

 Finally, a riskier pick for those of you who truly like to hoard the elite teams. The Saints are under 2% selected right now, and with so many other teams trending higher, they will likely remain low. New Orleans' remaining schedule is one of the easiest, but the Saints are ranked only 17th by ESPN Analytics, which is not the type of team you are obligated to save. Both of our models are higher on the Saints than the betting market, so they are a fine contrarian pick with risk.

 
 Chance to win: 65% (ESPN Analytics), 71% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Saints -3 (-185 moneyline) 
 Future value: 15th 
 ESPN Selection: 2% 
 

 5. Green Bay Packers (vs. Falcons ) 

 

 It's a tough spot for the Packers, coming off an overtime game on Sunday with a game on Thursday. Teams in that spot are 13-37 all-time. Combine that with injuries to Zach Bako-Bewele and Jayden Reed , while the Falcons get back Michael Penix Jr ., and it makes sense Atlanta is taking money. But our models like the Packers more than the betting market does. And out of all the teams favored by four-plus points, no team has a harder schedule than the Packers, despite a Week 15 home games against Miami. Ultimately, their ownership keeps them this low on the list. While I expect them to come in lower than 14%, there are too many other options to take on the risk.

 
 Chance to win: 74% (ESPN Analytics), 79% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Packers -5.5 (-265 moneyline) 
 Future value: 14th 
 ESPN Selection: 14% 
 

 6. Carolina Panthers (at Browns ) 
 

 The Panthers have too little of a win probability for me to trust them on ESPN, which is why they are ranked this low, but in contests with double-pick weeks this early, they are firmly in play. To survive the season undefeated in the Big Splash, you will use 26 teams, meaning that eventually you have to take some mediocre teams against bad teams. Despite last week's upset win, the Browns are still one of the three worst teams in the NFL. ESPN Analytics' model is high on the Panthers compared to the betting market, and with Carolina having little future value, this is a spot to gain leverage.

 
 Chance to win: 63% (ESPN Analytics), 54% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Panthers -2.5 (-148 moneyline) 
 Future value: 28th 
 ESPN Selection : 6%

title: Predicting the next five Super Bowl champions
summary: Ben Solak had some fun and did the impossible -- picked Super Bowl winners for the 2026 to 2030 seasons. And there are some surprises ...
full_text:
ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February 2027. We will count down to the big game with Super Bowl-centric stories every month. 

 Super Bowl winners are, by definition, improbable. It's not just the 1-out-of-32 math. It is mostly due to the fact that the NFL plays a best-of-one playoff series -- no best-of-five or best-of-seven series to save a good team that has a bad game or unlucky break. It's also the fact that injury attrition eliminates multiple playoff teams before the ball is ever snapped. It is so, so hard to win a Super Bowl.

 It's even harder to predict who will win a Super Bowl -- let alone the next five. (Why does nobody ever write about how much tougher my job is than an NFL head coach's?) We're two weeks into the 2026 season , and I have no idea who will win the Super Bowl in February. But I gave my best mid-September bet. Then, I went to next year (which is still kind of reasonable). And then I predicted the year after that (which was totally wacky). And then I did two more just because.

 To build this list, I tried not to be too scientific. A rigorous look at elite quarterbacks, elite coaches and a pedigree of winning would have given us ... the Chiefs, Rams and Seahawks in every Super Bowl down the way. I was reminded of Seth Walder's lovely FPI preseason simulation piece, in which he selects just one simulation from the set of thousands run during the preseason to determine team strength. It's a reminder that predicting an exact outcome -- not the likeliest outcome, but one exact outcome -- should carry with it some challenges to credulity. So ( spoiler alert ), if Ravens fans and Bills fans are upset that they are not included below, just know this: Browns fans and Dolphins fans also have the right to be upset.

 

 Remember to take these predictions as seriously as possible. Aggregate them with the headline "ESPN NFL analyst predicts [insert team] to win a Super Bowl within five seasons!" A lot of people will click. And more importantly, absolutely nobody will angrily DM me on social media.

 Jump to a season: 
 2026  |  2027  | 2028  | 2029  | 2030 

 

 

 2026 season: Seattle Seahawks 
 It's a little weird to pick a Super Bowl champion for the current season when we have only a two-game sample. It would be easier with no games (here are my preseason vibes) or something like eight games (OK, these guys are definitely good).

 I usually don't pick repeats -- it's so hard to get back to the dance after a long season the year before -- but it's difficult to argue any team has been better than Seattle through this short season. Quarterback  Sam Darnold  ( hip ) went down in the first quarter against the Patriots in Week 1 , and Mike Macdonald's group is still 2-0.

 

 What stands out about Macdonald's Seahawks -- and what makes them feel so repeatable -- is how the defense hasn't missed a beat despite offseason departures. We usually feel the brain drain (and long-season exhaustion) of a Super Bowl champion early in the ensuing season -- that is not so in Seattle. The entire defensive coaching staff remained and has easily accounted for the departures of safety  Coby Bryant , cornerback  Riq Woolen and edge rusher  Boye Mafe .

 The work of new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury with backup quarterback Drew Lock  has been impressive; Lock was ripping throws over the middle with timing and accuracy. Getting good play out of a QB2 is not the same skill set as getting good play out of a QB1, but all of the signs I've seen from Seattle thus far are that Fleury can keep up Klint Kubiak's momentum. The improvements in the running game -- even before Zach Charbonnet returns from injured reserve -- are noticeable, too.

 If the Seahawks repeat ... are they a dynasty? Probably not. Dynasties are made over a decade of dominance, not consecutive championships. Darnold would become the ninth quarterback to win consecutive Super Bowls, and with only one year left on his deal, he would likely demand -- and get -- a market-rate contract at the level of Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen . What are the Seahawks going to do,  not give it him?

 

 What I think happens: Seattle loses the NFC West title to the Rams by tiebreaker rules ... only to beat the Rams in an NFC Championship rematch as the fifth seed. That game ends 22-21 on a successful Seahawks two-point conversion at the end of regulation (no fumble hijinks this time).   Seattle goes on to face the Texans (yes, the currently 0-2 Texans) in one of the lowest-scoring Super Bowls of the 2000s -- not quite the 13-3 Patriots-Rams score from 2019 but close. The Seahawks win 16-10 at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles. Cornerback  Devon Witherspoon wins MVP (as he should have last season) with a stuffed stat sheet: seven tackles, three TFLs, one sack and one interception.

 
 

 2027 season: Cincinnati Bengals 
 It's actually quite rare to see a quarterback make a Super Bowl and then make his next one six years later. John Elway is perhaps the best example, though he made three close together (1986, 1987, 1989) and then another two after a long hiatus (1997,1998). Elway and Joe Burrow would be the only two to do it with the same franchise. Craig Morton did it back in the 1970s with two teams -- as a Cowboy in 1970 and a Bronco in 1977 -- and Kurt Warner did it with the Rams in 2002 and the Cardinals in 2009.

 But I think Burrow can do it by sticking with the Bengals, who have endured injury-ruined years and defensive decay ever since reaching the Super Bowl in 2021 . Their huge 2026 offseason bet on Dexter Lawrence II (and other defensive improvements aside) serves as proof of their desperation to get back before the current regime of coach Zac Taylor, de facto GM Duke Tobin and Burrow undergoes a major shake-up.

 

 The Bengals have a great shot at representing the AFC in 2026 because of their stars at premium positions: quarterback (Burrow), wide receiver ( Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins ), cornerback ( DJ Turner II ) and offensive tackle ( Amarius Mims ). Their lack of a true star edge rusher is mitigated by the presence of Lawrence, who through two games has been exactly the force multiplier they hoped on the interior.

 I am, however, concerned about the youth on the team in a 2026 playoff run. A lot of those key defensive players haven't taken serious playoff snaps. Demetrius Knight Jr. , Barrett Carter ,  Dax Hill , Turner -- even Lawrence himself has only two games of postseason action. For as clutch as Burrow is, and how dangerous that offense is, it's easy to forget that the defense powered the Bengals' AFC playoff run in 2021 -- holding Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs to three points in the second half of the AFC Championship Game, intercepting Ryan Tannehill with 20 seconds left in the divisional round and holding on fourth-and-goal against the Raiders in the wild-card round.

 

 What I think happens: The Bengals will use a deep 2026 playoff run that falls just short to propel themselves over the hump in 2027. In free agency, the team retains both Turner and Hill (somehow, don't ask me) to keep the secondary in a strong spot. Cincinnati also swings a bold trade for offensive tackle  Laremy Tunsil as the Commanders rebuild, banking that he has one last great year in him -- and he does. The Super Bowl victory comes a year later than they hoped, but the Bengals get revenge on the Rams -- in what ends up as Matthew Stafford 's final season -- with a 31-30 last-second win at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta.

 
 

 2028 season: Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Projecting 2026 and 2027 at least has some sort of tether in our current reality, but 2028 is where things slide quickly into dreamland. Consider projecting the Seahawks to win the Super Bowl two years ago. Pete Carroll was still the head coach,  Geno Smith was the quarterback, and  Jaxon Smith-Njigba was the No. 3 receiver. The NFL can change so fast over a two-year window.

 So who do I pick? The Browns? The Dolphins?…

title: Texans face troubling trend when they play without Nico Collins
summary: Houston has seen a dip in scoring, and quarterback C.J. Stroud has seen his QBR decrease when targeting others.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- The absence of Pro Bowl wideout Nico Collins has created a trend for the  Houston Texans .

 In the last three games, including the playoffs, that Collins has missed because of injury, Houston's ability to score has been a mixed bag. Even though quarterback C.J. Stroud threw for 353 yards last week, the Texans (0-2) lost 20-6 to the Cincinnati Bengals  without Collins (hamstring), and Houston has averaged 16 points in that span.

 Coach DeMeco Ryans understands how vital their No. 1 wideout is to the success of the offense, but he's challenging others to step up.

 "Everyone knows Nico is one of the top receivers in the league," Ryans said. "A lot of guys have to step up to fill that void left by Nico. The bottom line is everybody is here, everybody gets paid to go make plays. We have to find a way to do that. We definitely, of course, miss Nico. When you have such an explosive threat in Nico, it's hard on a defense."

 

 He also didn't practice Wednesday or Thursday as Houston prepared to travel to face the winless  Indianapolis Colts  on Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ). That usually is an indication in Houston that he won't play as the Texans tend to be cautious with soft tissue injuries.

 Collins rested in the Week 18 finale against the Colts last season, and Stroud and other starters didn't play in the second half of the 38-30 win. But in the last three games when Collins was injured and didn't play, Stroud averaged 294 passing yards per game and threw three touchdowns with five interceptions -- four coming in their playoff loss to the New England Patriots .

 Houston has struggled to find a receiver to step up in Collins' absence. In those three games, no receiver has eclipsed 70 receiving yards, and only three have gone over 55 in Xavier Hutchinson  (69) against the San Francisco 49ers in 2025, Jaylin Noel in that same game (63), and Jayden Higgins  (59) -- who is expected to miss the season -- against the Patriots. Being without Higgins and Collins means the Texans are down their top two wide receivers.

 In last week's loss to the Bengals, Houston failed to score a touchdown. Tight end Dalton Schultz had 140 yards on 12 catches, but when it came time to beat man coverage, the wideouts struggled -- as Stroud went 8-of-20 for 102 yards against that coverage in Week 2. Kayshon Boutte  (acquired in a trade before the season to help soften the blow after the loss of Higgins) and Hutchinson led the receiving corps with 37 yards a piece. 

 One way to help overcome the loss of Collins, who had 7 receptions for 75 yards and a touchdown in the opener against the Buffalo Bills , is an effective running game to help keep them out of third-and-long situations where teams tend to play more man coverage.

 Houston's 3.7 yards per carry ranks better than only nine teams, and the Colts have played man coverage on 50% of the snaps (third most this season) against third-and-7 or longer.

 Stroud admitted following last week's loss that the key to winning is on third downs, as Houston went 5-of-17 in those situations. An important caveat is Stroud faced third-and-7 or longer on 12 of his 16 dropbacks and only converted two first downs.

 

 "I think we just got to do a better job on the outside of just winning," Stroud said. "I think when we started to get in the flow of the game, started motioning, I think [Hutchinson] played great. I thought [Noel] did great. I thought [ Jared Wayne ] did good as well and of course, Boutte. It's tough sometimes when you don't get the call but you feel like you should. Can't rely on that. We have to be better."

 Since being selected No. 2 in 2023, Stroud's QBR when targeting Collins is 91 with a touchdown-to-interception ratio of 22-6. He has a QBR of 45 with a ratio of 48-25 when targeting anyone else. The biggest thing though is the red zone efficiency. Since the start of last season, the Texans rank last in red zone touchdown percentage (46% -- league average is 58%). But in those three games without Collins, the Texans' percentage sinks to 15%.

 But Stroud is optimistic as they head into Week 3.

 "I think it'll be a lot better," Stroud said. "Of course, a player like Nico, his presence is always felt when he's on the field. It's tough not having him, but I think this week could be better. We had a great day of practice today. We'll be able to hopefully take what we did in practice and execute on Sunday."

title: Ranking eight winless NFL teams: Texans, Bucs, others at 0-2
summary: Can the Texans turn it around (again)? Do the Buccaneers, Colts or Chargers have a chance to get right? Is the season already over for the Falcons and Dolphins?
full_text:
This time every year, I tell you that the NFL playoffs secretly start in Week 3 . For the league's 0-2 teams, Week 3 might as well be an eliminator game.

 In an era with 17 games and 14 playoff teams, it's possible to dig out of an 0-2 hole and make it to the postseason, something three teams managed to do in 2025. Two of them -- the Bears and Panthers -- even managed to win their divisions at the end of the year.

 But since 2002, 102 teams have started their seasons by losing three consecutive games. Even if we expand our scope and treat the seventh seed from 2002 to 2019 as a would-be playoff team, just four of those 102 teams overcame their 0-3 start and finished in the playoff picture, for an advancement rate of 3.9%. Two of them were Mike Tomlin-led Steelers teams that finished seventh in the AFC in 2013 and 2019, missing the postseason because the league hadn't yet gone to the 14-team field.

 The other two teams were both editions of the Texans -- and they actually did advance to the playoffs. One came in 2018. The other was last season's Houston squad. The Texans started 0-3, losing to the Rams, Buccaneers and Jaguars by a combined 13 points. From that point forward, they went 12-2, with their only losses coming to the eventual top seeds in the AFC (Broncos) and NFC (Seahawks).

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Here we are one year later, and the Texans are back again, joining seven other winless teams through two weeks of the 2026 season. They'll be in the only matchup of 0-2 teams in Week 3 as they travel to Indianapolis to play the Colts . Can they get back on track and avoid needing to defy history yet again ? Are there any other teams that have a shot at making it back from 0-2 to advance into the playoffs?

 Today, I'll take stock of the eight 0-2 teams around the NFL, break down why each has gotten off to a slow start and rank their chances of still sneaking into the postseason. I also included chances to make the playoffs via ESPN's Football Power Index .

 For teams such as the Dolphins, a playoff berth in 2026 wasn't really in the cards to begin with. For many of the teams ahead of Miami, though, there's going to be a sense of urgency to fix things quickly. Nobody wants to give up on their playoff dreams and start thinking about 2027 after three weeks. The Falcons have the first chance to get into the win column with a Thursday night matchup against Green Bay , but they aren't No. 1 on this list as the most likely 0-2 team to turn it around.

 

 
 Jump to an 0-2 team: 
 ATL | HOU | IND | LAC 
 MIA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Houston Texans 
 Chances of advancing to the postseason, via ESPN's FPI : 41.8% (16th highest)

 Well, as we just discussed, the Texans have been here before, starting 0-3 and living to tell the tale in January -- even after losing  quarterback  C.J. Stroud for a month. That 2025 team went 12-2 after its 0-3 start, driven by the league's best defense. From Week 4 onward, the Texans led the NFL in points allowed per drive (1.5) and were second in EPA per play (minus-0.1). There aren't many 0-3 teams that can count on being the best at anything in football over a three-month span moving forward, which might be why the Texans are one of the rare exceptions to the rule I build this column around each year.

 This season's defense, though, hasn't been quite up to the usual standard. Starting with games against  Josh Allen and Joe Burrow might do that to a team, but the Texans are 19th in points allowed per drive and 23rd in EPA per play through two weeks. This same defense had also famously flummoxed Allen in regular-season victories during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, but Allen threw for 334 yards and was responsible for four touchdowns in Buffalo's Week 1 victory .

 

 I'm not sure it's time to get alarmed about the Texans' defense.  Derek Stingley Jr . has been Mossed for spectacular catches in back-to-back weeks by Dalton Kincaid and  Ja'Marr Chase , something that isn't going to happen on a weekly basis. Houston has yet to generate a turnover despite forcing two fumbles and a wild throw from Allen with the game on the line in Week 1, which Kamari Lassiter dropped (Allen threw the winning touchdown pass on the next snap). The 2025 Texans had just two games without a takeaway across their 19 regular-season and postseason contests. The 2026 Texans have two in two.

 Instead, I'd just point out that it's really difficult to be one of the very best defenses in football for any sort of multiyear stretch of time. The Texans aren't going to be a below-average unit for very long, and they're going to look a lot better when they're facing the likes of Daniel Jones and Cam Ward in the weeks to come. It would be stunning if they really struggled for months on end.

 Consider, though, that the Texans finished second in scoring defense last year. If we take the second-best scoring defense for each season since 2002 and see where they ranked the following year, their average rank fell to 12th. I would be surprised if the Texans were outside the top 10 by the time we looked at the end of the season, but it would hardly be a surprise or unreasonable to expect something closer to the bottom half of the top 10 than a return to the top two.

 And that would be an issue, because while Stroud has righted the ship after last season's disastrous playoff run, the problems that have plagued the Texans' offense around Stroud during his time in the pros haven't improved. After adding running back  David Montgomery , re-signing guard  Ed Ingram and offensive tackle  Trent Brown  and adding offensive linemen  Keylan Rutledge , Evan Brown , Wyatt Teller  and Braden Smith , the hope was that general manager Nick Caserio had finally found a running game for his quarterback.

 Through two weeks, that running game hasn't been present. The Texans are 28th in success rate, 29th in EPA per snap and 30th in yards per carry on designed runs. Montgomery scored three touchdowns in the opener, but he has found space hard to come by, averaging 2.7 yards per attempt on the ground. Part of the problem has been availability. Ingram missed the loss to the Bengals , and Smith is on injured reserve because a foot injury .

 The run issues materially impacted the Texans against the Bengals. Despite Caserio expressing his confidence  that coach DeMeco Ryans had confidence in the running game after Week 1, Ryans quickly pivoted in the other direction one week later.

 After the Texans were stuffed on a fourth-and-1 in the first half and failed to pick up a yard on second-and-1 and third-and-1 on a drive in the second half, the Texans decided to attempt a 58-yard field goal in lieu of trying to convert on fourth-and-short, only for Ka'imi Fairbairn 's attempt to fall short. This isn't a situation where teams try to kick anymore; over the past three years, when teams have trailed by four points or more and faced a fourth-and-1 between 35 and 45 yards away from the opposing end zone, they've gone for it 180 out of 190 times.

 NFL Next Gen Stats saw the decision to attempt a field goal (let alone miss it) as one that cost the Texans 7.4 points of win probability. You can understand why Ryans thought the situation was hopeless, but the Texans can't afford to make those sort of decisions and survive against good football teams. It didn't really matter in the big picture given that the Texans lost by 14 points, but the Texans need to be able to run the ball effectively enough for their coach to at least retain a tiny bit of hope.

 

 A win against the Colts on Sunday in what amounts to a de facto playoff game would calm concerns in Houston. And after what happened in 2025, there isn't the same sort of panic after an 0-2 start that there would typically be for a team with championship aspirations. Given those expectations, though, starting the season by losing to a pair of teams that the Texans would expect to see again in the postseason picture is a…

title: Why are the Jaguars using CB/WR Travis Hunter sparingly?
summary: The highly anticipated two-way player is playing half of defensive snaps and has barely been seen on offense. But coach Liam Coen said it's by design.
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. --  Travis Hunter has had a relatively quiet start to his second season with the Jacksonville Jaguars .

 The 2025 No. 2 overall pick started both games at cornerback but is being rotated in and out during games. He has been on the field for only 57.4% of the team's defensive snaps. On offense, he has played 11 snaps and touched the ball twice for a total of 11 yards.

 That might raise some concern that the Jaguars are either misusing Hunter -- a player general manager James Gladstone said would "alter the trajectory of the sport" -- or he is struggling. However, the organization is not concerned. They say Hunter's decreased role, especially as part of the cornerback rotation, is by design.

 

 "We did it for the most part of the last season as well, before Travis got hurt," coach Liam Coen said. "It's something that we got to continue to do. We have corners that we have confidence in. Those guys can all make plays for us. They can all communicate for us. They've been in the system now.

 "But yeah, it's a rotation. Pre-game, we have it all laid out. The players know it. They all know the rotation. It's been clearly laid out to them what the expectations and standards are."

 Hunter doesn't seem to have a problem with the way he's being used.

 "Coaches tell me what I've got to do. I just follow the plan and follow their lead," Hunter said in the locker room after the Jaguars' 20-13 loss to Denver last Sunday. "My job is to play no matter when they put me out there so that's what I try to do."

 Hunter is rotating with Montaric Brown and Jarrian Jones at outside cornerback. Two of those three are on the field on each drive. Hunter has played 62 defensive snaps in the Jaguars' two games. Brown has played the most defensive snaps (85, 78.7%) of the trio, per ESPN Research. Jones has played 72 (66.7%).

 Defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile said that's not a knock on Hunter but more because they like the way Brown -- whom the Jaguars signed to a three-year, $31.8 million contract extension in the spring -- and Jones performed in the offseason and training camp.

 Through two games, Jones is allowing a 37.5% completion rate as the nearest defender, per NFL Next Gen Stats. Brown is at 66.7% and Hunter at 75%. Hunter and Jones each have a pass breakup while Brown leads the trio with six tackles (Hunter has five and Jones has one).

 

 "We feel like we had a bunch of good players there, guys that do a good job and have worked their tail off," Campanile said. "We feel good about all those guys. So keeping them fresh and rotating them all, that's kind of been the philosophy behind [the rotation]."

 What is a little surprising is that the Jaguars haven't played Hunter much on offense -- just four snaps against Cleveland and seven against Denver -- considering he played 67% of the team's offensive snaps in seven games last season before his season-ending knee injury. Hunter has one catch for 8 yards and one carry for 3 yards, both of which came in the opener against the Browns. He had 28 catches for 298 yards and a touchdown last season.

 However, it's not just Hunter whose usage is down. Receiver Parker Washington leads the Jaguars with 18 targets and receiver Brian Thomas Jr . is second with 12, but tight end Brenton Strange has just five and receiver Jakobi Meyers has three. This week, Coen said we could see Hunter be more involved offensively on Sunday against New England (1 p.m. ET, CBS).

 "Anytime you struggle, offensively specifically, you look at the totality of it all and Travis is a big part of [the offense]," Coen said. "We're looking at continuing to find different ways to get him involved. I thought he did a nice job, throughout the course of [last] week and we're going to look at giving him some more this week."

 Strange and Meyers need to be involved more, too, quarterback Trevor Lawrence said.

 "We got to do a better job getting everybody involved," he said. "... The offense is going to run through everyone at some point, though. It's not a one-man show. And I think everyone on our team knows that."

 Coen said Hunter's reduced playing time is partly due to the time he missed last season after suffering an LCL injury to his left knee during the team's bye week. He wasn't cleared for full participation until training camp in late July. But he did spend a lot of time rehabbing in the team's virtual meeting room, which allowed him to line up anywhere and get an immersive view of what the opposing offenses and defenses were doing.

 

 "I think it definitely has some form of an effect," Coen said. "You can walk through, you can do a million things in the walkthrough room, in the meeting room settings, but he just missed a lot of pitching and catching. Just missed a lot of chemistry with the quarterback."

 Hunter noted on Thursday that he has played only nine NFL games and feels he has made progress.

 "I feel like I just move a lot quicker. I know a lot more what I did last year, and I just feel like the guys are starting to trust me a little more every week," he said. "... I'm just happy that I can continue to get better. We got a game coming up, so that's the best thing."

title: The Rams are better when both RBs get the ball
summary: Through two weeks, Williams and Corum have nearly split the carries exactly.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- The night the Los Angeles Rams drafted running back Blake Corum in the third round in 2024, coach Sean McVay said Corum reminded him of another running back.

 He was referring to a running back already on the roster: Kyren Williams .

 At the time, Williams had finished up his second NFL season and was firmly the Rams' RB1. In 12 games that season, Williams ran for 1,144 yards and 12 touchdowns on 228 carries and had 32 catches for 206 yards and three touchdowns.

 But while Williams and Corum are similar, McVay said he believes the team is better when both are getting the ball. McVay said Williams and Corum are "similar in stature, but I also think they bring some unique things."

 "It's like a pitcher changing up his pitches," McVay said.

 Through two weeks, Williams and Corum have nearly split the carries exactly. Williams has 23 carries for 126 yards and a touchdown, while Corum has 22 carries for 133 yards. Last season, it was closer to a 65%-35% split in Williams' favor. 

 "We look at it like we have two great backs," McVay said. "Those guys being able to spell each other, I think, is when we're at our best."

 

 Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford said Corum and Williams are "as alike of two running backs" as he's played with during his 18-year NFL career, saying, "I feel like those two guys, we feel like we can call any play in our playbook at any time with either of those guys in there and feel really confident about it."

 "I could imagine as a playcaller that's a really comforting feeling knowing that whoever's out there, everything is up and we're ready to rock and roll," Stafford said. "They give us that great flexibility on offense."

 The pair know they'll be alternating drives, Williams said. Corum said there wasn't really a conversation this offseason in which McVay or running backs coach Ron Gould told them they'd be splitting carries, but "more so just building trust."

 "It's a long season and so we never really had a conversation [of] how we're going to split carries," Corum said. "It's more so of 'let's keep you guys fresh. You guys play really well off each other. I trust both of you guys and let's go from there.'"

 While Corum earned McVay's trust last season, he said his goal during the offseason was to work on being more explosive.

 Last year, Corum averaged 2.1 yards before contact per carry, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. That was the highest mark of any running back with at least 100 carries. In two games this season, he has found even more space before contact, gaining 3.1 yards before contact on average.

 "I feel like when I hit the hole, I'm hitting it pretty fast," Corum said. "I trust myself. Now it's just a sense of making more people miss, breaking that 60-yarder. Every time I get the ball, I try to be as explosive as I can."

 This offseason, Williams changed the way he worked out. In the past, the running back said, he wanted to make sure he was as versatile a player as could be. But during the offseason, he said he didn't do wide receiver drills and instead focused on drills specific for a running back. 

 On Wednesday, Williams said he thinks that work is showing up.

 "I think I continue to keep being grounded when I'm cutting, having great pad level and continuing to keep pressing those lines of scrimmage and being able to be patient," Williams said.

 And while the pair is competitive, Corum said, "it's a healthy competitiveness."

 "That's something that you want in a teammate, especially sharing a position," Corum said. "But we want what's best for each other and we truly believe we push each other to be great. On game day, we feel like we really do feed off each other's energy."

 Although just a small sample size of two games, the Rams' Week 3 opponent, the Denver Broncos  (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC), have allowed 157.5 rushing yards per game, which is the fourth most in the NFL. The Rams rank sixth in rushing yards per game (142.5), despite struggling to get in a rhythm as an offense in their season-opening loss to the San Francisco 49ers .

 "I think we've been pretty efficient," Corum said. "I think credit to the O-line and tight ends and you see we've been 13 personnel and been getting good removal, allowing Kyren and I to be able to press, be patient, hit our spots.

 "But saying all of that, there's still room for a lot of improvement. Maybe we can come out of more tackles and come out more explosive. That's where my mind's at. But it's been good. It's been efficient."

title: With Kyler Murray back, will Vikings open up passing attack?
summary: Coach Kevin O'Connell said he is "still a believer in explosives" despite a long stretch of tepid air production for Minnesota.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- Inside the visitors locker room Sunday at Soldier Field, Minnesota Vikings players peeled off layers of rain-soaked uniforms and equipment. Coach Kevin O'Connell soon launched into a postgame speech that precisely depicted his mindset, excitement -- and maybe even a bit of distress after a 9-3 victory over the Chicago Bears .

 O'Connell praised players for "trying to figure out a way to find a way."

 Later, he roared: "The only thing that matters is winning!"

 That line represented the culmination of a very public reckoning O'Connell has put himself through while heading into his fifth season in Minnesota. The Vikings (2-0) have won seven consecutive games, dating back to last season, in ways that are almost unrecognizable from the pass-happy teams he first fielded upon arrival in 2022. But as quarterback Kyler Murray returns to the field, and with a hot but otherwise clear weather forecast Sunday at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers ( 4:05 p.m. ET, Fox ), O'Connell has far from given up on the passing game he craves. 

 "I'm still a believer in explosives," he said Monday. "I'm still a believer in taking some yards when they present themselves and doing it at a level where we pitch and catch at a level that I know our guys are capable of."

 

 From 2022 to 2024, the Vikings put up the NFL's third-most passing yards (12,886) with the league's fifth-lowest rate of designed running plays (35.3%). They built their offense around receiver Justin Jefferson , who averaged a league-best 100.4 receiving yards per game over that period. Since that point, however, the Vikings rank No. 31 in passing yards (3,093) and have the league's fifth-fewest number of offensive plays -- rushing or passing -- that have gone for 10 yards or more (197). They've had fewer than 200 passing yards in 16 of their past 21 games.

 Fortunately for them, that stretch has coincided with a defense and special teams that have been among the NFL's best, ranking No. 3 and 7 in expected points added (EPA), respectively. 

 During their unbeaten start this season, with Murray playing only 11 snaps because of a concussion and leading rusher Jordan Mason  going on injured reserve with a thumb injury after one week, the Vikings have managed a league-low 13 plays of 10 or more yards. O'Connell has protected the offense, particularly last week in Chicago, by leaning on the run game more than all but one other NFL playcaller. His rate of designed runs (50%) is higher than every team but the Seattle Seahawks , who also lost their starting quarterback ( Sam Darnold ) early in Week 1. Relatedly, the Vikings are tied with the Seahawks and Cincinnati Bengals for the NFL's fewest turnovers this season (one). 

 "You've got to learn some things on how you approach trying to win one game every Sunday," O'Connell said this summer. "And they're all different. Every weekend is a challenge schematically, personnel-wise, where your team's at from a health standpoint, where your team's at with certain positions. Ultimately, all we're tasked with doing is trying to win a game for 60 minutes every week.

 "It sounds like a cliché until you learn [that] it doesn't matter what the stat box looks like. It doesn't matter what an EPA looks like. ... Ultimately, you learn that none of those other things matter because winning is the only thing that matters. That's what we were able to learn as a team. But most importantly, probably [for] me last year, figuring out different ways to win, however we had to, each week. The principles don't change."

 

 On a nicer day in Chicago, even with backup Carson Wentz behind center, the Vikings likely would have tried to exploit a Bears defense that had given up 387 passing yards in its previous game to the Carolina Panthers . Instead, after two games, Jefferson now ranks No. 20 in the NFL in receiving yards per game (73.5). Fellow starter Jordan Addison has a total of two receptions on seven targets, and no other wide receiver has caught a pass. 

 "Of course I would love to have 150 [yards], three touchdowns and just the fantasy stat line," Jefferson said in Chicago. "I definitely would love that. But with these conditions, with this type of game, it wasn't that type of day, which is totally fine. As long as us coming off the ball, executing our plays and just being a factor in the win, that's all that matters.

 "So just coming in here, difficult environment with the weather conditions, a lot of adversity in our way. It doesn't matter. We're just not going to really think about it. Just come in there and just lean on each other to get the done."

 

 O'Connell referenced that quote Monday, noting Jefferson has "enough experience now to see the big picture." But he also made clear that he connects the Vikings' offensive numbers this season to the unique circumstances of losing Murray in Week 1 and the weather in Week 2, and not a more fundamental issue of poor play.

 He jokingly lamented losing some yards when officials flagged the Bears for a 5-yard defensive holding foul rather than defensive pass interference -- a spot foul -- on a play that Jefferson otherwise would have likely caught for a 68-yard touchdown. O'Connell also praised Addison for his blocking and said: "His time's coming as far as registering the things he's capable of in the stat column."

 The same is true, the Vikings clearly hope, for the entire group.

 "We know that offensively we're going to continue to grow," offensive coordinator Wes Phillips said, "and we're going to make plays. And there's going to be some times when those other phases are going to have to lean on us. We're well aware of that and we're working hard every day to make sure that we're going to be the ones that step up when we're needed."

title: Seahawks encouraged by Jadarian Price leading RB room
summary: Seattle's running back committee has no touchdowns through two weeks, but there's another opportunity this week at Commanders.
full_text:
RENTON, Wash. -- Three things were apparent with running back Jadarian Price while watching the  Seattle Seahawks ' first-round pick during training camp.

 One, he has plenty of speed, even if not the same fifth gear as the guy he's replacing ( Kenneth Walker III ). Two, he's better in the passing game than his limited college production as a pass catcher would suggest. And three, while he will be the Seahawks' RB1, he has plenty of company in their backfield -- especially once Zach Charbonnet returns.

 So, much of what we've learned about Price during Seattle's 2-0 start has merely been confirmation of what was already assumed.

 After not playing a down in the preseason, the Seahawks limited Price's workload to 24 snaps in Week 1 . He gained 58 yards on 12 touches against the New England Patriots . That included a 13-yard run on the first play of his NFL career. In a Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals , Price played 24 snaps and touched the ball 14 times for 60 yards. That included a 25-yard run that set up their second touchdown, as well as an 11-yard run when the Seahawks went right back to the rookie after he lost a fumble on the previous drive.

 "I've thought he's done well," offensive coordinator Brian Fleury said Thursday. "We gave him a little more last week and he showed up, had a couple explosive runs that he was able to break and run through contact. So I'm happy with the development we've seen, and I think it'll just continue to show itself."

 Price was sidelined against the Cardinals after hurting his chest/shoulder late in the third quarter. However, he took part in the first two practices of this week as a limited participant and appears to have a good chance of playing Sunday against the Washington Commanders (1 p.m. ET, Fox).

 

 Through two games, Price leads Seattle's backfield in snaps with 47 and in touches with 26. George Holani has looked like the clear RB2 since the start of the offseason program, and he has out-snapped Emanuel Wilson 38 to 31. But Wilson has 23 touches compared to Holani's 13.

 However, that trio is still looking for its first touchdown. Wilson couldn't find the end zone on three consecutive carries from inside the 5-yard line late in the second quarter against Arizona, leading to a turnover on downs. But he came through on the Seahawks' final possession to help close it out.

 With Price out and Holani briefly joining him on the sideline, Wilson carried the ball 10 times for 48 yards on a 16-play touchdown drive that took more than 10 minutes off the clock. He finished with 92 yards on 21 attempts after playing just three snaps in the opener.

 "It's the things that we saw him do throughout training camp before he had that minor setback," coach Mike Macdonald said of Wilson, who was sidelined for part of the summer with a hamstring injury after signing a one-year deal with Seattle in March. "Glad to see him do his thing. A decisive runner. He gets downhill, not just on the inside run game, it's on the perimeter game, as well. Had a great run on third down where he kept the drive going on the last drive, which is awesome. Lot of great stuff, so we're happy to have him."

 Seattle's backfield equation will change once Charbonnet -- a co-starter last season -- returns from last season's ACL tear in his left knee. He will miss at least two more games while on the physically unable to perform list. The Seahawks did not open his 21-day practice window this week, but Macdonald's comments suggested that should happen in the near future.

 

 As for Seattle's available tailbacks, their roles look defined when all are healthy. Price has started both games, and all of his work has come on first or second down. Holani, an excellent pass blocker, has played 18 of the team's 24 third-down snaps. Wilson, listed at 5-foot-10 and 226 pounds, is the power runner.

 While Holani is the best receiving threat of the three, Price continues to look plenty capable in that regard. After catching only 15 passes over three seasons at Notre Dame -- and backing up No. 4-overall pick  Jeremiyah Love  for much of that time -- Price has three receptions for 14 yards on four targets.

 His last touch against Arizona was a screen pass late in the third quarter that gained 8 yards. While Price was being tackled, his right shoulder hit the turf hard as former Seahawks defensive lineman L.J. Collier landed on him with all 300 pounds of his body weight. Macdonald said X-rays were negative.

 "It's something we'll monitor throughout the week," he said. "Shouldn't be a long-term thing."

 Through two games, Fleury's offense has the NFL's highest designed rush rate (52.2%), a metric in which they also led the league last season (47.6%) under Klint Kubiak. After totaling 162 yards on the ground against Arizona, the Seahawks rank ninth in rushing yards per game (129.5) and 14th in yards per carry (4.2).

 "I think as an offense, I think we have great opportunity for growth to really just get the one more block," Macdonald said. "We have the right mentality -- I'll tell you that -- on offense. I think the guys want that. It's just, when you watch the tape, there's a hunger there for more explosive runs, which is really cool. We've got a great opportunity in front of us."

title: What's next for Jayden Daniels, Commanders after elbow injury?
summary: Experts weigh in on Daniels' latest injury and what it means for him, the Commanders and their collective futures.
full_text:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- For nearly an entire half on Sunday, Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels resembled the player from 2024, the one who was named NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year and mentioned as a future league MVP.

 On the final drive of the first half at the  Dallas Cowboys , Daniels provided reminders of that season: He ran for 24 yards and threw for another 27, including a strike on third-and-6 to Stefon Diggs for 10 yards.

 

 Then, on the final play of the half, the 2025 version of Daniels showed up, the one who missed 10 games with three different injuries. He suffered a dislocated left elbow, leaving the Commanders with plenty of questions about the future -- from his durability to whether they had built a good enough roster to withstand his absence for even a short period.

 After visiting specialists Tuesday through Thursday, Washington general manager Adam Peters told 106.7 The Fan radio that Daniels would not need surgery nor would he be placed on injured reserve.

 Still, his latest injury has left Washington in a familiar spot: wondering what this means for Daniels' future and trying to piece together wins. Last season, the Commanders struggled to do the latter and finished 5-12. Washington is 0-2 now and will face the defending Super Bowl champion  Seattle Seahawks  in its home opener Sunday.

 "0-2 is not where we wanted to be, that's for sure," Quinn said. "But we also are resolute that that's not where we're going to be staying."

 Commanders reporter John Keim, ESPN draft expert Jordan Reid and senior fantasy writer Eric Karabell weigh in on Daniels' latest injury and what it means for him, the Commanders and their collective futures.

 

 

 Is the season lost? 
 It's only two games. But after last season, when injuries -- notably the one to Daniels -- derailed the Commanders, it would require a leap of faith to think otherwise at this point, particularly in the NFC East. Even if Daniels had remained healthy, Washington is now 0-2 in the division. So, the road would have been tough regardless. Also, the Commanders will next face Seattle in their home opener and in the coming six weeks will play the Giants twice, the 49ers, the Rams and the Eagles. However, the Giants' game looks different with quarterback Jaxson Dart out for the season. The Colts in Week 4 in London also is winnable. A bleak picture could change in a hurry.

 But if Daniels is out multiple weeks, that's a steep task - especially because the defense continues to struggle in coverage. But there is still a chance he only misses one week. As one teammate said, the shame of the injury is that he looked terrific in the first half vs. Dallas - and that meant good things for the future. His return and subsequent performance changes everything about their future.

 It's also a big year for Quinn; while ownership values him this is a results-based industry and another bad season wouldn't help him. But any decision for when Daniels' returns will be led by medical personnel.

 

 And this isn't about backup quarterback Marcus Mariota , who will start Sunday, as much as it is about what the Commanders haven't shown in other areas.

 Against Dallas, Daniels was sharp and showed the dynamic ability that made him the No. 2 pick in the 2024 draft, and a player multiple high-profile coaches liked best in that class.

 "I loved everything about the first half, how he was playing," Quinn said of Sunday's performance, as Daniels rushed for 69 yards and threw for 96 yards and a touchdown before the injury.

 But Daniels also covers up a lot of flaws. Those flaws will now be magnified during his absence, and that's the concerning part. Washington's defense has allowed seven touchdowns in two games. A new system always brings growing pains, but the Commanders are faster and more talented in the front seven as compared with 2025's unit, and new coordinator Daronte Jones has a strong reputation. Defensive backs say his scheme requires a lot of preparation and knowledge; that also could lead to early issues in coverage until they have more games in the system.

 On multiple plays Sunday, a cornerback could be seen communicating with a safety right before the ball was snapped. In one case, there appeared to be confusion; and in another, the corner was looking at the safety when the ball was snapped. At other times, it appeared players went to the same coverage area.

 Quinn said they know what it looks like when they do it right, so after two games, "It's not good enough."

 But can that overcome all the issues? The Commanders' defense struggles unless it applies pressure. They don't create turnovers. That's a bad combination. Last season, the Bears' defense ranked 24th in scoring and 29th in yards but led the NFL with 33 takeaways (23 more than Washington).

 Washington has forced only 27 turnovers since the start of the 2024 campaign and hasn't taken the ball away in two games this season.

 If the Commanders had a proven defense and a strong, consistent run game, then they could survive for a few weeks. But their offensive line, already down left tackle Laremy Tunsil , now has right guard Sam Cosmi -- their top remaining lineman -- in concussion protocol. Tunsil and Daniels are Washington's best offensive players. It's tough to survive those absences.

 Could they develop those other aspects? Sure. But when? And will it happen quickly enough for Washington to withstand Daniels' absence? The Commanders have lost 12 of their past 14 games dating to last season, but they changed coordinators and spent heavily on defense in the offseason. If not a new team, it should be a different one. After two games, Washington ranks 27th in yards and 25th in points. The Commanders are 28th in yards per pass attempt.

 After Sunday's game, one player, without prompting, expressed confidence in what the offense and the team could still do. He was encouraged by a lot of what he had seen by the offense, despite the loss. And he remained convinced it could get the season pointed in a better direction. Others share his belief. If that belief doesn't turn into a win real soon, then hope will once more lead to despair for Washington fans. -- Keim 

 

 Should the Commanders have serious concerns about Daniels' viability as their QB of the present and future? 

 If he missed another long stretch, it would be hard not to have those concerns. But even with a short absence there's risk involved that impacts his future.

 What they'll never have to worry about is his approach. Few work harder or study more; he continues to arrive at work by 5:30 a.m. every week. He organized film sessions with the receivers. He picks the brains of athletes in other sports -- Steph Curry, Draymond Green and LeBron James -- and has talked to Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka about Kobe Bryant's mindset.

 Daniels has been focused on improving and winning; he has said he doesn't care about fame and celebrity status.

 However, he has now dislocated his left elbow twice in his past four games and reinjured it in another. He has finished only four games since the start of last season and left four others early. He suffered a knee injury in one game that cost him two weeks and a hamstring in another that sidelined him for one.

 The question is: Can anything be done to prevent another dislocation? One source close to the situation said surgery was never recommended last year and multiple medical experts said surgery is almost never performed after a first one because the risk for recurrence is around 2 percent.

 Indeed, Quinn said surgery was not discussed and after consulting with multiple outside specialists it wasn't recommended this time either. According to Dr. Marc Kowalsky, an orthopedic surgeon with ONS in Connecticut, and an expert on elbow and shoulder injuries the likelihood of another dislocation increases - even if Daniels plays with a brace.
